SUNDAY: Everton and Crystal Palace in advanced talks over McNeil-Johnson swap

SATURDAY: West Ham and Tottenham agree £5m fee for Manor Solomon

FRIDAY: Rodri tells Real Madrid he wishes to join Barcelona

THURSDAY: Man City target new goalkeeper after James Trafford sale

WEDNESDAY: Aston Villa braced for fresh Arsenal bid to sign Ezri Konsa

TUESDAY: Man City step up chase for Chelsea's Pedro Neto

Sports.title: Man United's lack of transfer business risks undermining all their good work under Ineos. It's time to back up talk of grand plans with action - or fans' patience will run out, writes NATHAN SALT
Sports.content:
Heading into the summer transfer window, the expectation outside of Manchester United was that this was a club ready to splash the cash. A third-place finish - and crucially a return to Champions League football - was to be supplemented by a record-breaking access fee for Amazon’s All or Nothing documentary, a record training kit sponsorship with Betway, upticks in sponsorship deals with existing partners and huge salaries for the likes of Casemiro and Jadon Sancho now officially off the books. All signs pointed to a £200million midfield rebuild, with players of the quality of Elliot Anderson, Sandro Tonali, Bruno Guimaraes, Mateus Fernandes and Aurelien Tchouameni on the shortlist, to help transform United back into one of England and Europe’s elite. After the club's new-look recruitment team hit the mark with four summer signings a year ago, transforming the club’s fortunes in attack and in goal, excitement was through the roof. But now, as United’s players and staff enjoy a five-day training and team-bonding retreat in Ireland, fingers are again being pointed at the powers-that-be by supporters. Just how serious are you about competing with the very best? Man United's decision-makers (from left to right) Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox are starting to come under pressure from fans over a lack of transfer activity Actions speak louder than words There are a handful of things that Ineos and the decision-makers at Manchester United love. They love to tell supporters about the ‘clear plan’ to take them back to contending for Premier League titles. They love self-imposed frugality and how that shift in approach no longer leaves United open to being a pawn in the game of chess that is the transfer window. And they love project players in the mould of Chido Obi, Ayden Heaven, Sekou Kone, Enzo Kana-Biyik, Diego Leon, Cristian Orozco and Tynan Thompson. ‘We have a clear plan,’ director of football Jason Wilcox said back in October. ‘I am sure there are going to be bumps in the road but we have just got to make sure we stay calm irrespective of the noise outside.’ Only this summer, that same phrase was repeated by chief executive Omar Berrada through the club’s internal podcast arm Inside Carrington. ‘We have a clear plan,’ Berrada said. ‘[Director of football] Jason Wilcox and his team are well set up to execute that plan. ‘What we saw last season is a good way forward for us. We want a mix of experience and youth. A mix of players who have demonstrated they can perform in the Premier League and players that are doing very well outside the Premier League. ‘Whatever decisions we take will not just be for the short term but the long term.’ The issue Manchester United are facing is that talking about a plan doesn't represent fun for supporters.

Your browser does not support iframes.

Restraint isn’t fun. Projects tend to be a slow process that take years to pay off, with the likes of Leon, Orozco and Kana-Biyik some way off first team football. Fans of any club crave the dopamine rush a new transfer provides. The transfer window has become an addictive loop of rumour and reward, and the absence of business quickly causes inquests online. And there is some legitimacy to the frustrations of many United fans. They didn’t get Anderson, their undisputed No 1 target. He ended up at Manchester City in a £116million record-breaking deal for an English midfielder. An obvious ‘bump in the road’, as Wilcox put it. They didn’t get Mateus Fernandes, a player that felt much more attainable internally before the finances involved exploded and Ineos’ frugality kicked in. He ended up at Tottenham Hotspur for £85million. United were frustrated that the player didn’t push more to end up at Old Trafford. Bruno Guimaraes and Sandro Tonali have both long been admired but figures close to both parties have explained to Daily Mail Sport how any hope United would get close to the financials to land one of Newcastle's star men was quickly extinguished under their new, more austere regime. They ended up at Arsenal and Tottenham Hotspur for a combined £175million. ‘We have to be really disciplined. We have a plan, we know what we can invest and we need to stick to it,’ Berrada added back in June. ‘In some cases, we may decide to make an investment knowing it is the right thing, not for the next two or three years but the next ten. ‘We need to stay very focused on what we are trying to achieve. It's very important you don't let the market or the agents dictate what we should be doing.’ The final line is the kicker. In a market where the base price for a good-to-great Premier League midfielder is around £75-80million, United are determined not to fall into the traps of the previous regime, where big-money signings would lead to years of expensive repayments, all for little-to-no on-pitch success. United pivoted to Aston Villa's Youri Tielemans, triggering his release clause. It was a smart signing As was the addition of Andrey Santos from Chelsea. But United need more numbers in midfield So, United pivoted. First to Andrey Santos, a player United first brought up to Chelsea when the terms of Alejandro Garnacho’s move were discussed a year ago, before finally getting him for £50million earlier this summer. Then it was Youri Tielemans, triggering his £35million release clause. Having landed the Premier League's official ‘Signing of the Season’ in Senne Lammens last term, internally there is a belief that his fellow Belgian Tielemans can make it two-for-two in 2026-27. Both are smart signings with huge upside. Adding to Bryan Mbeumo, Matheus Cunha, Benjamin Sesko and Lammens, Ineos can point to a track record of their way being a successful one. Internally, too, there has been a real eagerness to no longer be seen as a club that can be ripped off, a club that agents can manipulate or bully. This was one of the main reasons they didn’t cave on their valuation of Jorge Mendes client Fernandes when Tottenham upped the ante. The desire to limit leaks is stronger than ever, too. Wilcox and Berrada have placed immense emphasis on acting in the shadows and out of the court of public opinion. The Tielemans signing appeared to outsiders to come from nowhere, much to the delight of bosses. They have been decisive in moving on from Rasmus Hojlund, in getting all the wages covered in the loans for Andre Onana (Trabzonspor) and Altay Bayindir (Celta Vigo), and insiders believe United are close to escaping the dreaded cycle of being seen as a poor recruiter, blinded by star power. But with three weeks left to go in this transfer window, Ineos and United’s decision makers are at a crossroads. It’s an expensive market and Michael Carrick needs more. With Champions League football on the horizon, and the first seven games coming in a 29-day stretch, Carrick needs help. United proved against Paris Saint-Germain in Gothenburg that they are ready to be aggressive on the pitch, with their exciting style of play. The question now is, can Ineos be aggressive off it? With his team set to play seven games in the first 29 days of the new season, Michael Carrick needs more quality players to call upon So, where do they need to strengthen? Signing a left back is absolutely essential. Two enquiries to Newcastle United for Lewis Hall – both strongly rebuffed – show that United know that, too. For as much credit as Luke Shaw deserves for starting every single Premier League game last season, asking him to replicate it amid the added strain of European football feels like wishful thinking. The options in front of United are to make a big play for Hall, a player that could be United’s and England’s left back for the next decade. Newcastle will want record money for a full back. That won’t change. Or there is the youth route, promoting Harry Amass, who has looked bright during pre-season. Yet he has been told his best chance for regular game-time is elsewhere. United are understood to be open to both loan and permanent deals. And then there is the cheap option of keeping faith with Shaw and leaning on Noussair Mazraoui, who plays left back for Morocco, in case of injury. Luke Shaw deserves credit for starting every Premier League game last season. But to expect him to do the same in 2026-27 feels like wishful thinking Lewis Hall would be an ambitious and exciting signing at left back. But United's efforts so far haven't extended beyond an enquiry Only one of those three options would signal that United are heading towards the very top, and it’s not options two or three. Patrick Dorgu, despite being listed as a defender in every squad list, is only seen as an option further forward on the wing. Then there is the conundrum of the midfield, and whether United do or don’t need a third recruit in that area (they do). Mason Mount, who has been a huge success across pre-season, came off in Gothenburg after 20 minutes and that highlighted the fragility of United’s side just a fortnight out from the season. Mount is popular with every manager he plays under but his reliability is an issue. He has started just 25 league games since joining United for £55million three years ago. Tielemans, as exciting a signing as he is, missed over 20 games with injury last season. Manuel Ugarte is a long-term absentee and the plan was to move him on. Casemiro has gone. Santos is a smart addition and Kobbie Mainoo will rightly be an important figure. But United need another body. Shifting too much onus, too soon onto the likes of Tyler Fletcher, who is expected to be the young midfielder United place the most effort into developing for the first team this season, is unfair. ‘For us to get in the top four and consistently challenge for Champions League places, win the Champions League, win the Premier League, we have got to invest in the squad,’ Wilcox said back in that October sit-down. ‘We have got to buy the right players.’ And so far they’ve done that. Of the 13 first-team signings to this point under Ineos, only Ugarte has proven a major disappointment. In bringing in (from left) Bryan Mbeumo, Benjamin Sesko and Matheus Cunha last summer, Ineos worked wonders in the transfer market. But they need to be more active this time around But if Project 150 – the stated aim of winning the Premier League title by 2028 in United’s 150th anniversary year – is legitimate and not just a piece of catchy PR, United face a defining three weeks to set the tone for where they are going. Ineos deserve trust and patience to navigate ‘bumps in the road’ after their success in moving on the deadwood, bringing down the wage bill, transforming the team’s fortunes with hits in the transfer market, and committing to plans for a new stadium. But patience doesn’t last for ever and if, in three weeks' time, United are still light in midfield, relying on Shaw as a sole left back option, and there is no back-up to Sesko, don’t be surprised if many fans' patience has run out.

Sports.title: Chelsea hero John Obi Mikel brutally mocks Arsenal fans, telling them Vinicius Junior was 'using you' to get bumper new Real Madrid deal: 'I don't know what they were smoking'
Sports.content:
Chelsea hero John Obi Mikel brutally mocks Arsenal fans, telling them Vinicius Junior was 'using you' to get bumper new Real Madrid deal: 'I don't know what they were smoking'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Former Chelsea midfielder John Obi Mikel has ruthlessly mocked Arsenal fans who got carried away by the prospect of signing Real Madrid superstar Vinicius Junior, after the Brazilian committed his future to the Spanish giants with a bumper new deal.

The Gunners opportunistically targeted the 26-year-old forward while he was locked in lengthy contract talks with Real Madrid, and were prepared to make him the highest-paid player in Premier League history if he agreed to the move.

Arsenal fans were bouncing off the walls at the prospect of luring Vinicius Junior away from Madrid, in a move that would have been viewed as one of the most seismic transfers in modern English football history.

Even Mikel Arteta admitted he was 'absolutely smitten' with the idea of signing him after the prospective move was approved 'at all levels' at the Emirates.

Ultimately, to Arsenal's disappointment, the Brazilian international penned a new six-year deal at the Bernabeu to commit his future to Real Madrid, calling an end to the 18-month contract saga.

His lucrative new deal reportedly makes Vinicius Junior the second-highest earner at the club, ahead of Jude Bellingham and captain Federico Valverde while narrowly behind superstar forward Kylian Mbappe.

Arsenal target Vinicius Junior committed his future to Real Madrid, signing a new bumper deal

Ex-Chelsea star John Obi Mikel joked that the Brazilian was simply 'using' the Gunners and that the prospective move was never on the cards: 'I don’t know what they were smoking'

Mikel joked that Arsenal's proposed signing of Vinicius was never on the cards, insisting they aren't 'one of the big boys' despite winning the Premier League last campaign.

‘Of course, mate. F***ing hell. I don’t know what the Arsenal fans were expecting,' he said on The Obi One Podcast.

‘You win the league after 22 years and then you all of a sudden think: that’s it, you’ve arrived, you’re one of the big boys again. No, you’re not.

‘They’ve just been humbled because I said it: there’s no way Vinicius Junior is leaving Real Madrid to go to Arsenal, a club that’s won one title in 22 years.

‘This guy wins titles, he’s won lots of titles at Real Madrid. He wants to win titles season after season, the Champions League, La Liga, competing year after year and winning those titles.

‘He’s tasted what it feels like winning the Champions League, Arsenal have never won the Champions League. Zero.

‘You expect a player who has won the Champions League with Real Madrid to leave that, everything that he’s built at Real Madrid, and the squad that Jose Mourinho is assembling right now? They look to me like a team that at the end of the season, you probably see them in the Champions League final.

‘There’s some team there at Real Madrid when you look at the players that they have. You expect him to leave that and go to a team that has won one league title in 22 years? F***ing hell.’

Mikel went on claim that Vinicius simply 'used' the north London club to get a new bumper deal at the Bernabeu.

He added: ‘All the Arsenal fans when I said that before, in my DMs, I saw messages, “We’ve clipped this, we’ve sent this video, and when it happens we’re absolutely going to come on here and destroy you…”

‘I was looking at it and thinking that’s just my opinion. I never thought he was going to leave.

‘He was using you guys [Arsenal] to get a better deal, he was using them to get a better deal.

Arsenal have bolsted Mikel Arteta's ranks with the £75million signing of Bruno Guimaraes

‘I have no idea why Arsenal fans would genuinely believe that Vinicius Junior was going to go from Real Madrid to Arsenal. If you ask anybody… I think it was only Arsenal fans who believed that was going to happen. I don’t know what they were smoking.’

Following last season’s title triumph, Arsenal have bolstered Arteta’s squad with the £75million signing of Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle, alongside Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge and Illan Meslier from Leeds.

It is understood Juventus star Kenan Yildiz and PSG's Bradley Barcola remain firmly on Arsenal's summer wishlist, although the latter is also wanted by Liverpool.

Sports.title: Beware Premier League rivals: Enzo Maresca's Man City are made for Erling Haaland and could help him produce his best season yet, writes JACK GAUGHAN
Sports.content:
Back home 5,000 miles away, there ought to have been a certain Norwegian licking his lips at what Manchester City served up before they headed home from Asia. Presuming he has a subscription for the club’s in-house TV channel, that is.

This performance was made for Erling Haaland. The attacking style Enzo Maresca hopes to implement is made for Haaland. Atletico Madrid struggled for answers in how to counter City’s wingers – boldly direct all game – as they fizzed balls across the six-yard box.

That is Haaland’s zone and even before Omar Marmoush netted effectively the same goal twice in two minutes just before the hour – Antoine Semenyo hitting an area, the Egyptian tapping in – there came very real evidence that Haaland is going to be labelled a tap-in merchant. And City will not mind that one bit: that is where their goals are coming from this season.

It looks a game plan reliant on a man with a killer’s instinct, knowing exactly where to plonk himself. Haaland is the best in world football at that and City’s idea is clearly to lean into his strengths even further than they had done already.

Maresca had twice shown frustration before Marmoush’s double when Savinho had seemingly laid certain goals on a plate for a striker, only for nobody to arrive. The Italian bowed his head once and then outstretched the arms as Marmoush and others failed to fly in.

‘We cannot create the amount of situations and not finish the action,’ Maresca said. ‘There we need to be clinical. We need to improve. We are getting better there. With Erling we can be even more dangerous.’

Omar Marmoush produced two close range finishes from crosses aimed towards the six-yard box

Enzo Maresca's gameplan looks to have been devised with Erling Haaland in mind

Rayan Ait-Nouri scored Manchester City's third goal in their 3-1 victory over Atletico Madrid

Words were had at half time and it was noticeable that not only Marmoush but Phil Foden would later be readier to meet Semenyo’s crosses, crashing into the box in the way that had been replicated over and over in training the evening before. The victory was topped off by Rayan Ait-Nouri’s late third.

‘The players want to play,’ Maresca said as he left the door open for Marmoush’s potential exit, with Tottenham monitoring his situation.

‘They want to play. When they don’t play, they’re not happy. Omar’s desire is probably to play more minutes. It doesn't mean that he isn't going to play more minutes here but it's also his decision.’

Spurs target Savinho shows what he can offer City

Spurs still hold a keen interest in landing the £70million-rated Savinho, who had intimated a willingness to seek a new challenge earlier in the summer.

But the Brazilian has shown Maresca what he can offer out on the right wing with this style of play. There were the dangerous cutbacks, the sort reminiscent of a bygone era in the early years of Pep Guardiola, that suggested more of an end product than had been evident in his first two seasons.

That was the positive side of a lively Savinho, who relentlessly beat his full back around the outside. And yet, there were reminders of his profligacy that has seen him score just seven times in 84 games across all competitions.

When pouncing on a mistake, the 22-year-old should have driven towards goal and forced Jan Oblak to commit, instead deciding to check back and attempt a curling effort into the far corner from outside the box. It whipped wide.

And one of Maresca’s other disappointments came as Semenyo hit a dangerous area, only for City’s other winger to still be on his heels. There is work to do and decisions to be made before the end of the transfer window.

Savinho produced dangerous cutbacks and reliably beat his full back, but still showed reminders of his profligacy

City will need Anderson to quickly get up to speed

Despite dominating, City had fallen behind before Marmoush’s brace. A scrappy opener by Jorge Dominguez, a 16-year-old defender who towers over most. The teenager stabbed past Gianluigi Donnarumma from the second phase of a corner. City should have cleared their lines but it wasn’t the end of the world.

What will have concerned Maresca more were the spaces between the lines that Rodrigo Mendoza, a 21-year-old signed from Elche in February, was afforded. Mendoza proved a problem for Mateo Kovacic, ghosting off the back of the central midfielder and creating two decent chances. City will need to be more robust in that area of the pitch when they meet Arsenal in Sunday’s Community Shield.

Elliot Anderson is not linking up with the team until Wednesday and so it is likely that Kovacic will feature alongside Tijjani Reijnders in Cardiff. The pair have been strong on the ball in South Korea while having obvious things to work through defensively from a positioning sense.

As Barcelona expect to wrap up a deal to land metronome Rodri, City will need Anderson to quickly get himself up to speed.

Sports.title: Amazon founder and billionaire Jeff Bezos closes in on deal to buy minority stake in Liverpool as consortium's £1.35billion investment nears approval
Sports.content:
Amazon founder and billionaire Jeff Bezos closes in on deal to buy minority stake in Liverpool as consortium's £1.35billion investment nears approval

Amazon founder and billionaire Jeff Bezos is closing in on a deal to buy a minority stake in Liverpool.

Bezos is part of a billionaire boys' club featuring the owner of Facebook and the son-in-law of an Indian steel magnate, with the consortium set to purchase a share of the Premier League giants that equates to around 30 per cent.

Daily Mail Sport reported three weeks ago that a group led by Amit Bhatia, the former co-owner of Championship side Queens Park Rangers, were serious and confident of buying that percentage of the club for roughly £1.35billion from Liverpool's American owners Fenway Sports Group (FSG).

And now sources indicate the process is ticking along nicely, with suggestions it could be rubber-stamped in the next week.

Bezos, who has an estimated net worth of £207.4billion, per Forbes, is the most notable name involved in the deal alongside Mark Zuckerberg’s classmate and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin, valued at £24.5bn.

Bhatia will lead the bid. He stepped down after nearly two decades as QPR supremo last month – he has a stand named after him at Loftus Road – and he is the son-in-law of steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal, who is the world’s 65th-richest man with £24.8bn to his name.

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos is part of a group set to buy a minority stake in Liverpool

John W Henry, the principal chair of Fenway Sports Group, who own Liverpool, has always been eager for additional investment while still being keen to hold the majority stake

It is understood the 46-year-old British-Indian business leader Bhatia has also entrusted the help of a senior PR executive who previously worked for Manchester United and King Charles when he was the Prince of Wales.

Bezos' net worth ranks him as the third-richest man in the world, and while he is no longer the CEO of Amazon, he retains the title of executive chairman.

He has never previously invested in sport, although he was interested in buying the current Super Bowl winners Seattle Seahawks and fellow NFL team Washington Commanders before pulling out.

Liverpool are already one of 11 Premier League clubs under American ownership, which includes fellow Big Six teams Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester United.

Arsenal owner Stan Kroenke made his money in commercial real estate development by developing a strategic business relationship with American supermarket Walmart, with his wife Ann Walton the daughter of Bud Walton, who co-founded the chain. He also has a significant sports and land empire.

Meanwhile, Chelsea are owned by a consortium named Blue Co, which is co-led by Clearlake Capital, an LA-based private equity firm, and American businessman Todd Boehly.

Manchester United are owned by the Glazer Family, who are from the US and valued at around £8.87bn, while Sheikh Mansour, a member of the ruling family of Abu Dhabi and the vice-president of the UAE, is Man City's majority owner.

Newcastle United were taken over in 2021 by a consortium of the Saudi Public Investment Fund.

In terms of what a potential Bezos takeover means for Liverpool, there are warnings to fans getting excited about the mega-money set to come in: the club itself won’t have direct access to an infinite supply of cash, as the funds will go to FSG and not the team.

The Premier League has recently introduced a modern version of financial fair play with the ‘squad cost ratio’ rules which state that clubs can only spend a set percentage of its football-related revenue and profit/loss from player sales.

It is around 85 per cent but can be 70 per cent for those competing in Europe, as Liverpool often is.

However, if the club was looking to borrow money at a future date, they will be in a position to do so on an interest-free basis which can only benefit cash flow. Bezos and Saverin’s names help with commercial deals.

Some fans are also worried that this is a sign of FSG slowly selling up, with principal owner John W Henry now 76. FSG sources say this is the opposite and insist this is another way the owner is looking to further position the club for success.

The Boston-based owners, with Mike Gordon more hands-on again now Michael Edwards has departed, will still make the day-to-day decisions despite selling off 30 per cent of the club.

When approached for comment, FSG referred to an earlier statement which said Bhatia and a consortium had expressed interest in an investment. Bezos was also approached.

MEET THE KEY PLAYERS

JEFF BEZOS

Bezos is the third-richest man in the world, according to Forbes. In 1994, he read that web usage was growing at a rate of 2,300 per cent a year and wanted to open an online book store, so set one up in his garage in Seattle alongside his then wife Mackenzie Scott.

He changed the name from Cadabra to Amazon after the South American river as, at the time, website listings were alphabetised so an ‘A’ listing would be near the top. They slowly started selling more products and are now one of the most recognisable companies in the world.

Bezos is no longer the CEO of Amazon but retains the title of executive chairman. He is also the owner of the Washington Post and founder of Blue Origin which competes with Elon Musk in the modern-day space race. He flew to space in 2021.

The 62-year-old has dabbled in the idea of sports investment before but this time appears to be different. He was interested in buying the current Super Bowl winners Seattle Seahawks and fellow NFL team Washington Commanders but pulled out.

He married former American journalist Lauren Sanchez last year.

Bezos has dabbled with the idea of sports ownership in the past but this time appears to be different

EDUARDO SAVERIN

Saverin was born in Brazil with Romanian heritage. He moved to Miami at age 13 and attended Harvard University. He became friends with fellow undergraduate Mark Zuckerberg and the pair wanted to set up a website for students to communicate, making a $1,000 investment each.

The site was originally named ‘The Facebook’ and soon grew to other universities, later anyone in the world aged 13 or older. It now has more than 3billion users and its parent company, Meta Platforms, has a market value of around £1.12trillion.

Saverin is played by Andrew Garfield in The Social Network film based on the book Accidental Billionaires about his rise at Facebook. Weeks before Facebook became a public company, he moved to Singapore and renounced his US citizenship.

The 44-year-old is now head of B Capital, a venture capital firm.

Eduardo Saverin was a co-founder of Facebook and is now head of venture capital firm B Capital

Amit Bhatia, the son in law of Lakshmi Mittal, previously worked for QPR for 19 years

AMIT BHATIA

Bhatia is a 46-year-old British-Indian with an investment banking background in sectors such as technology, media, property, real estate and health.

He formerly worked on Wall Street before founding a construction company aged 32, which has more than 5,000 UK employees. He won the young entrepreneur of the year award in 2013.

Bhatia married Vanisha Mittal in 2004 in a six-day wedding which the Guinness World Records recorded as the most-expensive ceremony of all time at £41m. Vanisha’s father is Lakshmi Mittal, the world’s 65th-richest man with £24.8bn as per Forbes.

Bhatia worked at QPR for 19 years and his company, AyBe Capital, owns shares in the cricket franchise London Spirit, former England cricketer Kevin Pietersen’s YouTube channel and an indoor golf league founded by Rory McIlroy.

The tycoon recently played a round of golf with basketball legend LeBron James and is regularly on the course with Indian cricketing icon Sachin Tendulkar.

Sports.title: Jose Mourinho's Netflix documentary gives fans the chance to see a version of the Special One they have never seen before. It's a must-watch with added stardust from Sir Alex Ferguson, Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Co: TV REVIEW
Sports.content:
Jose Mourinho's Netflix documentary gives fans the chance to see a version of the Special One they have never seen before. It's a must-watch with added stardust from Sir Alex Ferguson, Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Co: TV REVIEW

'You don’t want to make me cry, because I don’t want.’ Then there is a long pause as an uncomfortable Jose Mourinho looks around, taps the table, and attempts to suppress his emotions.

This is Mourinho as we have never seen him before.

The 63-year-old had just been asked about how he processed the death of his father while he was manager of Manchester United in 2017. He fights back the tears for as long as he can, battling to keep his enigmatic personal persona intact.

This is something that Mourinho tries to do throughout his new hit three-part docu-series on Netflix. The legendary manager wants to give football fans an insight into his outrageously successful career on the touchline, which has seen him win 26 major trophies across England, Spain, Portugal and Italy, rather than delve into his private life.

Speaking in the latter stages of the documentary, Mourinho says: ‘People think they know me, but they don’t know me. And I’m happy they don’t. It’s a privilege for the people that know me.

‘You want to do a documentary because of my career. You don’t do a documentary with a guy that wins nothing in football.’

Jose Mourinho shows vulnerability like never before in his new Netflix docu-series

The documentary goes through the highs and lows of Mourinho's life and career

Mourinho is right; there is no world in which he would be sat on a sofa in his luxurious mansion, with the sunshine beating down on his swimming pool in the background (a Netflix cameraman’s dream setting) and be speaking to director Joe Pearlman if he had not achieved what he has done in his trophy-laden 30-year coaching career. That said, that doesn’t mean we don’t want to know what makes him tick.

Pearlman, who has directed documentaries about pop stars Robbie Williams and Lewis Capaldi, and BECKHAM producer John Battsek do an exemplary job of respecting Mourinho’s wishes to maintain his privacy while also providing a window into Jose the man and what he has been through.

From how his children ‘enjoy life more without me’ to how his father shaped the person he is, the docu-series showed us a more vulnerable Mourinho than he has ever allowed us to see previously.

Now, these small snippets are only really delved into towards the end of the final episode. The majority of the show takes us through the box office rollercoaster of a career Mourinho has had in the beautiful game. And boy, does it do a great job.

To make a sporting documentary enjoyable, it needs heaps of insight from those closest to the subject, untold anecdotes and exclusive information we haven't heard before. MOURINHO ticks all three of these boxes, and some.

It has bucket loads of insight from the likes of Frank Lampard, John Terry, Sir Alex Ferguson, Iker Casillas, Zlatan Ibrahimovic, and that’s just to name a few. These household names show just what a mammoth impact Mourinho has had on the game. I mean, they aren’t exactly nobodies, are they?

Not all of them drop in to shower the manager with compliments and praise. Former Real Madrid captain Casillas spoke of the ‘very cold’ relationship he had with Mourinho and how it was ‘taken to a limit’ during his first tenure.

This is Mourinho, after all; he has created a whole host of enemies throughout his time on the touchline. The programme doesn’t hold back from showing that; it takes us on a journey through the good and the bad, the highs and the lows. It doesn't shy away from anything.

There is plenty of insight into Mourinho from big names such as Sir Alex Ferguson

Zlatan Ibrahimovic also spoke of how Mourinho impacted his career when at Inter Milan

This is a man adored by Chelsea fans for his successes in England and by Inter Milan supporters for putting them back on their pedestal with a magical Champions League triumph.

But he is also the same man who had an acrimonious exit from Madrid, after forming what Sami Khedira calls a ‘nightmare’ and poisonous dressing room, and who was forced to agree a settlement with former Chelsea club doctor Eva Carneiro over claims that the manager discriminated against her.

There are also some incredible revelations, such as Mourinho discussing how he had meetings about returning to Barcelona in 2008 as manager, almost a decade after working tirelessly as an assistant and how, to this day, he doesn't like to be described as, 'the translator'.

But by far the biggest revelation of them all was Mourinho admitting, for the very first time, that he had verbally agreed to become Sir Alex Ferguson's replacement at Manchester United in 2013. However, the desire to feel 'loved' again changed his mind, so he made a dramatic U-turn and rejoined Chelsea.

'The objective of the work that we are doing is to tell the truth,' Mourinho eloquently said when revealing his big United bombshell. And well, that's what he is in this documentary: honest. He is, as always, unapologetically Mourinho.

Sports.title: Former Chelsea doctor Eva Carneiro aims thinly-veiled dig at Jose Mourinho on social media after his refusal to apologise over infamous touchline row in Netflix documentary
Sports.content:
Former Chelsea team doctor Dr Eva Carneiro has made a tongue-in-cheek jibe at Jose Mourinho in light of his comments about their infamous touchline row in a new documentary.

Mourinho avoided apologising to Carneiro when opening up about their infamous touchline row for the first time in over a decade in his new three-part Netflix docu-series titled MOURINHO, which is released on Tuesday.

The former Blues boss claimed he sees 'a lady doctor is the same as a man’s doctor' when addressing the incident which led to him agreeing a settlement with Carneiro after she took them to a tribunal in 2016 over claims that she was discriminated against by the manager.

And on the same day that Mourinho's quotes hit the headlines, Carneiro took to social media to make a light-hearted joke toward her former boss when announcing an exciting new chapter in her career.

Taking to X, Carneiro wrote that her announcement, which will be revealed in Autumn, was a 'Special One' before adding a winky face emoji.

'Bom Dia,' her post started. 'I have an announcement to make. A truly Special One.'

Bom Dia 😁⚽️!!!!!



I have an announcement to make.



A truly Special One 😉



A project close to my heart which I have been working on for years and is almost ready for launch.



Not an old set piece!



Watch this space. This autumn!!!! pic.twitter.com/kVXyNqJ3DD — Dr Eva Carneiro (@evacarneiro) August 10, 2026

Dr Eva Carneiro (left, pictured in 2015) has aimed a tongue-in-cheek dig at Joe Mourinho on social media

'A project close to my heart which I have been working on for years and is almost ready for launch. Not an old set piece! Watch this space. This autumn!!!!'

During a Premier League clash with Swansea City at the start of the 2015-16 season, Mourinho hit the roof when Carneiro and physio Jon Fearn went onto the pitch to treat Eden Hazard, who had gone down seemingly injured.

Dr Carneiro claimed that Mourinho sexually discriminated against her during his tirade and called her the 'daughter of a wh***' in his native Portuguese.

Back in 2015, Mourinho called her 'impulsive and naive' in his first public reaction to her decision to treat Hazard. She was then dropped from first-team duties and left the club just a month later.

Mourinho and Chelsea eventually agreed a settlement after Carneiro took them to a tribunal over claims that she was discriminated against by the manager, and constructively dismissed by the club.

But 11 years on, Mourinho believes he treated Carneiro in the same manner that he would treat any other doctor who made what he deemed as a mistake.

‘For me, a lady doctor is the same as a man’s doctor,' Mourinho said in the docu-series. 'So, as always, I use my vocabulary when I’m not happy.

'There are words in moments where the tension is very, very high. Normally, people with football culture, with football DNA, with football background, they go over it in one second. In that case, it was different.’

The 63-year-old has spoken up about the incident for the first time in over a decade in Netflix's new three-part docu-series MOURINHO

Hazard, who played under the now-63-year-old for two years, claimed 'it was nothing special' in the documentary, which is set to air on Tuesday, but 'with Jose everything is bigger'.

Footage shows that the Portuguese coach, who is now Real Madrid manager, shouted a whole host of expletives toward Carneiro and Fearn as they treated Hazard. He screamed phrases such as 'f*** off, man' and 'f*** you, man'.

'I’m not a doctor, but my eyes know when a player is injured, and they know when a player is not injured,' Mourinho said in the docu-series.

'I knew that he was not injured, but the doctors went to the pitch, and in that moment we were left with nine players.’

Hazard was forced to come off the pitch for a brief period, as is the rule when a player receives medical treatment, leaving Chelsea with nine men after Thibaut Courtois had been sent off.

Chelsea gave Dr Carneiro an unreserved apology, but Mourinho refused to say sorry and grinned as he left the tribunal.

A deal was done in a back corridor of the court and Chelsea then issued a statement saying it 'regretted the circumstances' which led to the former club doctor leaving and 'apologises unreservedly to her and her family for the distress caused'.

The terms of the settlement remain secret, but during the tribunal it was revealed that Chelsea had previously offered £1.2million to silence Carneiro.

Mourinho did not apologise after the incident or at the tribunal and there were no signs of an apology in the docu-series either.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
