World.title: Security operatives rescue kidnapped Catholic seminarian, one other worshipper
World.content:
Security operatives in Enugu State have rescued a Catholic seminarian and one other worshipper, about one week after they were kidnapped.

The Secretary to the Enugu State Government (SSG), Chidiebere Onyia, announced the rescue of the kidnapped victims at the headquarters of the State Security Service (SSS) in Enugu on Monday evening.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that suspected kidnappers invaded a Catholic Church in Enugu State and abducted the seminarian, Lawrence Chidera Igbo, and one other worshipper, Emmanuel Onwudi.

The incident occurred on 2 August when the attackers invaded St. Joseph Catholic Church, Inoyi, in Affa, Udi Local Government Area of the state.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Arrest and killing of suspects

While making the announcement, Mr Onyia, a professor, said apart from the rescue of the abducted victims, three suspected kidnappers were arrested, while one was shot dead during a shootout with security operatives.

The SSG said the SSS, the army, the police, and the Enugu State Forest Guard jointly conducted the operation.

He acknowledged that ransom was paid to the kidnappers, but it was deployed as a strategy which helped security operatives track down the criminals by deploying the state’s hi-tech security assets.

Mr Onyia said the ransom has been recovered from the kidnappers after the operation.

“There was one fatality in this process. It was one of the criminals who died in the process of apprehending them.

“Usually, criminal elements will not want to be apprehended easily without a fight, but our people were ready, and we have one fatality, while the others are here now, as you could see; and they will face the full wrath of the law,” he said.

The SSG pointed out that the rescued victims had equally identified the arrested suspects as their abductors.

He said some arms, including AK-47 rifles, and seven ammunition magazines were recovered from the suspects during the operation.

Mr Onyia boasted that the Enugu State Government was ready to fight criminality head-on and warned criminals to leave the state.

“We made it very clear that if criminality becomes your venture, Enugu State is not the location to do that business; that we will pursue you, we will make sure we bring you to justice, and that was why we put the robust security architecture across the state, working in collaboration with the security forces to ensure that Enugu is uncomfortable for anybody that plans criminality.

“We are intentional in investing in and organising our security architecture to prevent crime. You can’t commit these crimes in Enugu State and get away with it. No way,” he said.

The SSG also warned residents who collude with criminals or serve as their informants, vowing to come after them as well.

“We will find you also, just as we have found these people, and we will prosecute you as part of this evil operation and this evil syndicate,” he stressed.

Mr Onyia praised the security operatives for the success of the operation and rescue of the victims.

“We also want to very highly commend all the security agencies: the SSS, Nigerian Army, the Nigerian police, the Enugu State Forest Guard, the military services, and others for being very instrumental in some of the work that was done, and continue to do in Enugu State,” he added.

World.title: Nigeria is building a sustainable health financing future, By Muhammad Ali Pate
World.content:
Nigeria welcomes Gavi’s US$500 million support as part of the shared effort to protect our children over the next five years. Within that period, we will continue to strengthen the domestic financing and institutional capacity needed to sustain immunisation beyond 2030, as Nigeria assumes greater responsibility for financing the programme and meeting the health needs of our citizens.

For much of the past three decades, global health financing rested on the expectation that external assistance would continue to expand alongside the health needs of developing countries. That expectation is now less certain, as fiscal pressures in donor countries, changing political priorities and recent disruptions to established programmes reshape how health partnerships are financed and managed. Nigeria must prepare for that change without surrendering the gains those partnerships have helped to achieve.

The implications are especially clear in immunisation, where nearly 10 million children are born in Nigeria each year. Each cohort must be reached with the vaccines already in the national schedule, while new vaccines are introduced only where the burden of disease, the evidence and the capacity of the health system justify them. With one of the largest birth cohorts in the world, Nigeria is among the most demanding immunisation settings globally.

Against this background, Gavi’s announced support of about US$500 million between 2026 and 2030 at a meeting with President Tinubu is a welcome boost. It will help finance vaccines, strengthen delivery and surveillance, maintain the cold chain and reach children who remain outside routine services. The support is provided within Gavi’s co-financing model, under which participating governments meet a share of vaccine costs and take on more as their capacity grows. Under Gavi 6.0, the Alliance’s 2026–2030 strategy, country leadership and the long-term sustainability of national immunisation programmes remain central to the way support is provided.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Financing a National Commitment

Nigeria has already co-financed vaccines at a level only few countries in the Gavi portfolio have matched. Over the course of the partnership, more than US$500 million has come from domestic resources. This scale of commitment reflects Nigeria’s demographic weight and a routine schedule of nearly 13 antigens; vaccines are consequently among the highest commodity cost items in the budget of the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare.

This investment reflects the priority President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration has given to immunisation, maternal and child health and primary healthcare. Sustaining that commitment as the programme expands will require counterpart financing to keep pace and responsibility to be shared more evenly across the federation. The Federal Government has historically borne most of the co-financing cost, while states are expected to provide much of the workforce, facilities, transport and community outreach through which vaccines reach children. A lasting financing framework should therefore reflect the shared responsibility between the federal and state levels.

That balance becomes more important with every vaccine introduced, because each addition creates a recurrent obligation as successive cohorts become eligible. Each new vaccine must therefore be judged not only by disease burden, but also by equity, affordability and the ability of the health system to deliver it consistently. Expanding the schedule without sustaining reliable coverage would defeat the purpose of doing so.

Within that framework, domestic financing has risen incrementally under President Tinubu. Health represented about 3.48 per cent of the federal budget when the administration began; it moved to 4.3 per cent, then about 5.28 per cent, and reached 6 per cent of the 2026 budget net of liabilities. Although Nigeria’s needs remain greater, this progression establishes a stronger domestic base over successive budgets instead of resting policy on promises that cannot be sustained.

The Design of the NHSRII

These financing choices cannot be separated from the way the wider health system is organised. The Nigeria Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative (NHSRII) was designed in response to a system in which priorities, financing and implementation had too often been dispersed across separate programmes. It provides the framework through which government sets national priorities, states and partners align behind them, and resources are connected more clearly to results.

External assistance has contributed immensely to Nigeria’s health gains, much of it delivered through separate plans, procurement channels, contractors and reporting systems. These programmes saved lives and built important capabilities, but they also produced fragmentation, duplication and limited visibility across the sector, leaving national institutions to assume responsibilities without always inheriting the systems, data and financing required to sustain them.

The Sector-Wide Approach (SWAp) was introduced to change that pattern. Under the Health Sector Renewal Compact, the Federal Government, all 36 states, the Federal Capital Territory and development partners have committed to work from one national plan, one budget and one reporting system. Because Nigeria’s health system remains decentralised, national progress still depends on state and local performance; the reform therefore gives the federation a shared direction while making responsibilities, resources and results easier to track.

The HOPE for Quality Primary Healthcare (HOPE-PHC) programme gives practical effect to this approach by linking financing to measurable improvements in primary healthcare at state level.

Building the Domestic Financing Base

Within that framework, domestic financing has risen incrementally under President Tinubu. Health represented about 3.48 per cent of the federal budget when the administration began; it moved to 4.3 per cent, then about 5.28 per cent, and reached 6 per cent of the 2026 budget net of liabilities. Although Nigeria’s needs remain greater, this progression establishes a stronger domestic base over successive budgets instead of resting policy on promises that cannot be sustained.

These increases are intended to support better services, stronger financial protection and improved population health. Achieving that purpose requires sound planning, predictable financing, disciplined procurement and clear reporting, so that Nigerians can see the connection between increased health investment and medicines in stock, functioning facilities, frontline workers and protection from catastrophic costs.

We expect the Gavi commitment to leave Nigeria with more than the vaccines purchased over five years. By 2030, fewer children should remain outside routine immunisation, differences between states should have narrowed, and federal and state governments should have a clearer and more durable arrangement for sharing recurrent costs. Data, supply chains and programme management should also sit more securely within Nigerian institutions.

From Imports to Domestic Production

As domestic financing grows, it should also change what Nigeria buys and what it is able to produce. Replacing donor money with public money to import the same finished products would leave the country exposed to foreign-exchange volatility, supply disruptions and production decisions made elsewhere.

This is why President Tinubu established the Presidential Initiative to Unlock the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC). Its mandate covers pharmaceuticals, vaccines, biologics, diagnostics, medical devices, logistics and health technology, with the aim of reducing that dependence by attracting investment into domestic production and building a stronger healthcare economy.

Vaccine manufacturing is technically demanding and requires capital, technology transfer, regulation, quality assurance and dependable demand over many years. Nigeria has the market to support such investment, but viability will depend on pooled procurement, development finance, strong regulation and credible technology partnerships working together. Gavi’s growing support for African vaccine manufacturing can assist countries prepared to build that capacity on sound commercial and regulatory foundations.

Beyond 2030

We expect the Gavi commitment to leave Nigeria with more than the vaccines purchased over five years. By 2030, fewer children should remain outside routine immunisation, differences between states should have narrowed, and federal and state governments should have a clearer and more durable arrangement for sharing recurrent costs. Data, supply chains and programme management should also sit more securely within Nigerian institutions.

The Gavi funding, rising domestic budgets and the drive for local manufacturing are therefore parts of one reform programme under the NHSRII. This approach is enabling Nigeria to build a health system in which international cooperation serves national priorities and domestic institutions carry a growing share of responsibility.

That transition is taking place amid constrained public revenues, unequal fiscal capacity across states and rising costs for essential commodities. Meeting these pressures will require careful priority-setting, greater efficiency and a steady expansion of domestic financing without weakening services on which people already depend.

Nigeria welcomes Gavi’s US$500 million support as part of the shared effort to protect our children over the next five years. Within that period, we will continue to strengthen the domestic financing and institutional capacity needed to sustain immunisation beyond 2030, as Nigeria assumes greater responsibility for financing the programme and meeting the health needs of our citizens.

Muhammad Ali Pate (CON) is the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Federal Republic of Nigeria.

World.title: SSS frees, compensates man wrongly linked to Oyo schoolchildren abduction
World.content:
The State Security Service (SSS) says it has freed and compensated a man who was wrongly detained for an alleged role in the abduction of 46 pupils, including seven teachers, from three schools in Oriire Local Government Area of Oyo State.

The SSS media unit disclosed this in a press statement shared with PREMIUM TIMES on Tuesday. According to the statement, the man, identified as Mustapha Marwana, was initially linked to the Ansaru terror group.

However, the SSS director general, Oluwatosin Ajayi, ordered his “immediate release” following an investigation by a panel “which established that Katsina -born Mustapha is not a member of any terrorist organisation and had no operational links with the Ansaru terrorist group.”

“Mustapha was arrested in connection with the abduction and killing of school pupils and teachers in Oriire LGA, Oyo State,” the statement reads. “He was subsequently subjected to thorough investigation to establish the extent, if any, of his involvement in the activities under investigation.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

PREMIUM TIMES reported that terrorists invaded the schools on 15 May, kidnapping the students and their teachers. The assailants killed one teacher before leaving the scene and another in captivity.

A few days later, the Defence Headquarters identified the terrorist responsible for the abduction as Boko Haram members. The captives regained freedom nearly 60 days after their abduction following security operations.

President Bola Tinubu later issued a statement blaming the Ansaru terror group for the abduction. The president also said the terror group demanded the release of its arrested leaders as a condition for freeing the kidnapped victims, but the government made no concessions and instead secured the release through targeted security operations.

The federal government, thereafter, charged and sentenced three men, including two Ansaru leaders already in custody in connection with the abduction.

Mr Marwana’s case

However, Mr Marwana, a carpenter, has never been named in any of these charges.

The SSS said investigators found no evidence linking him to the attack and membership of the terror group. In addition to the release order, the SSS said its director-general also approved “the payment of initial N3 million as compensation to assist him in meeting his immediate needs and restarting livelihood.”

The SSS said the man was released to his lawyer, Oghene Forgive.

It said Mr Marwana expressed appreciation to the director general for his compassionate and humane intervention.

His lawyer, Mr Forgive, also reportedly thanked the SSS boss “for his generosity and dedication to establishing Mustapha’s innocence.”

The SSS explained that the compensation was part of measures being adopted by the current SSS leadership to support persons cleared after investigations and facilitate their reintegration into society.

This newspaper reported how the service awarded a N20 million compensation to a Sokoto-based businessman who was accidentally shot and injured in 2016. The man was mistaken for another person during a pre-dawn raid in Jos, Plateau State.

In another instance, the SSS also released an Abuja-based businesswoman, Chineze Ozoadibe, and gave her N10 million as compensation in October 2025 after reviewing her case.

The SSS said that since the appointment of Mr Ajayi as its director-general, he has resolved and prioritised cases of human rights, resulting in the payment of over N300 million as compensation.

World.title: Nigeria’s condition in debate: Reviewing the Bishops–Presidency conversation, By Samuel Aruwan
World.content:
It was the Presidency that first informed Nigerians about President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s meeting with the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Nigeria (CBCN) on 28 July 2026.

In a statement issued by presidential spokesperson Bayo Onanuga⁠, the Presidency said the President received a CBCN delegation led by its President, the Most Rev. Matthew Man-Oso Ndagoso, Archbishop of Kaduna.

The statement, titled “We Are Stabilising the Nation, Prosperity on the Horizon, President Tinubu Tells Catholic Bishops⁠,” said the restructuring of security operations and institutions would deliver victory over terrorism, banditry and kidnapping.

“I have just approved the expansion of the armed forces,” the President was quoted as saying. “We are getting more equipment, building new barracks. We will defeat terrorism.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The composition of the delegation showed that this was an engagement between the President and a broad representation of the Catholic hierarchy. The presidential statement acknowledged that the bishops raised concerns about security, tertiary education, limited university spaces, democracy, credible elections and poverty. It also reported their requests concerning mission schools and equal access to places of worship.

President Tinubu responded by pointing to the Nigerian Education Loan Fund, the absence of a prolonged strike by the Academic Staff Union of Universities and what he described as the recovery of the economy.

“I can tell you categorically with sincerity that the country has been placed on a sound footing. The economy has recovered,” the President said. “This government has stabilised, and there is prosperity on the horizon. Life is improving.”

On the 2027 elections, he defended the Independent National Electoral Commission: “The opportunities are equal. INEC is neutral. They have never intimidated anyone.”

Soon after the meeting, the full text of Archbishop Ndagoso’s address, titled “Partners in Building a Just, Peaceful and Prosperous Nigeria,” entered the public domain. It showed that the bishops had presented a wider and more troubling assessment than the summary contained in the Presidency’s statement.

Their address was not a complete condemnation of the administration. They commended NELFund, thanked the government for its reception of Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Holy See’s Secretary for Relations with States and International Organisations, and acknowledged the rescue of kidnapped schoolchildren and their teachers. They recognised specific government efforts while questioning whether those efforts had produced sufficient improvement.

The bishops expressed concern about the place of Christians following the departure from the informal Christian–Muslim balance in the presidency. They did not claim that the Muslim–Muslim ticket was unconstitutional. They asked the President to reassure Christians of their equal rights and place in Nigeria through deliberate policies and actions.

On education, they commended the student loan programme but observed that loans could not solve the shortage of university places. They also questioned the wisdom of the recent federal moratorium on establishing new tertiary institutions, fearing that it could restrict the expansion needed to accommodate Nigeria’s growing youth population.

The moratorium itself raises a genuine policy dilemma. Nigeria has many underfunded and underused institutions, and indiscriminate expansion could weaken academic standards. Yet restricting new institutions does not remove the shortage of places. Access, affordability, staffing, infrastructure and quality must be addressed together.

The bishops also warned about the possibility of a one-party-dominant state. They asked President Tinubu, as leader of the governing party, to ensure a genuine level playing field and strengthen the democratic institutions he once relied upon as an opposition figure.

They connected this concern to declining voter turnout and growing public distrust of elections. They called for easier access to permanent voter cards, adequate and timely funding for INEC, transparent procedures and results that reflect voters’ choices. Anything short of a credible election in 2027, they warned, would be an “invitation to avoidable disaster.”

Insecurity was among the most urgent issues raised. The bishops recognised successful rescues but argued that these remained isolated when compared with attacks on schools, farms, homes, places of worship and highways. Their declaration that Nigeria was “bleeding” presented insecurity as a moral and humanitarian crisis, not merely an operational challenge.

They connected insecurity with economic hardship, unreliable electricity, poor roads and policies whose promised gains had been slow to reach citizens. They renewed their request for the return of mission schools and called for the equal application of religious freedom, particularly for Christians who reportedly face difficulty obtaining land for churches in parts of northern Nigeria.

The disagreement became sharper when john Cardinal Onaiyekan, a member of the delegation, appeared on ARISE News⁠ on 31 July 2026.

“His reply is that the nation is not bleeding,” Onaiyekan said of the President. “We told him our economy is not helping our poor people. He told us the economy is doing fine.”

The Cardinal alleged that people around the President were “giving him a rosy picture of what the country is, which it is not.” He said the bishops believed they had an obligation to help Tinubu appreciate the country’s reality as they understood it.

“When the nation is bleeding, you can’t expect a polite meeting with the head of state,” he said. “We need to let him know.”

Onaiyekan also attributed to the President the statement, “In politics, all is fair.” He interpreted it as evidence of an excessive determination to win elections and argued that the government was “bent on winning by all means.”

The alleged remark does not appear in the Presidency’s original account of the meeting, and no independently available transcript establishes its exact wording or context. It should therefore be treated as Onaiyekan’s recollection rather than an independently verified quotation.

On 1 August, the official State House website published “Cardinal Onaiyekan’s Abuse of Clerical Privilege⁠,” a response by Temitope Ajayi, Senior Special Assistant to the President on Media and Publicity.

Although Ajayi wrote in his own name and described the accusation as his view, the article appeared on the State House website and constituted a public defence of the President by a senior presidential aide.

Ajayi described Onaiyekan’s decision to recount and interpret the private meeting as “fundamentally inappropriate” and “an abuse of clerical privilege.” He said the bishops had requested the meeting, presented what he called a “notably acerbic” submission and received the President’s response. Reciprocity, he argued, required them to preserve the confidentiality and dignity of the engagement.

He also defended the administration on substance. The bishops’ assessment, he wrote, was “neither scripture nor an article of faith,” but a perspective that could be challenged with facts and evidence.

According to Ajayi, Tinubu acknowledged that serious economic and security problems remained but believed Nigeria had emerged from a “dark tunnel” and laid the foundations for recovery. Ajayi cited fiscal stability, more regular payment of salaries and pensions, and gains by the armed forces and intelligence agencies.

He rejected the suggestion that officials were shielding Tinubu from the truth, saying the President receives information through newspapers, television, intelligence assessments, operational briefings and contacts across the country.

One sentence sharpened the central issue: “The real question is not whether they know the truth but what choices they make in response to it.”

On 3 August 2026, Catholic priest Ugochukwu Ugwoke publicly rejected Ajayi’s confidentiality argument⁠. He maintained that the meeting was neither a sacramental confession nor a legally protected proceeding and argued that, without an express agreement, no absolute obligation of secrecy had been established.

This later intervention does not determine whether Onaiyekan exercised good judgment. It does, however, reinforce the distinction between a legal or ecclesiastical duty of confidentiality and a political expectation of discretion.

My purpose in revisiting the exchange is to examine what each side said, the evidence supporting its position and the questions that remain unresolved. Neutrality does not require avoiding difficult conclusions. It requires applying the same standards of evidence, fairness and context to every side.

The difference between the two accounts arose largely from how they measured the country. The Presidency emphasised fiscal stability, government programmes, university stability and security operations. The bishops concentrated on household welfare, political competition, public confidence and citizens’ experience of insecurity.

On Christian inclusion, the issue is not simply whether the Muslim–Muslim ticket was lawful. A political decision may be constitutional and still create a feeling of exclusion. The bishops’ concern should therefore be tested against the administration’s record of appointments, policies and equal treatment, rather than answered only by reference to electoral legality.

On political competition, one-party dominance can develop without opposition parties being formally banned. It may emerge through pressure on opponents, unequal access to state institutions or misuse of incumbency. Defections alone, however, do not prove that competition has ended. The relevant test is whether opposition parties can organise, campaign and contest elections without unlawful disadvantage.

Neither presidential assurance nor public distrust settles the question of INEC’s independence. Its credibility must be judged by the transparency of appointments, the adequacy of its funding, the consistency of its procedures, the integrity of collation and the verifiability of results.

INEC’s 2024 “Review of the 2023 General Election⁠” recorded 93,469,008 registered voters. Approximately 26.7 per cent participated in the presidential election of 25 February 2023, held alongside the National Assembly elections, when total votes cast are measured against the complete register.

That figure does not prove electoral manipulation. Low turnout can result from voter apathy, distrust, insecurity, logistical failures, non-collection of permanent voter cards and difficulties encountered at polling units. It nevertheless establishes a serious problem of low electoral participation, even if its causes require further evidence.

Having once been involved in the security management of one of Nigeria’s most sensitive and complex states, I recognise that the present crisis is not today’s creation. It reflects social tensions, institutional failures, policy weaknesses and warnings neglected over many years. I examined part of this history in my article, “National Security Reflections on Maitatsine, Bullum-Kuttu and Boko Haram Uprisings.”

That history explains the complexity of the problem without removing the responsibility of the government in office. Although the current administration did not create every part of the crisis, it carries the constitutional duty to address it. Progress must be measured not only by operations conducted, arrests made or weapons recovered, but by whether those efforts produce lasting safety.

Classified intelligence and citizens’ experience measure different aspects of security. Operational briefings may show what security agencies are doing; citizens judge the results by whether they can travel, farm, attend school and worship without fear. Both are necessary for a fair assessment.

The economic disagreement can also be examined against published data. The economic disagreement can also be examined against published data from the fact-checking standpoint of a journalist researching conflict and security governance. That is what I have done, as the next paragraph demonstrates.

According to the National Bureau of Statistics’ “Nigerian Gross Domestic Product Report Q1 2026⁠,” Nigeria’s real Gross Domestic Product grew by 3.89 per cent year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026, compared with 3.13 per cent in the corresponding quarter of 2025.

The NBS “June 2026 CPI Report⁠,” dated 15 July 2026, recorded year-on-year headline inflation of 15.91 per cent and food inflation of 17.52 per cent. Although headline inflation was marginally lower than May’s 15.93 per cent, food inflation rose from 16.96 per cent in May.

These figures indicate growth in aggregate real output and a much lower headline inflation rate than Nigeria recorded earlier. They do not establish that living standards or purchasing power have recovered. Inflation remaining positive means that the general price level is still rising, while June’s increase in food inflation shows that the improvement was not uniform.

The World Bank’s October 2025 “Nigeria Development Update⁠,” titled “From Policy to People: Bringing the Reform Gains Home,” recognised “substantial progress on macroeconomic stabilization.” It also observed that those gains had “yet to substantially improve Nigerians’ livelihoods.”

These findings explain how the Presidency and the bishops could present different accounts of the same economy. The Presidency can point to measurable macroeconomic progress, while the bishops can point to households struggling with food prices, transportation costs, unreliable electricity and reduced purchasing power.

The two positions address different stages of the same process: stabilisation at the national level and its incomplete transmission to families. Government revenue may increase while households remain under pressure. Salaries may be paid regularly but buy fewer essential goods.

On mission schools, the Presidency was broadly correct that decisions concerning schools taken over and administered by state governments ordinarily rest with those states. The President could nevertheless use his political influence to encourage governors to engage the original proprietors.

On religious freedom, the bishops did not object to the Supreme Court’s protection of Muslim students at Rivers State University. They asked that the same constitutional principle be applied to Christians who reportedly face difficulty obtaining land for churches or practising their faith. Their position was that equality should exist in practice, not only in law.

Onaiyekan’s presence at the meeting gives direct value to his recollection of what was said. A distinction must still be made between his recollection of statements and his interpretation of the President’s expression and advisers. He did not identify those allegedly presenting a rosy picture or specify what information they withheld. That part of his account remains an interpretation rather than an independently established fact.

The Presidency’s objection rests largely on an expectation of discretion following a closed-door meeting. Yet its statement of 28 July 2026 had already disclosed parts of the President’s responses on the economy, security, education, INEC and mission schools. Ajayi’s subsequent article disclosed further details.

The disagreement was therefore not only about privacy. It was also about who was entitled to frame the meeting for the public.

The bishops presented an account centred on insecurity, hardship, electoral distrust and equal citizenship. Onaiyekan reinforced that account but added recollections and interpretations requiring separate evaluation. The Presidency defended its record and its right to disagree while questioning the propriety of the Cardinal’s comments.

Nigeria’s condition will ultimately be judged by outcomes: whether people are safer, whether their earnings buy more, whether electricity and roads become more reliable, whether opposition parties can compete fairly, whether confidence in INEC improves and whether religious rights receive equal protection.

Presidential assurances and episcopal declarations can shape the debate. Neither can settle it. That requires credible evidence, honest public engagement and a willingness to examine Nigeria’s condition as it is.

Samuel Aruwan is a postgraduate student at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria.

World.title: Afolabi assumes duty as 35th Abia Commissioner of Police
World.content:
By Ben Ngwakwe, Gombe

UMUAHIA — The Abia State Police Command has welcomed a new Commissioner of Police, CP Wilfred Olutokunbo Afolabi, who has assumed duty as the 35th Commissioner of Police in the state.

Afolabi takes over from AIG Danladi Isa, who was promoted and redeployed to the Force Criminal Investigation Department (FCID), Annex, Kaduna.

In a statement issued on August 10, 2026, the Command’s Police Public Relations Officer, DSP Maureen Chioma Chinaka, described the new commissioner as a seasoned police officer with more than three decades of service in the Nigeria Police Force.

Afolabi joined the force as a Cadet Assistant Superintendent of Police on May 18, 1992, and has served in various strategic command, operational, administrative and international policing positions.

He holds a Bachelor of Science degree in Botany from the University of Ilorin, as well as a Postgraduate Diploma and a Master’s degree in Peace and Security Studies from the University of Port Harcourt.

His professional training includes the Strategic Leadership and Command Course at the National Institute of Police Studies, Abuja; Tactical Leadership Command Course at the Police Staff College, Jos; Internal Security/Low Intensity Conflict Course at the Armed Forces Command and Staff College, Jaji; and Peacekeeping Negotiation Course at the Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre, Ghana.

Afolabi also has extensive international policing experience.

Between 2004 and 2005, he served as pioneer Sector Commander of Sector 2, Nyala, and pioneer Regional Commander of Southern Darfur under the African Union Mission in Sudan.

During the assignment, he helped establish operational and administrative structures, set up police stations in internally displaced persons’ camps and coordinated civil police activities.

Earlier, between 2001 and 2002, he served as Nigeria Contingent Commander and Special Response Unit Officer under the Human Rights Section of the United Nations Mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where he contributed to law enforcement reforms, system analysis and training programmes for local police personnel.

Before his deployment to Abia, Afolabi served as Commissioner of Police, Administration, Training and Development, at the Force Headquarters, Abuja.

He had also served as Commissioner of Police in Ondo State, where he coordinated administrative and operational activities, strengthened intelligence gathering, improved investigative efficiency and promoted community policing initiatives.

He also served as Commissioner of Police, Force Equitation Officer, Mounted Troop, at the Force Headquarters, Abuja, supervising mounted police operations and ensuring operational readiness and professionalism in crowd control and ceremonial duties.

Between 2021 and 2023, Afolabi served as Deputy Commissioner of Police, Administration, Delta State Command; DCP, Criminal Investigation Department, Katsina State Command; and DCP, Operations, Bayelsa State Command.

As DCP Administration in Delta, he handled high-level administrative responsibilities and enforcement of police regulations. In Katsina, he coordinated criminal investigations, while in Bayelsa, he planned and supervised crime prevention and operational activities across the state.

Between 2016 and 2021, he served in various capacities, including Area Commander in Anambra State Command, Assistant Commissioner of Police, Operations, Imo State Command, and Assistant Commissioner of Police, Intelligence, Abuja.

From 2014 to 2016, Afolabi served as a Divisional Police Officer in several divisions within the Federal Capital Territory before becoming a Directing Staff at the Police Staff College, Jos, where he trained and mentored senior police officers.

His career also includes service as Sector Commander and Second-in-Command in Joint Task Force operations in Warri, Staff Officer at the Force Headquarters and Unit Commander of the Police Mobile Force in Plateau State, where he participated in specialised policing operations.

Afolabi has undertaken several national and international assignments, including serving among the first Nigerian police officers deployed to the African Union Mission in Darfur.

He was also the last Contingent Commander of the Nigeria Police Team to the United Nations Mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina and served as Aide-de-Camp to visiting Heads of State.

He participated in the organisation of major international events, including the All African Games and Commonwealth Summit.

Afolabi is a Fellow of the Peace and Security Studies Department of the University of Port Harcourt and a Justice of the Peace.

The Command described him as a disciplined, strategic and result-oriented police officer whose career reflects a commitment to public safety, professional excellence and international policing standards.

It called on stakeholders, traditional and community leaders, civil society organisations and members of the public to extend their cooperation to the new commissioner as he begins his tenure.

According to the Command, such cooperation would be critical to Afolabi’s efforts to strengthen security, improve policing and safeguard lives and property across Abia State.

Afolabi is married with children. His hobbies include travelling and reading.

World.title: Inuwa intensifies push for federal road projects, meets Umahi
World.content:
By Ben Ngwakwe, Gombe

GOMBE — Gombe State Governor, Muhammadu Inuwa Yahaya, has intensified efforts to attract Federal Government intervention in major road projects across the state, particularly those considered critical to agricultural, commercial, industrial and tourism development.

Yahaya renewed the push during a meeting with the Minister of Works, Senator David Umahi, on Monday in Abuja, where he canvassed accelerated action on strategic federal road projects in the state.

According to a statement by the Director-General, Press Affairs, Government House, Gombe, Ismaila Uba Misilli, the meeting formed part of the governor’s sustained engagements with the Federal Government to improve road connectivity and unlock economic opportunities across the state.

A major focus of the meeting was the Gombe-Biu axis of the Akwanga-Jos-Bauchi-Gombe-Biu-Maiduguri Super Highway, recently approved and flagged off by the Federal Government.

Yahaya has consistently advocated the early commencement of work on the Gombe-Biu section, describing the corridor as strategically important to Gombe and the entire North-East.

His advocacy has included repeated engagements with the Ministry of Works and other relevant federal authorities, culminating in Umahi’s recent visit to Gombe, where he joined the governor and members of the National Assembly for the groundbreaking ceremony of the project.

Following the groundbreaking, the governor is seeking sustained momentum towards the commencement of full-scale construction and timely completion of the road.

Another major request by the governor is the construction of northern and southern bypasses for Gombe metropolis.

According to Yahaya, the proposed bypasses would open up the state capital from both ends, create strategic links to the Gombe-Biu corridor, decongest existing roads and facilitate the movement of people and goods.

Responding, Umahi described the Gombe-Biu axis of the super highway as a priority project of the President Bola Ahmed Tinubu administration, assuring the governor that his request for construction to commence from the proposed point of interest would be given due consideration.

The minister also expressed confidence in the capacity of Hitech Construction Company, the contractor handling the project, describing it as one of the competent firms executing major infrastructure projects in the country.

Umahi commended Yahaya for his persistence and commitment to pursuing development projects for the people of Gombe State.

Reflecting on his recent visit to the state, the minister said the experience had deepened his appreciation of the scale and quality of infrastructure development under the Yahaya administration.

“Since my visit to Gombe, I have become like your ambassador. Anywhere I go, I talk about your state and the developmental strides I have witnessed. I tell people, when you want to see genuine development and visionary leadership, go to Gombe,” Umahi said.

He assured the governor that the Federal Government would deliver the project, expressing optimism that its completion would have a significant impact on the people of Gombe and further demonstrate the infrastructure agenda of the Tinubu administration.

The minister also acknowledged Yahaya’s sustained advocacy for the rehabilitation and reconstruction of other strategic highways linking Gombe with neighbouring states and economic centres.

They include the Gombe-Bajoga-Potiskum, Gombe-Dukku-Darazo and Gombe-Bauchi corridors.

The roads, which connect several communities and agricultural areas to major markets and commercial centres, are regarded as critical economic links for Gombe State and the wider North-East.

The governor’s renewed push is expected to strengthen federal-state collaboration on road infrastructure, improve regional connectivity and create new opportunities for trade, agriculture, investment and industrial development across the state.

World.title: Why I am supporting Donkemezuo for House of Reps — Dokubo-Asari
World.content:
By Adesina Wahab

Da Amakiri Tubo, Alhaji Mujahid Abubakr Dokubo-Asari, Amanyanabo of The Source, Elem Kalabari, Torusarama Piri, has explained his decision to support the aspiration of Hon. Engr. Elvis Donkemezuo to represent Yenagoa–Kolokuma/Opokuma Federal Constituency in the House of Representatives in 2027.

Dokubo-Asari, who publicly endorsed the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) candidate during an event in Abuja on Monday, said Donkemezuo had been involved in the struggle for the advancement of the Ijaw people and understood the challenges confronting the Niger Delta.

“He has fought alongside me for the Ijaw cause; he understands our struggle and will give the Ijaw people a voice in Abuja,” he said.

The endorsement was made during a gathering of prominent Ijaw sons in Abuja, where Donkemezuo paid homage to the monarch and formally presented his political ambition.

The meeting, which began as a traditional courtesy visit, provided an opportunity for the two men to reflect on their involvement, in different capacities, in the struggle for the rights and development of the Ijaw people.

Following introductions by Prince Jude Tabai, Dokubo-Asari spoke about Donkemezuo’s record and his involvement in the Ijaw struggle.

He described Donkemezuo as “a great son of Ijaw land,” recalling his participation in efforts aimed at advancing the interests and welfare of the Ijaw people.

Dokubo-Asari said the 2027 election should not be viewed solely from the perspective of party politics, stressing that the Ijaw people needed representatives at the National Assembly who understood their history, challenges and aspirations.

He expressed confidence that Donkemezuo had the experience and understanding required to effectively represent the people at the National Assembly.

“With people like Engr. Elvis, who are conversant with the problems of the Ijaw people, the voice of the Ijaws and our challenges will be heard in the National Assembly,” he said.

Donkemezuo’s Ijaw activism

Donkemezuo was the pioneer coordinator of the Ijaw Youth Council (IYC), Abuja Chapter, and later served as president of the IYC in 2013.

He was also involved in processes surrounding the establishment of the Presidential Amnesty Programme for former Niger Delta militants and has advocated environmental protection, justice and development in the Niger Delta.

His memoir, The Vain Ijaw Struggle, chronicles his experiences during the Niger Delta struggle and the efforts to draw international attention to environmental degradation, injustice and socio-economic challenges in the region.

‘I will support you’

Dokubo-Asari also pledged his support for Donkemezuo’s political ambition, saying he would use his words and actions to support the aspiration and work towards his emergence in 2027.

The monarch further prayed for divine guidance, protection, wisdom and strength for Donkemezuo as he embarks on his political journey.

Also present at the gathering was Chief Ebikabowei Victor-Ben, popularly known as Boyloaf, who described Donkemezuo as “trusted and tested” and pledged his support for the aspiration.

Others in attendance included Hon. Chief Raphael Kuku, Elder Edward Alagoa, a pioneer founding member of IYC Abuja, Tuedere Victor Ben, Hon. Romeo Bekeyai and Prince Jude Tabai, among others.

The gathering brought together prominent figures associated with the Ijaw struggle and underscored the growing political attention surrounding the 2027 contest for the Yenagoa–Kolokuma/Opokuma Federal Constituency.

World.title: 2027: Kogi Central PDP inaugurates campaign council, names Etudaiye DG
World.content:
…As Natasha says campaign must be house-to-house

By John Alechenu

ABUJA — The Kogi Central chapter of the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, has inaugurated its campaign organisation for the 2027 general elections, with a charge to members to take the party’s campaign to the grassroots.

The campaign council was inaugurated in Okene under the leadership of Senator Natasha Akpoti-Uduaghan, who represents Kogi Central in the Senate.

The development was contained in a statement issued by her Media Aide, Sam Idoko, in Abuja on Tuesday.

According to the statement, Dr Salami Etudaiye was appointed Director-General of the campaign, while Hon. Alhaji Abubakar Yahaya Karaku will serve as Campaign Chairman.

Other members of the campaign team are Hon. Jacob Ogirima Anebe, Secretary; Hon. Ilyasu Zubair, Head of Operations; Hon. Isiaka Uhuanaye, Head of Technicals; and Hon. Jane Onoba, Head of Welfare.

Speaking at the inauguration, Senator Natasha charged members of the campaign council to focus on winning the election, stressing that victory must begin at the grassroots.

She said the campaign must be taken directly to voters through house-to-house and polling-unit-to-polling-unit mobilisation.

“This campaign must be house-to-house and polling-unit-by-polling-unit. We must reach our people directly, listen to them, engage them and explain clearly why the PDP remains the best platform for the development and progress of our people,” she said.

The senator said the party’s doors remained open to new members, urging supporters to work together to build a stronger political movement in the district.

“We must open our doors for everyone who wants to join this moving train and this winning team. There is room for everyone who believes in the PDP and in the future we are building for Kogi Central,” she said.

She also urged members of the campaign organisation to maintain discipline and unity while ensuring full coverage of all wards and polling units.

“The election ahead will take all of us — leaders, women, youths, ward executives, coordinators, volunteers. We must work as one,” she said.

In his acceptance speech, the campaign Director-General, Dr Etudaiye, described his appointment as a responsibility that required commitment and determination.

“I stand before you today with a heart full of gratitude and a spirit on fire. I accept, with humility and with steely resolve, the sacred responsibility you have placed upon me as Director-General of this campaign.

“This is not a ceremonial title. This is a call to battle. I did not accept this assignment to manage a campaign of polite handshakes and quiet meetings. I accepted it to organise a movement,” he said.

Etudaiye said the campaign organisation would reach every part of Kogi Central, including Okene, Adavi, Ajaokuta, Okehi and Ogori-Magongo, as well as streets, markets, campuses and homes.

“We are not going into this election to beg. We are going in to win and to win decisively,” he said.

He urged women and youths to play leading roles in the campaign, particularly in grassroots and digital mobilisation.

“To our youth: your energy, your digital power, your courage — this campaign will be incomplete without you. Come and own it,” he said.

Etudaiye pledged to lead the campaign with transparency and competence, with a focus on securing votes for the party.

“I will listen. I will coordinate. I will fight for every vote,” he said.

“This is not just a campaign. This is a revolution of hope for Kogi Central. I accept this charge. I embrace this duty. And by the grace of God and the collective will of our people, we shall prevail,” he added.

The Campaign Chairman, Karaku, urged members to put aside personal interests and differences and work towards the collective objective of strengthening the PDP and securing victory for its candidates.

“This is the time for every member of our great party to come together. We must put aside whatever differences we may have and concentrate on the larger objective of building a stronger PDP and securing victory for our candidates,” he said.

Karaku urged the campaign team to promote positive and issue-based messaging while strengthening its grassroots mobilisation.

“Our message must be positive, our conduct must be responsible, and our mobilisation must be strategic. We must convince the people through our programmes, our commitment and our presence at the grassroots.

“Elections are won by organisation, unity and the ability to connect with the people,” he said.

He urged members to work collectively, stressing that every vote, ward and polling unit mattered.

“Nobody should consider himself or herself too important to work with another person. Every vote matters, every ward matters and every polling unit matters. If we remain united, disciplined and focused, we can achieve the victory we desire,” Karaku said.

He also appealed to party members and supporters to promote peace and issue-based politics throughout the election period.

Campaign Council

Director-General: Dr Salami Etudaiye

Campaign Chairman: Hon. Alhaji Abubakar Yahaya Karaku

Secretary: Hon. Jacob Ogirima Anebe

Head of Operations: Hon. Ilyasu Zubair

Head of Technicals: Hon. Isiaka Uhuanaye

Head of Welfare: Hon. Jane Onoba

World.title: ‘I WANT TO BE A NURSE’:  Trafficked Delta girl finds hope after escaping Abidjan prostitution ring
World.content:
•Annabel with Olorogun Egbo, Ughelli North LG Chairman.

By Egufe Yafugborhi

For 19-year-old Annabel, the dream of becoming a nurse was almost swallowed by a journey that took her from her community in Delta State to the streets of Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire, where she was trafficked into prostitution.

Today, that dream is alive again.

After weeks of uncertainty and abandonment in a foreign land, Annabel is back home in Ovwiamuge, Agbarho, Ughelli South Local Government Area, Delta State, reunited with her parents and receiving support to rebuild her life and return to school.

Rescue

Her rescue began with a viral video. In the footage, which circulated widely on social media, an unidentified interviewer found the young Nigerian on the streets of Abidjan and began asking questions to establish her identity and trace her family.

“Annabel,” she replied when asked her name. She identified her state as Delta and her village as Ovwiamuge. Her parents, she said, were both alive and still in Nigeria.

But there was a painful revelation: they did not know she was in Côte d’Ivoire.

Asked whether she knew the people who had taken her there, Annabel indicated that she could identify her “Madam” and had her phone number. She also knew the place where she had been taken, although she did not know its name.

Firm resolve

The narrator explained that Annabel had been taken to Côte d’Ivoire for prostitution but was thrown out after she refused to yield.

“I was told I was coming to earn from a decent job,” she said. The narrator’s appeal was simple: share the video and help locate her family.

That triggered a chain of community intervention that eventually brought the teenager home.

Among those who championed her return was Stella Okotete, Executive Director of Business Development at the Nigerian Export-Import Bank, who received Annabel back in Nigeria through her Erhuvwuoghene Girl Child Right Foundation.

Homecoming

For Okotete, the rescue could not end with bringing Annabel across the border. The bigger task was helping her recover, reintegrate into society, and reclaim a future that trafficking had threatened to destroy.

“Thank God, Annabel has returned home safely. Her joyful homecoming is a moment of relief, gratitude, and hope for all of us.

•Stella Okotete (bespectacled) of ErhuvwuOghene Foundation

addressing Ovwiamuge residents who came in numbers to welcome

their daughter back home.

“This incident reminds us that the responsibility of protecting our children rests with every parent, guardian, and society. I call on mothers to pay closer attention to the welfare, safety, and well-being of their children, particularly the girl child.

“Human trafficking remains a grave threat to our communities. We must remain vigilant, educate our children, speak up against suspicious activities, and work together to protect every child from exploitation.”

Hope Renew

Perhaps the most significant part of Annabel’s rescue is what comes next. Okotete’s foundation is championing her return to school to rebuild her aspirations.

The teenager has already expressed her ambition: to become a nurse. That dream has also received the backing of the Chairman of Ughelli North LG, Olorogun Jaro Egbo, who received Annabel from Okotete.

“I am overjoyed that our daughter, Annabel, is back,” he said.

Egbo said the community’s response to Annabel’s ordeal demonstrated what collective action could achieve when the safety of a vulnerable person became a shared responsibility. We are going to get her back to school. She wants to be a nurse so that she can also take care of others,” he underscored.

“I call on other people elsewhere… parents should be very, very mindful of their children,” he emphasised.

Back in her community, Annabel was reunited with her parents and a joyful community who agreed that she should undergo medical examinations and receive the necessary support for reintegration.

“We’ll try our best to integrate her back into society and give her all necessary support,” Okotete assured.

Caution

The case has revived concerns about the vulnerability of young Nigerians to trafficking, particularly through promises of opportunities outside their communities. Annabel’s ordeal is therefore both a rescue story and a warning. A teenager left home, apparently without her parents knowing, only to find herself in a foreign country facing pressure to enter prostitution.

Her refusal placed her in an even more precarious position, leaving her stranded until a chance encounter brought her plight to public attention.What followed demonstrated how social media, community leadership, and intervention by individuals and organisations can blend to rescue the vulnerable.

But the circumstances that led to Annabel’s ordeal remain concerning. For Okotete, preventing another Annabel will require more than rescuing victims after trafficking has occurred. It requires vigilance, education, and stronger family and community protection.

“Together, we can fight human trafficking, safeguard our daughters, and build a future where every girl is free to dream, grow, and achieve her full potential,” she said.

For Annabel, the road ahead is now different. Not another foreign street.

Not another trafficker’s promise.

A classroom and eventually, a hospital ward, where she hopes to become the nurse she has always wanted to be.

World.title: ₦1.5bn mass wedding: Kano children deserve greater investment — APC stalwart
World.content:
By Golok Nanmwa

JOS — An All Progressives Congress, APC, stalwart and businessman, Bashir Abdullahi II, has criticised the Kano State Government over its reported expenditure of more than ₦1.5 billion on a mass wedding programme involving 1,500 couples.

Abdullahi described the reported expenditure as a “costly misplaced priority,” arguing that Kano State required greater investment in education, healthcare, employment and human capital development.

In a statement made available to newsmen in Jos on Tuesday, he said while supporting vulnerable citizens remained a legitimate responsibility of government, public resources should be deployed in ways that could deliver sustainable benefits to a wider segment of the population.

He said the issue was not whether the beneficiaries deserved assistance but whether the reported ₦1.5 billion was the most effective way to provide such support.

“There is nothing wrong with supporting vulnerable citizens. There is nothing wrong with helping people who cannot afford the cost of marriage.

“But when government spends ₦1.5 billion on a mass wedding in a state facing major development challenges, citizens are entitled to ask whether that money could have achieved a greater and more lasting impact elsewhere,” he said.

The Kano State Government has said the expenditure covered medical screening, dowries, business grants, furniture, food and other essential items provided to the couples.

Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf said the government gave each bride ₦100,000 as dowry and another ₦100,000 as a capital grant, alongside household furniture and other necessities.

Yusuf described the programme as one of his administration’s key campaign promises, saying it was designed to support vulnerable residents, strengthen families and promote social stability.

However, Abdullahi urged the government to look beyond the immediate benefits of the programme and consider its long-term development impact.

He argued that a one-off intervention could provide immediate relief without addressing the underlying economic challenges confronting beneficiaries.

“Marriage comes with responsibilities that last for years. Families need food, housing, healthcare and education for their children.

“A government that wants to fight poverty must therefore think beyond the wedding ceremony and invest in the economic capacity of families to sustain themselves,” he said.

Abdullahi said the reported ₦1.5 billion could, in his view, have been channelled into classroom construction, teacher training, school feeding, healthcare, vocational education and youth employment.

He argued that such investments had the potential to benefit citizens over a longer period.

“A classroom remains after the ceremony.

“A trained teacher can educate generations of children.

“A young person equipped with a useful skill can earn an income and support a family.

“These are investments that create lasting capacity,” he said.

The APC stalwart stressed that his criticism was not directed at marriage or the beneficiaries of the programme.

“This is not an argument against marriage. It is not an argument against helping widows, divorcees or poor families.

“It is an argument about priorities and opportunity cost,” he said.

He urged the Kano State Government to provide details of the expenditure and explain the long-term development outcomes expected from the programme.

According to him, the government should demonstrate how many beneficiaries are expected to become economically independent, how many businesses would be established and the mechanisms put in place to monitor the programme after the initial assistance.

Abdullahi also urged governments in the North to give greater attention to education and human capital development, arguing that poverty could not be sustainably addressed through short-term interventions alone.

He said Kano’s development challenges required sustained investment in schools, teachers, healthcare, skills acquisition, infrastructure and productive employment.

“Government must learn to distinguish between what is politically attractive and what is developmentally necessary.

“A mass wedding may provide a new beginning for individual couples, but a good school can provide a new beginning for an entire generation,” he said.

According to the Kano State Government, the mass wedding involved 1,500 couples drawn from the state’s 44 Local Government Areas and was coordinated by the Kano State Hisbah Board.

The government also said the beneficiaries underwent medical screening and counselling before the ceremonies.

Abdullahi said the programme should ultimately be assessed not by the scale of the ceremony but by the long-term improvement it brought to the lives of the beneficiaries.

He added that social intervention programmes should combine immediate assistance with sustainable livelihood opportunities.

“The real question is not how many weddings government can sponsor.

“The real question is how many lives it can permanently transform,” he said.

World.title: Delta federal roads: Gridlock, anguish as farmers, motorists groan
World.content:
•The failed Asaba-Ugbolu-Illah-Ebu federal highway in Delta State.

By Ochuko Akuopha

EBU — Farmers and traders in the Ebu community in Oshimili North Local Government Area, Delta State, have been cut off from major markets across the South-South and Northern regions as the Asaba-Ugbolu-Illah-Ebu federal highway has become virtually impassable due to persistent neglect and torrential rains at the peak of the rainy season.

The critical single-lane road, which serves as a primary gateway to Edo, Kogi, and the vast expanse of Northern Nigeria, has severely restricted the movement of agricultural produce and essential goods, triggering a fresh wave of economic hardship for the agrarian community.

A Road That Swallows Dreams

Drive through this corridor and you’ll witness a scene that defies belief. Where smooth asphalt once carried the hopes of traders and transporters, there now yawn deep gullies, potholes that have spread into muddy graves for vehicles. Heavy-duty trucks lie on their sides, their loads scattered, their drivers cursing the fate that brought them here.

“My brother, for the past four months, it has been a nightmare,” said Azuka, a transporter who has plied the route for fifteen years, his eyes betraying the exhaustion of countless sleepless nights spent stranded on this road.

He gestured toward a section where three trailers have crashed into each other, creating a metal sculpture of frustration. “Most drivers have decided not to follow the road anymore. We have broken down trailers everywhere.”

The statistics tell a grim story. A journey that once cost a passenger N1000 now demands N5000 and that’s if you can find a transporter willing to risk the journey at all. The cost of repairs has become prohibitive, and many vehicles simply give up, joining the growing number of abandoned cars along the roadside.

Farmers Bearing the Heaviest Load

But the human toll transcends economics. It is measured in the faces of farmers whose yams, cassava, maize, plantain, and potatoes rot in their fields because they cannot reach the markets of Asaba, Ugbolu, and Onitsha.

“The situation of the road is actually disturbing,” Mr. Andrew Onlaye, an indigene of Illah community, told NDV. “The neighbouring communities are agrarian communities that cultivate yam, cassava, maize, plantain, potatoes. The deplorable nature of the road has made it difficult for the farmers to take their goods to the market,” he added.

What the farmers have cultivated with their sweat and prayers now becomes a source of anguish. The road that should carry their produce to hungry markets instead swallows their livelihoods whole.

A Highway of Tears

But the most devastating cost cannot be counted in naira or kobo. It is measured in lives lost, in families shattered, in dreams that ended on this stretch of asphalt.

“In fact, more than two, three deaths were recorded because of the heavy duty trucks on the road. Many youths have been involved in accidents because of the deplorable nature of the road. Okada versus trailer, it killed some of them instantly. Some of them were maimed and injured. Some of the cases are still being discussed in the police station,” Onlaye revealed.

The road has become a predator. When trucks fall, when Okadas collide with trailers and when vehicles break down in the middle of nowhere, the darkness descends and with it.

“Because of the inability to pass through the road, it is very easy for people to fall victim to bandits, armed robbers and others attack,” Onlaye added, painting a picture of a community under siege from all sides.

The Politics of Neglect

As the rainy season intensifies; the road continues to steadily worsen. The heavy-duty trucks that the road was never designed to handle have accelerated its collapse. Four months ago, there were still stretches where drivers could find relief but this is no longer possible.

“The trailers are using the road too often,” Onlaye explained. “The heavy duty trucks passing through the roads especially during this rainy season have made the situation worse to the extent that small vehicles cannot pass through. It is not easy to maintain vehicles after passing through the roads.”

Mr. Nathan Oswe, another road user, expresses fears that the communities could be completely cut off. “Even during the electioneering period, many places may not be accessed and INEC officials may not be able to move election materials to the affected areas.”

A Cry for Help

The people have not suffered in silence, they have raised their voices to the Federal Government, cried out to the state government and prayed for intervention.

“These are some of the reasons why the people are crying out,” Onlaye said. “When the people are crying to the Federal Government, they are also crying to the state government to intervene and do some palliative to enable the people in the community to move with ease.”

“We need the federal and state government to come to our aid to see if they can do any palliative work, because transportation is the only way we can fend for ourselves,” Azuka added.

A Glimmer of Hope

When contacted, former Controller of the Federal Ministry of Works in Delta State, Mr. Matthew Ogar offered these words: “We are trying to see what we can do on that road; the road is under design.”

However, the question that haunts every traveller and every farmer, who must navigate this treacherous path, is not whether the road will be fixed, but whether it will be fixed before more lives are lost, more dreams are shattered and before another community is cut off from the nation it serves.

World.title: 2027 Polls: NHRC asks FG to arrest, prosecute Sheikh Jingir for hate speech
World.content:
By Ikechukwu Nnochiri

ABUJA — Ahead of the 2027 general elections, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), on Tuesday, urged the Federal Government to immediately arrest and prosecute Islamic cleric, Sheikh Yahaya Jingir, for hate speech and incitement.

The Commission, in a statement signed by its Executive Secretary, Chief Tony Ojukwu, SAN, said it condemned in strong terms “the hateful and inciting remarks” it said were made by the cleric in a viral video on Sunday.

The NHRC said it watched with grave concern as the cleric openly canvassed for religiously exclusive politics ahead of the general elections and used derogatory language referring to “infidels” while urging supporters to obtain voter cards to “show their limit.”

The rights body described the statements as a direct attack on the principles of equality, non-discrimination, and peaceful coexistence guaranteed under the 1999 Constitution, as amended, and Nigeria’s international human rights obligations.

“The Commission finds these remarks to be hate speech and incitement to religious hatred and potential violence. At a time when we are preparing for another general election, such utterances are reckless and dangerous.

“They serve no purpose other than to divide Nigerians along religious lines and set citizens against one another.

“We cannot afford to look away. If we fail to speak and act now, we embolden both Christian and Muslim clerics and other influential persons to make worse statements in the coming months. That path leads only to crisis,” the Commission stated.

Consequently, it called on the Inspector General of Police, the Director General of the Department of State Services, and other relevant authorities to immediately arrest and prosecute Sheikh Jingir for hate speech and incitement.

The Commission implored religious leaders, traditional rulers, and politicians to refrain from divisive rhetoric, even as it urged Nigerians to reject identity politics and to hold leaders accountable based on competence, service delivery, and respect for human rights.

“Prosecution must proceed irrespective of status or political affiliation in order to serve as a deterrent to others who may seek to exploit religion for political gain during this election period.

“The Commission will continue to monitor compliance and will engage with security agencies, INEC, and civil society to ensure that the 2027 elections are free from hate and violence,” the statement further read.

World.title: ‘Nigeria Loses 600,000 People Annually over Administration of Medical Oxygen’
World.content:
Benjamin Nworie in Abakaliki

The Vice Chancellor of David Umahi Federal University of Health Sciences (DUFUS), Ebonyi State, Professor Jesse Uneke, has said that Nigeria is losing over 600,000 people yearly due to issues relating to the administration of medical oxygen.

Uneke, who is the Nigerian and State Lead/Principal Investigator for the EQUI-RESP Africa Research Project, disclosed this in Abakaliki, the Ebonyi State capital, during the First Stakeholders’ Engagement Event/Co-Creation Workshop on Medical Oxygen Economy organised by the university in conjunction with the University of Edinburgh, UK, supported by the National Institute for Health and Research (NIHR), UK.

He explained that the administration of medical oxygen issues was happening because there was no platform where stakeholders in the medical oxygen space could come together to discuss the research-policy interface and see how to contextualise some of the strategies against the problems for the country.

“That is why, in this phase of this project, we have decided to start with this kind of stakeholders’ engagement. I am excited that we have every key stakeholder in the medical oxygen space represented here,” Uneke said.

He opined that the project started its first phase by carrying out intervention work in three industrial areas of the state: quarry industrial site in Onueke, rice mill in Abakaliki, and timber market.

According to him, “This project has to do with respiratory health, and the idea is to come up with strategies that will lead to interventions that will improve health outcomes as far as respiratory health is concerned.

“We carried out intervention research in these three areas, where the project was able to treat between 300 and 400 people free of charge.

“We provided them with inhalers, carried out other free diagnoses and guided them on how to stay healthy regarding their respiratory health.

“We are very grateful to the founders of this project for selecting Nigeria as one of the five countries in Africa where the EQUI RESP project is being implemented.

“The project is significantly placed within the global health space because, if anything is going to happen in terms of research aimed at identifying strategies that will enhance health outcomes in Africa, Nigeria cannot be excluded.

“We are fortunate that Nigeria was not just selected as one of the five African countries. We also have Côte d’Ivoire, Kenya, South Africa, Cameroon, and, of course, Nigeria. We have two centres in Nigeria, one in Ebonyi State and one in Lagos State.

“Because the project also has to do with health policy and health systems, particularly moving evidence into policy, I was brought into the project and asked to lead the Ebonyi State research. So, we are very grateful that this project came to Nigeria and, specifically, to Ebonyi State.”

He added that: “Ebonyi State was selected because of the very excellent work that the current administration under Governor Francis Nwifuru is doing.

“Ebonyi is one of the states where partners can easily come and carry out projects in collaboration with not only the state government, but also institutions like our university and other institutions within the state, including the two teaching hospitals. There is also an enabling environment and the excellent work being done by the state Commissioner for Health.

“We are now getting into the second phase. We have moved from the community-based project to the hospital-based phase. In this hospital-based phase, we are focusing on medical oxygen and the medical oxygen economy.

“From what we have seen, this is one of the areas that is not well emphasised as far as the health sector is concerned. Nigeria is said to be losing over 600,000 people yearly due to issues related to the administration of medical oxygen. The problem is that these deaths are very preventable.”

In his remarks, the Chief Medical Director, Alex Ekwueme Federal University Teaching Hospital, Abakaliki (AE-FUTHA), Professor Robinson Onoh, described the EQUI-RESP Africa Research project as multi-country research involving Nigeria and other countries and also a multi-centre research involving different centres.

He commended Governor Francis Nwifuru for creating the enabling environment for oxygen production centres in the state, which were not in existence before he came on board.

He said: “I want to commend the governor of Ebonyi State because before he came in as governor, there was no place where oxygen was produced in Ebonyi State. But by the time he came up and created an enabling environment, we now have areas in Ebonyi State where oxygen is being produced.

“And today, we can boast of multiple centres in Ebonyi State where medical oxygen is being produced. The importance of medical oxygen was noticed during the era of COVID. That was when it became obvious that we have an issue with that in Nigeria.

“Because it was discovered that for COVID patients to survive, you need oxygen. And when you now have multiple persons needing oxygen, we now discovered that there was a problem. And that’s why oxygen is being produced in a lot of places.

“And I want to inform you that one of the oxygen production centres in Ebonyi State is located in AE-FUTHA. So, I commend the governor for that.”

World.title: CMFC Shows Bright Prospects Three Months after Transformation
World.content:
Three months after shareholders approved the change from Deap Capital

Management & Trust Plc to Critical Minerals Financing Corp Plc (CMFC), the company has started showing very bright prospects going by its latest financial results for nine months ended June 30, 2026.

The company was restructured following the entry of Banklink Africa Private

Equities Limited as a core investor, making CMFC as a specialised financing and investment Banking institution focused on developing Africa’s critical minerals, metals, and commodities sectors.

Unaudited interim financial statements of the company for the nine month ended

June 30, 2026 submitted to the NGX on August5, showed that CMFC has started to earn income and closing period with a robust cash position.

Specifically, unlike the nine months ended June 2025 when the company recorded zero income, it ended nine months in 2026 with an income of N82.641 million. A further analysis of the earnings showed that 90 per cent was recorded between

March and June 2026. Also, the company closed the period with a robust cash position of over N6 billion, a situation market analysts said gives the company opportunity for business funding to earn more income in the coming months.

Besides, the company has paid off the AMCON negotiated debt of N430 million for which they were originally claiming N2.5 billion. Also, AMCON, which used to be the largest shareholder with 16 per cent of the paid-up capital, is no longer a shareholder in the company, freeing the company from issues related to its painful past years.

Banlink Africa Private Equities Limited is now the majority shareholder and has

committed a total of N6 billion to accelerate the corporate transition of CMFC. Investors in the Nigeria Exchange Limited ( NGX) have embraced these developments in CMFC with a lot of optimism. Since August 2025 when the company and Banklink Africa Private Equities Limited started their discussions about Banklink’s strategic investment in the company to August 7, 2026 more than 1.44 billion shares of the company have been traded out of the total issued and fully paid up share capital of 1,500,660,000. This shows a turnover of 97 per cent compared to 946 million shares of the company traded between May 2023 when the company restarted operation after 10 years of inactivity and July 31, 2025. The stock has also become very liquid since the new investors showed interest in the company with daily deals being in excess of 190 transactions compared to less than 40 deals in the period from May 2023 to July 31, 2025 before Banklink Africa Private Equities Limited invested in the company. At the same time the price has moved from N1.35 per shares in the first week of August 2025 to N11.43 on January 31, 2026 before it came down from February 2026 to the present level of N3.01 on August 5, 2026 when the nine months result for 2026 was released to the market.

The result has given a complete picture of the turnaround and transformation of the company from negative shareholders fund of N2.3 billion as at September 30 , 2025 to a positive shareholders funds of N4.3 billion as at June 30, 2026, a positive movement of 272 per cent.
