Mexico’s envoys are made up of experienced personnel from the National Forestry Commission (Conafor), the National Commission of Protected Natural Areas (Conanp), state and municipal environmental agencies, Civil Protection, rural fire management brigades and civil society organizations.

The arrival of the firefighting crews comes as B.C. faces more than 100 active wildfires spanning 156 square kilometers. In addition to Mexico, British Columbia has received support from Australia, New Zealand and other Canadian provinces and territories.

With reports from Now Toronto, Publimetro, CBN Noticias and the CBC

World.title: Navy ramps up security presence in Mazatlán after high July homicide count
World.content:
After Mazatlán in July recorded its highest monthly homicide total of the year, the Mexican Navy on Saturday announced the deployment of more than 1,700 of its personnel to the Sinaloa port and resort city.

In a statement, the Navy Ministry (SEMAR) said that the deployment was occurring “within the framework of ‘Operation Sable’ Mazatlán” and was aimed at the “strengthening of security” in the city, the second largest in Sinaloa after state capital Culiacán.

The deployment comes after 36 homicides in Mazatlán in July, the city’s highest monthly total of murders in 2026, according to the newspaper El Sol de Mazatlán. It also follows the arrival of 900 Mexican Army troops in Mazatlán on July 23. The bolstering of the army’s presence in the city was part of a security reinforcement in response to a series of armed attacks.

In its statement, SEMAR said that the navy deployment reflects “the institution’s ongoing commitment to the well-being” of Mazatlán residents and tourists.

The ministry said that “operational actions will be focused on strategic areas … with the priority objective of reestablishing peace and public order and weakening illicit infrastructure that fuels schemes of violence and places the health of the population at risk.”

The term “illicit infrastructure” was a reference to clandestine drug laboratories and the cartel assets that support the distribution of narcotics, such as vehicles.

In its statement, SEMAR also issued what it called a “respectful call” for citizens and tourists to have “full confidence and certainty in the deployed forces.”

The ministry said that the central focus of the Mexican Navy’s operations is to “protect Mexican families while acting at all times with strict adherence to human rights, the proportional use of force and the current legal framework.”

“Its presence in the streets and on the coast has the sole aim of providing a safe and protected environment,” SEMAR said.

Violence in Mazatlán

Of the 36 people murdered in Mazatlán in July, 32 were men and four were women, El Sol de Mazatlán reported on Monday. The newspaper wrote that two cases were investigated as femicides, while two of the victims were minors.

Among the armed attacks in Mazatlán last month was one allegedly perpetrated by the “Los Chapitos” faction of the Sinaloa Cartel against marines, two of whom died from wounds they sustained. Marines returned fire and killed 10 criminals.

Much of the violence in Sinaloa is related to an ongoing battle between Los Chapitos, led by sons of convicted drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, and “Los Mayos,” a Sinaloa Cartel faction formerly led by Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada. The battle intensified in 2024 after Zambada was kidnapped by Joaquín Guzmán López and forced onto a plane that flew him to New Mexico. Both Zambada and Guzmán López, a son of “El Chapo,” were arrested by U.S. authorities at the Doña Ana County International Jetport in the U.S. border state in July 2024.

While the majority of the fighting between Los Chapitos and Los Mayos has occurred in Culiacán and surrounding areas, the battle has spilled into other parts of Sinaloa, including Mazatlán.

As Mexico News Daily reported last month, on July 17 and 18, six armed attacks were reported in Mazatlán in less than 24 hours, leaving four people dead and three others wounded. Between July 22 and 23, five more people were murdered.

El Sol de Mazatlán reported that episodes of violence in Mazatlán in July, including attacks on homes with firearms and explosives, occurred in rural and urban areas of the municipality of Mazatlán, including parts of the city frequented by tourists. Among those areas, the newspaper reported, were San Marcos, Lomas de Monterrey, Santa Fe, Infonavit Alarcón, Hacienda del Seminario, Lomas del Ébano, Zona Dorada and Pradera Dorada.

With reports from Expansión and El Sol de Mazatlán

World.title: Most avocado exports to the US have resumed after last week’s suspension
World.content:
Approximately 75% of avocado packing facilities in Mexico’s Michoacán state have been cleared for export following a pause in the avocado trade with the United States over security concerns, Julio Berdegué, Mexico’s advisor for international agri-food affairs and strategic issues under the USMCA, announced on Saturday.

The re-approved facilities handle roughly 85% of Michoacán’s avocado exports and the rest will be restored soon, according to Berdegué.

Mexico exports over 1 million tonnes of avocados a year, according to data from the Mexican Agriculture Ministry. Meanwhile, Michoacán contributes the highest avocado production of any Mexican state, with an export market valued at US $3.65 billion.

U.S. avocado imports from Michoacán were temporarily suspended on Wednesday after the U.S. Embassy issued an alert regarding a “threat to U.S. interests.” It marked the third time in just over four years that the United States has suspended avocado trade with Mexico for security reasons.

The embassy statement announcing the suspension did not reveal the nature of the threat, but President Sheinbaum has since said that the suspension followed a meeting at the U.S. embassy related to threats against some of the inspectors hired by the United States to monitor sanitary quality.

A meeting scheduled for the following day with an organization of avocado producers revealed that there had been an increase in extortion cases in certain regions of Michoacán.

In response to the news, Mexico worked to “rapidly strengthen” security in the state for the “immediate and gradual” resumption of the export program, said U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson.

Following the suspension, Michoacán Governor Alfredo Ramírez Bedolla deployed an extra 300 security operatives to Michoacán’s avocado-growing region “as a preventive measure.” Then, on Thursday morning, the federal Defense Ministry announced it had sent more than 1,500 soldiers to the state to “protect avocado producers and packing plants in the region.”

Exports resumed from the municipalities of Tancítaro, Tacámbaro and Uruapan, as well as the area between Morelia and Pátzcuaro, on Saturday.

To prevent future security issues, the Mexican government has established a permanent working group to monitor security in the region and prevent extortion of producers.

With reports from ABC Noticias and La Jornada

World.title: Opinion: After growing up in Mexico, was I prepared for US high school?
World.content:
My parents took a big risk when they moved their newborn twins from Manhattan to a small town in central Mexico. Yet, I couldn’t be more grateful that they did.

My family came to San Miguel de Allende when I was six months old, and I lived there until I was 15. And although we love San Miguel, my parents thought it best to send me back to the United States for high school. Having mastered the arts of reading, writing and calculating in Mexican schools, I think it’s safe to say that I learned to be a student there.

I attended SMA-based Academia Internacional from preschool through third grade. Their school emphasizes diversity and individuality, with a multicultural student body comprising both Mexican and American students. At Academia, I met my best friends and made my favorite childhood memories. I began studying French in the third grade, took advanced English classes through the Cambridge program at school, performed dance shows at the local theater and, most importantly, became queen of the monkey bars.

In fourth grade, I transferred to Colegio Newland, another bilingual and diverse school that emphasizes leadership and hands-on learning. The school follows an innovative curriculum that integrates technology into the classroom, with much of our learning centered around a platform called Knotion. At Newland, I was the middle school student body president, competed in spelling bees, traveled to geography competitions in other cities and even created a haircare brand for my entrepreneurship class. I also played tennis and took piano lessons outside of school.

As I reflect on my schooling, I realize many people assume the Mexican education system is mediocre or easy. But in reality, it challenged me while providing a foundation I needed to comfortably transition to a U.S. high school. I recall my middle school teachers constantly assigning pop quizzes, and to make matters worse, they would hand back our tests from lowest grade to highest — yikes. I struggled a lot in the subject of history, and after failing an exam, I spent weeks studying to improve my grade, only to discover that the content was fascinating. Thanks to Newland, I found a passion for it.

My parents loved raising my brother and me in San Miguel and considered it the perfect place for young children. However, they believed it made sense for us to return to the United States for high school. And like many parents, mine worried about the transition and whether I was academically prepared for a more “rigorous” school. Nevertheless, they were confident my brother and I would be okay because of the values we grew up learning. In San Miguel, people respect each other, always offer help and love to joke around. My brother and I were raised with those same values. And because of them, we adapted and made friends quickly.

I started by studying for the SSAT, the entrance exam required by most private high schools in the U.S., and it was rough. In Mexico, standardized tests barely exist, so I was unfamiliar with the idea of them. Additionally, I had never taken an exam in English, making it difficult to understand academic vocabulary. However, being fluent in Spanish often helped me identify the meaning of words with Latin roots. And ironically, my Mexican upbringing was the strongest part of my application as I drew on my childhood experiences in my essays. I wrote about Christmas, listening to mariachis and visiting Oaxaca.

After a long admissions process, I enrolled in a small boarding school in northern California. At first, the Spanish-to-English transition was difficult. My first year, I remember getting a 60% on a physics exam and feeling completely defeated. But seeing my international friends excel after going through the same transition motivated me to keep trying my best.

It’s crazy to think that I moved away from home at just 15. My parents still live in Mexico while I’m at school thousands of miles away. Of course I was scared to be on my own, but growing up between two cultures has made adapting to a new environment much easier, and California has quickly become my second home.

Throughout the two years that I’ve studied in the U.S., I’ve learned so much. My love for history persists and I have even grown to like math! (sort of). I found that attending Spanish-speaking schools didn’t hold me back, but rather, it is one of the most fascinating parts of who I am.

Now, I am going into my senior year, in which I will be editor-in-chief of the school newspaper and a prefect in the dorms. I continue to challenge myself academically with Advanced Placement (AP) and Honors courses, and can’t wait to have as much fun as possible with my friends.

As the college application process begins, I continue to write about my Mexican upbringing in every essay. I couldn’t be more grateful to have grown up and studied in such a beautiful place. I truly believe that I wouldn’t be as outgoing, determined or academically accomplished had my parents chosen to raise me in Manhattan instead.

Zella Golden grew up in San Miguel de Allende and is a senior in high school in Marin, California. Golden is completing an internship with MND.

World.title: Taylor Farms recalls its Mexico-sourced jalapeños, cuts ties with Sinaloa supplier over salmonella scare
World.content:
Just weeks after Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled iceberg lettuce products sourced from central Mexico, the Salinas, California-based company is voluntarily recalling some products that include jalapeño chiles due to concerns about possible salmonella contamination.

The decision by Taylor Fresh Foods — the parent company — is linked to a recall issued by San Diego-based Coast Citrus Distributors, which announced it was voluntarily recalling fresh jalapeños due to food safety concerns.

Taylor Fresh Foods said in a statement that it is not aware of any reported illnesses linked to its products containing jalapeños.

In its own statement, Coast Citrus said it will “no longer” source peppers from a farmer based in the northwestern Mexican state of Sinaloa, while it “seeks alternative suppliers.”

Taylor Fresh Foods also stated that it no longer purchases products from the Sinaloa farmer and “will fulfill orders with alternative suppliers.”

Besides the chiles themselves, guacamole, pico de gallo, taco salsa, burritos and spicy sandwiches are among the jalapeño-containing prepared foods included in the latest Taylor Farms recall.

Several U.S. states have been notified that all such products that feature a “Best If Used By” date up to and including Aug. 16, 2026, have been recalled. The products were sold at stores such as Kroger, Stop & Shop, Target, Whole Foods, Trader Joe’s and Walmart.

The recall comes as a result of a salmonella outbreak in the U.S. linked to jalapeño peppers imported from Mexico that had sickened 345 people in 27 states and led to 36 hospitalizations as of last Wednesday.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued an alert on Aug. 5, while the Food and Drug Administration is “working to determine if recalled jalapeños went to grocery stores,” so additional recalls could be announced.

As a result of the alert, Coast Citrus immediately agreed to recall the affected products and notify its customers. The Chipotle Mexican Grill and Qdoba restaurant chains also stopped serving the jalapeños in question.

Salmonella infections can cause diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps, and can be especially serious in young children, the elderly and people with weakened immune systems. The illness usually lasts four to seven days, and most people recover without treatment.

The latest recall comes amid heightened scrutiny of food safety in the U.S. restaurant industry, following last month’s outbreak of cyclosporiasis — a parasitic disease — linked to iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell restaurants that was reportedly sourced from central Mexico.

With reports from RTV Noticias, The Associated Press, the BBC and La Jornada

World.title: MND Local: Why is Puerto Vallarta so quiet right now?
World.content:
Walk around Puerto Vallarta right now and something feels different.

It’s not simply quieter in the way Vallarta is meant to feel during low season. There aren’t just shorter waits at restaurants, and there isn’t just a little more room on the beach.

It’s empty.

Restaurants have tables sitting unused. Tour operators are seeing smaller groups. Businesses that depend on visitors are wondering when the crowds will return.

More than just the ‘low season’

Anyone who has lived here for a while knows that summer is slower. That’s nothing new. But this one? This one feels different.

And the question being asked across the city is simple: “Where did everybody go?”

The events of Feb. 22 certainly didn’t help. The violence that followed the military operation against cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as El Mencho, brought roadblocks, burned vehicles, disruptions and international headlines. Several airlines temporarily suspended flights to Puerto Vallarta as the situation unfolded.

For those here at the time, the reality was more complicated than the images broadcast around the world. The immediate crisis passed quickly, and Puerto Vallarta reopened even faster.

But for people watching those images thousands of kilometers away, they may have been all they saw. Fear has a far longer memory than a roadblock.

A viewer in Canada or the United States doesn’t necessarily distinguish between what happened that day and what Puerto Vallarta was like the day after, let alone what it’s like six months later.

If your only knowledge of a place comes from television footage showing burning vehicles and blocked roads, you might think twice about booking a holiday there, too.

However, February isn’t the whole story.

Increased competition for travelers

Travelers have more choices now, and Puerto Vallarta is competing harder for holiday dollars. Airfares and promotions matter, and more destinations are competing for the same travelers than ever before.

People can visit somewhere new, find a cheaper flight, take advantage of a resort promotion elsewhere or simply decide after several trips to Vallarta that they would like a change of scenery.

For a family deciding where to spend a week, a few hundred dollars makes a big difference.

Travelers don’t owe Puerto Vallarta their vacation, which means the city has to keep earning their business. That includes offering solid value.

Some may point out the prices certain restaurants are charging right now.

There are places in Puerto Vallarta where prices have climbed to the point that visitors can legitimately ask whether the experience still represents good value for money, particularly when compared with other destinations.

Yet there is another side to that conversation.

The economics of tourism

Restaurant owners still have employees to pay. They have rent, electricity, ingredients, maintenance, taxes and a list of other costs that don’t disappear because it’s August and the tables are empty.

When fewer people come through the door, every customer matters more. That doesn’t make every price reasonable, nor does it mean visitors should simply pay whatever they are asked. But to encourage lower prices, businesses need both a reason and a way to reduce them.

Volume matters. A restaurant with full tables can afford to make a little less per customer. A tour operator with full boats can offer a better deal. A shop with steady foot traffic can move more product at a smaller margin.

When the customers aren’t there, the math changes. That’s where the impact of a quiet tourism season spreads far beyond the hotel lobby.

Tourism isn’t just hotels. It’s the taxi driver waiting for a fare. It’s the server whose income depends partly on tips. The boat captain. The tour guide. The massage therapist. The shop owner. The market vendor. The person cleaning vacation rentals. It’s an enormous economic ecosystem that most people don’t consider until something goes wrong.

Why locals matter

The question isn’t necessarily whether businesses have any customers. It’s whether they have enough to make the numbers work. That’s where full-time residents come in, because local residents have far more influence than they realize.

Foreign residents often fall into the trap of thinking, “I’m not a tourist. Tourism doesn’t really affect me.”

It does. Local restaurants employ neighbors. Local shops generate community income. Taxis, tours and business recommendations all drive the surrounding economy.

One response to a quiet summer is surprisingly simple: Go out.

Try the restaurant you’ve been meaning to visit. Use the independent shop with the quirky knickknack that caught your eye. Book the local tour you’ve thought about taking. Catch a bus and venture beyond the tourist zone.

Leave a review. Recommend a business. Spend money locally. And when someone back home asks whether Puerto Vallarta is still worth visiting, tell the truth.

A shared investment

Yes, there was violence on Feb. 22. Yes, Vallarta deals with crime, traffic, construction and infrastructure issues. But it also offers extraordinary natural beauty, remarkable food, generous people, neighborhoods full of character and a community that continues to evolve.

Both things can be true.

Don’t sell a fantasy. Tell people why you still live here. Long-term residents offer something tourism campaigns never will: personal credibility.

When a government campaign says Puerto Vallarta is wonderful, people expect it — it’s a sales pitch. But when someone who has lived here for five, 10 or 20 years says, “I know the problems. I know what happened. And I still think you should come,” that carries real weight.

Maybe this unusually quiet summer is a warning. Maybe it’s simply a blip. Either way, it would be foolish not to pay attention.

The question shouldn’t only be “Where did everybody go?” It should also be “What can residents do to make sure they want to come back?” That starts with remembering that tourism isn’t an entitlement; it’s an investment everyone shares.

When those tables sit empty, the impact doesn’t stop with the restaurant owner. It ripples out, eventually reaching everyone who calls Puerto Vallarta home.

And when home is hurting, no one is untouched.

Charlotte Smith is a writer and journalist based in Mexico. Her work focuses on travel, politics and community. You can follow along with her travel stories at www.salsaandserendipity.com.

World.title: Has Mexico reined in its inflation rate? Not yet, says Banxico chief
World.content:
Inflation in Mexico fell to just 0.12 points above the Bank of Mexico’s 3% target in July, but the central bank’s governor says it’s too early to declare victory in the fight against rising prices.

“At the Bank of Mexico, we’re not claiming victory yet,” Victoria Rodríguez Ceja told the newspaper El Financiero in an interview published on Monday.

Her remarks came after the national statistics agency INEGI reported on Friday that Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate was 3.12% in July, down from 3.37% in June.

Rodríguez noted that the headline rate in July was the lowest since May 2020. However, “even though inflation is practically at the [3%] target,” the Bank of Mexico will continue to seek low and stable price rises, the central bank governor told El Financiero.

INEGI’s 3.12% annual inflation reading in July was the product of 3.95% year-over-year core inflation and 0.29% non-core inflation. Annual core inflation remained reasonably high due to factors such as 4.85% year-over-year price rises for processed food, beverages and tobacco and 4.36% year-over-year increases for services.

The low non-core reading was the product of a 3.34% annual drop in prices for agricultural products (fruit, vegetables and meat) and a 3.31% increase in energy prices, including those for electricity and gasoline. Prices for agricultural products also declined on a month-over-month basis in July, falling 1.51%.

Rodríguez: Lower prices for agricultural products won’t last

Rodríguez’s interview with El Financiero came after Mexico’s headline inflation rate fell during four consecutive months from April to July. The headline rate last month was 1.47 percentage points below the 2026 peak of 4.59% in March.

Rodríguez said that the recent decline in inflation is explained, in part, by “changes in relative prices caused by favorable supply shocks.”

That was a reference to increased supply of fresh food, such as fruit and vegetables, and, as a result, lower prices for such products, as reflected in INEGI’s latest inflation data.

Rodríguez said that the Bank of Mexico doesn’t anticipate that lower prices for agricultural products will last due to “the unique characteristics of these prices and their exposure to meteorological phenomena.”

The easing of drought conditions in Mexico is a major reason why fresh food prices have recently come down, but there is no guarantee that weather-related factors won’t cause increases in the future.

Further explaining why the Bank of Mexico isn’t yet declaring victory in the fight against rising prices, Rodríguez noted that core inflation was 3.95% in July, while services were 4.36% more expensive than a year earlier. Inflation for services has recently trended down, but is still higher than the central bank would like. One factor driving the increase in prices for services was a 5.93% year-over-year increase in private school fees in July.

The Bank of Mexico’s inflation outlook

The Bank of Mexico (Banxico) forecasts that Mexico’s average annual headline inflation rate will be 3.5% in both the third and fourth quarters of 2026. In other words, the central bank anticipates that inflation will be higher between August and December than the 3.12% reading in July.

Banxico sees inflation declining in every quarter next year. It anticipates an average rate of 3.4% in Q1 of 2027, 3.3% in Q2, 3.2% in Q3 and 3% in Q4.

Those forecasts are included in a monetary policy statement released by Banxico last Thursday after its governing board voted in favor of maintaining the central bank’s key interest rate at 6.50%. Rodríguez told El Financiero that the bank’s current benchmark rate will contribute to the consolidation of “inflation’s downward path toward the [3%] target.”

However, she noted that the bank’s interest rate is subject to change based on “our assessment of the inflation outlook.”

In its Aug. 6 statement, the Bank of Mexico noted that headline inflation is “expected to converge to the target in the fourth quarter of 2027,” two quarters later than the bank anticipated when announcing its board’s interest rate decision in late June.

It said that its inflation forecasts “are subject to various risks.”

On the upside, they include “persistence of core inflation; disruptions due to foreign trade policies or to an inflationary impact from geopolitical conflicts; climate-related impacts; cost-related pressures, and a trend towards depreciation of the Mexican peso.”

On the downside, the risks include “lower-than-anticipated economic activity in Mexico and/or the United States; lower pass-through from increased costs, and lower pressures stemming from the appreciation that the national currency has been registering since last year.”

In her interview with El Financiero, Rodríguez stressed that the Bank of Mexico’s focus when making monetary policy decisions is the “inflation dynamic,” rather than economic growth, which had been very weak — or non-existent on a quarter-over-quarter basis — until a 1.5% sequential expansion in the second quarter of 2026.

With reports from El Financiero

World.title: The Colombian State Owns 62 Companies. Here’s What They’re Worth
World.content:
Colombia · Economy

Key Facts State portfolio The Colombian state controls 62 companies with a combined equity of COP 197.27 trillion (about US$62.5 billion), a finance-ministry report shows.

The oil group Ecopetrol dominates, with equity of COP 83.7 trillion (about US$26.5 billion). Finance arm Grupo Bicentenario bundles 13 financial entities worth COP 27.98 trillion (about US$8.9 billion), including the FDN, FNG and Banco Agrario.

Grupo Bicentenario bundles 13 financial entities worth COP 27.98 trillion (about US$8.9 billion), including the FDN, FNG and Banco Agrario. Wide reach The holdings span energy, finance, infrastructure, transport, insurance and utilities.

A finance-ministry tally lays bare how much of Colombia’s economy the state still owns — and how much rides on one oil company.

If you want to understand who really runs Colombia’s economy, start with the Colombia state companies the government owns outright. A new Ministry of Finance report, reported by La República on August 10, 2026, counts 62 of them, worth a combined COP 197.27 trillion (about US$62.5 billion) in equity. That is a big footprint for a market economy — and it lands just as a new, market-leaning government decides what to do with it.

Ecopetrol’s headquarters in Bogotá; the oil firm anchors the state’s corporate portfolio. (Photo: SajoR, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What the Colombia state companies portfolio holds

The list runs across the economy: energy, finance, infrastructure, transport, insurance and utilities. But it is not evenly spread. As the analyst Francisco Miranda, of Orza, put it, the portfolio is “profoundly concentrated” — varied on paper, but dominated by one name.

That name is Ecopetrol, with equity of COP 83.7 trillion (about US$26.5 billion). Two of its own subsidiaries come next: ISA, the power-transmission and infrastructure group, at COP 28.3 trillion (about US$9 billion), and Reficar, the refiner, at COP 23.37 trillion (about US$7.4 billion). Add them up and the oil complex alone accounts for most of the portfolio’s value. After that comes Grupo Bicentenario, which groups 13 state financial entities worth COP 27.98 trillion (about US$8.9 billion) together — among them the FDN development bank, the FNG guarantee fund and Banco Agrario. Within that group the FDN is the largest, at COP 9.94 trillion (about US$3.1 billion), ahead of the FNG at COP 3.87 trillion (about US$1.2 billion) and Banco Agrario at COP 3.48 trillion (about US$1.1 billion). Further down sit household names like Icetex, the student-loan agency, Colpensiones, the public pension manager, the arms maker Indumil, and a string of regional electricity firms. Between them, these companies keep the lights on, lend to farmers, back mortgages and pay pensions — which is why the state has been reluctant to let go.

The numbers behind the balance sheet

The portfolio is still making money, but momentum has slipped. In 2025, the 62 companies pulled in operating revenues of COP 174.8 trillion (about US$55 billion), down 4.5% from COP 182.9 trillion (about US$58 billion) a year earlier. Net profits came to COP 19.5 trillion (about US$6.2 billion). Four firms lost money.

The revenue drop is not trivial. Miranda linked it to the difficulties facing several sectors at once, and because the portfolio leans so heavily on Ecopetrol, the state’s corporate income rises and falls with oil. When crude is strong, the dividends flow; when it is not, the whole balance sheet feels it. That concentration is the single most important fact about these holdings — and it means the fortunes of 62 companies, and a chunk of the national budget, hang on one commodity and one firm.

Why this matters for investors and the region

This is not an academic tally. Ecopetrol is the crown jewel, and its dividends are a major source of revenue for the national budget. So the health of these companies is not just a corporate story — it is a public-finance story. When their profits shrink, the government has less to spend, which matters at a time when Colombia is wrestling with a wide fiscal deficit.

It also arrives at a hinge moment. President Abelardo de la Espriella, inaugurated on August 7, 2026, leads a market-leaning government that is rethinking the state’s role after the statist Petro years — on fracking, on Ecopetrol’s direction, and on how actively the state should own and run companies. For anyone invested in Colombia, or in the region’s energy and infrastructure names, the direction of this debate is worth following: it will shape dividend policy, investment plans and the balance between public and private hands.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many companies does the Colombian state control, and what are they worth? According to a Ministry of Finance report reported in August 2026, the state controls 62 companies with a combined equity of COP 197.27 trillion, about US$62.5 billion. They span energy, finance, infrastructure, transport, insurance and utilities. Which state company is the biggest? Ecopetrol, the oil group, is by far the largest, with equity of about COP 83.7 trillion, roughly US$26.5 billion. Its subsidiaries ISA and Reficar rank next, so the oil complex accounts for most of the portfolio value. Why does this matter for Colombia’s budget? Ecopetrol’s dividends are a major source of revenue for the national government. When the state companies earn less, the budget has less to work with, which is significant while Colombia manages a wide fiscal deficit.

Sources: La República (“De incluir a gobernar”); Colombia’s Ministry of Finance and Public Credit; Orza.

World.title: Why Argentina’s Credit Keeps Shrinking Even as Inflation Cools
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts Credit decline Real private-sector peso lending fell 1.0% month-on-month in July 2026, per First Capital Group using BCRA data.

Real private-sector peso lending fell 1.0% month-on-month in July 2026, per First Capital Group using BCRA data. Annual slide Total peso loans to the private sector dropped 1.3% in real terms year-on-year.

Total peso loans to the private sector dropped 1.3% in real terms year-on-year. Personal pain Personal loans fell 5.4% in real terms year-on-year — a tenth straight monthly decline.

Personal loans fell 5.4% in real terms year-on-year — a tenth straight monthly decline. Card crunch Credit-card lending dropped 3.7% real month-on-month and 9.8% year-on-year.

Credit-card lending dropped 3.7% real month-on-month and 9.8% year-on-year. Rate pressure The private-bank benchmark rate, TAMAR, was seen near 22.4% a year in August 2026.

The private-bank benchmark rate, TAMAR, was seen near 22.4% a year in August 2026. Policy stance The BCRA left monetary policy unchanged, prioritising disinflation over growth.

Inflation is cooling, yet lending keeps falling in real terms — a squeeze analysts have nicknamed the “absorption trap.”

Here is a puzzle at the heart of Argentina’s economy right now: inflation is cooling, yet Argentina private credit keeps shrinking. July’s figures confirm it — bank lending to the private sector fell again in real, inflation-adjusted terms. The central bank is winning its fight on prices, but businesses and households are getting less credit, not more.

The Banco Central de la República Argentina in Buenos Aires. (Photo: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

Why Argentina private credit keeps shrinking

The July numbers are not a blip. First Capital Group, using BCRA data, reported on August 6 that total peso loans to the private sector fell 1.0% in real terms from June, and 1.3% from a year earlier. Analysts have a name for the mechanism behind it: the “absorption trap,” a phrase popularised by the economist Christian Buteler. To hold down inflation and steady the peso, the authorities drain pesos from the system — through central-bank operations and, increasingly, the Treasury’s high-yield debt sales. That leaves banks with less to lend.

High rates do the rest. The private-bank benchmark rate, TAMAR, was seen near 22.4% a year in August — about 1.84% a month. At those levels borrowing is dear, fewer firms and families take loans, and rising delinquency, or mora, makes banks more cautious still. It becomes a loop: high rates, more defaults, tighter lending, and credit that stays flat on the floor.

What the July numbers show

The pain is broad. Personal loans fell 0.7% in real terms month-on-month and 5.4% year-on-year — a real decline now stretching ten months. Credit-card lending dropped 3.7% on the month and 9.8% on the year. Commercial loans, the working capital that small and medium firms live on, slipped 0.3%. Only mortgages managed to grow in real terms.

The BCRA’s own second-quarter 2026 Monetary Policy Report, presented on August 6, kept the policy stance unchanged. The message is plain: disinflation comes first, and the credit recovery will have to wait. The figures are not forecasts — they are what actually happened in July, drawn from the central bank’s own data.

How the absorption trap works

Think of the central bank as a sponge. To keep inflation down and the peso stable, it soaks up spare pesos from the banks, and the Treasury adds to the drain by rolling over debt at high rates. Every peso parked in those instruments is a peso not lent to a factory, a shop or a family. Banks take the deal because it is safe and pays well, but their spare cash for new lending shrinks in the process.

That is the trap. Tight money is needed to beat inflation, yet the same tight money starves the credit market. Ease too soon and inflation could flare again; stay tight and lending stays frozen. There is no comfortable exit, which is why the debate in Buenos Aires is less about whether the policy is working on prices — it is — and more about how long the real economy can wait.

Why it matters beyond Argentina

Credit is the fuel for a recovery, and Argentina cannot rebound without it. Small firms rely on working-capital lines to stock shelves and make payroll; households lean on instalments and cards to buy durable goods. When lending shrinks in real terms, consumption stays flat — the Buenos Aires Herald recently flagged a “red alert” as spending failed to pick up. Household loan defaults climbed to a record 12.7% in June, a measure of how stretched Argentine borrowers have become, and a warning sign for banks weighing whether to lend more.

President Javier Milei and Economy Minister Luis Caputo have made a deliberate trade-off, betting that lower inflation now is worth softer activity today. For the rest of the region, Argentina is a live test of whether that bet pays off — and a reminder that beating inflation and reviving credit do not always arrive at the same time.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the “absorption trap” in Argentina? It is a term used by analysts for a squeeze in which the central bank and the Treasury absorb pesos to control inflation and steady the currency, leaving banks with less liquidity to lend to the private sector. Why is inflation falling while private credit shrinks? Bringing inflation down requires tight money and high interest rates. Those same conditions make borrowing expensive and reduce the real value of new lending, so credit contracts even as prices cool. What did the BCRA decide in its latest report? In its second-quarter 2026 Monetary Policy Report, published on August 6, the BCRA kept its policy stance unchanged, signalling that disinflation remains its priority.

Sources: First Capital Group; Banco Central de la República Argentina (BCRA); Infobae; La Nación; Ámbito; Buenos Aires Herald.

World.title: Explosive Drones Are the New Weapon in Colombia’s Conflict
World.content:
Key Facts Drone cluster Explosive-laden drones struck police posts, a town hall and a military target in Colombia in early August 2026.

Explosive-laden drones struck police posts, a town hall and a military target in Colombia in early August 2026. Officer killed A drone strike on the San Roque substation in Cesar killed Subintendente Argemiro Rodelo Canchila on the night of Aug 7.

A drone strike on the San Roque substation in Cesar killed Subintendente Argemiro Rodelo Canchila on the night of Aug 7. Tolima hit Drones struck Rioblanco’s town hall and police station on Aug 9; a separate attempt on a Planadas base was intercepted.

Drones struck Rioblanco’s town hall and police station on Aug 9; a separate attempt on a Planadas base was intercepted. Tactics, not training Groups are using Ukraine-war-style drones, but there is no credible evidence they were trained in Ukraine.

Groups are using Ukraine-war-style drones, but there is no credible evidence they were trained in Ukraine. Antioquia risk Police say about 35 stations have anti-drone countermeasures, concentrated in the Bajo Cauca region.

Police say about 35 stations have anti-drone countermeasures, concentrated in the Bajo Cauca region. Hardline response President de la Espriella’s forces killed six armed-group members over the weekend of Aug 9–10.

Colombia · Security

Explosive drones have become a routine weapon for Colombia’s armed groups, with a deadly police strike and scattered attacks in early August.

You may have seen news of the Colombia drone attacks in early August 2026, but the pattern is what matters. This was not a one-off. A cluster of strikes with explosive-laden drones hit the country’s southwest and north, and the army has named specific FARC dissident fronts. The ELN and the Clan del Golfo are in the picture too. If you live in or invest in rural Colombia, it marks a sobering shift in how the conflict is fought.

Inside the wave of Colombia drone attacks

The deadliest incident came on the night of August 7, 2026, in Cesar. A drone loaded with explosives struck the police substation in San Roque, in the municipality of Curumaní, killing Subintendente Argemiro Rodelo Canchila, 43, who had 18 years of service. This was a deliberate strike on a small, fixed post — and it shows that police stations are now targets from the air.

Two days later, on August 9, drones hit the town hall and a police station in Rioblanco, Tolima. No one was hurt; the army blamed the Ismael Ruiz front of FARC dissidents. On August 7, a separate attempt targeted the General Domingo Caicedo infantry battalion in Planadas, also in Tolima — but the army said it detected and neutralised the explosive-laden drones before they reached the base. The targets — town halls, police posts, an army battalion — point to a coordinated effort to test defences and challenge state authority.

A tactic borrowed from Ukraine — not training

Here is the crucial point. Credible reporting says these groups are adopting Ukraine-war-style drone tactics: cheap commercial drones modified to drop explosives, and first-person-view (FPV) drones flown straight into a target. There is no reliable evidence that any of them were trained in Ukraine. The method has spread; the training claim has not been shown. Do not mistake one for the other.

That distinction matters for risk. You do not need an army to run this kind of attack — just a commercial drone, some explosives and the know-how to marry the two. That lowers the barrier for every armed group in the region. In Antioquia, the police commander, Colonel Luis Muñoz, said about 35 stations and substations now have countermeasures, with the risk concentrated in the Norte, Nordeste and Bajo Cauca subregions — Segovia, Ituango, Cáceres, Tarazá and Caucasia. The catch: anti-drone systems are mostly under army control, and they are not everywhere.

Why this matters for investors and residents

A drone strike on a rural police post is not a distant worry. Rural investment — mining, agriculture, energy — depends on secure supply chains and safe staff movement, and a hit near a mine or a farm is a direct operational threat. Roads matter too. On August 8, attackers detonated explosives that destroyed a toll booth under construction on the Pan-American Highway near Santander de Quilichao, in the Mondomo sector of Cauca. Accounts of injuries conflict, with leading Colombian outlets reporting none, and FARC dissidents linked to alias “Iván Mordisco” are suspected, though authorities had not formally confirmed responsibility.

An explosives attack on a toll booth is an attack on mobility and trade, not just a building. And the bigger story runs past Colombia: cheap drone warfare is spreading to non-state actors across Latin America, and Colombia is simply the frontline. If these tactics work here, they will surface elsewhere — which is why security planners around the region are watching.

The government’s response

President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office on August 7, is leaning hard into a “firm hand” security line. Over the weekend of August 9–10, security forces killed six members of illegal armed groups — four FARC dissidents in Meta and two Clan del Golfo members in Antioquia. It is a clear signal of intent.

But hardline operations have limits without technology. The anti-drone systems are thin on the ground, and smaller-town police posts stay exposed. The drones are not going away, so the state will need sustained investment in detection and interception. Until then, the southwest and northern subregions like Bajo Cauca will remain fragile — and the sky above them contested.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the Colombia drone attacks of August 2026? They are a cluster of explosive-drone strikes on police posts, a town hall and a military target in the southwest and north in early August 2026. The army attributed several to FARC dissident fronts. The ELN and the Clan del Golfo also pose a threat. Were these groups trained in Ukraine? No. Credible reporting indicates armed groups are adopting Ukraine-war-style drone tactics, using cheap commercial drones modified to drop explosives. There is no reliable evidence of Ukrainian training; the tactic has spread on its own. Which regions face the highest drone risk? Antioquia is a key area, especially the Norte, Nordeste and Bajo Cauca subregions, including Segovia, Ituango, Cáceres, Tarazá and Caucasia. Tolima, Cesar and Cauca also saw attacks in early August 2026.

Sources: Infobae Colombia; El Espectador; Vanguardia; Pulzo; Semana; El Pilón; Blu Radio; Al Jazeera.

World.title: Peru’s New Government Takes Four Spending Laws to Court
World.content:
Peru · Economy

Key Facts Legal challenge Finance Minister Elmer Cuba and the MEF will file constitutional challenges against four spending laws passed by the previous Congress.

Finance Minister Elmer Cuba and the MEF will file constitutional challenges against four spending laws passed by the previous Congress. Which laws They cover teacher pensions, military and police pensions, CAS worker bonuses, and a CAFAE incentive homologation.

They cover teacher pensions, military and police pensions, CAS worker bonuses, and a CAFAE incentive homologation. Teacher cost The teacher-pension law carries a reported cost of about S/8 billion a year (about US$2.4 billion) for more than 160,000 retired educators.

The teacher-pension law carries a reported cost of about S/8 billion a year (about US$2.4 billion) for more than 160,000 retired educators. Security cost The military and police pension law is put at around S/46 billion in present value (about US$13.6 billion) by the Fiscal Council and the MEF.

The military and police pension law is put at around S/46 billion in present value (about US$13.6 billion) by the Fiscal Council and the MEF. Fiscal rule The MEF argues the laws threaten Peru’s fiscal rule and the government’s control of public spending.

The MEF argues the laws threaten Peru’s fiscal rule and the government’s control of public spending. No ruling yet No case number or filing date has been reported; this is an announced challenge, not a court decision.

Peru’s new government is moving to strike down pension and spending laws it says blow a hole in the budget, setting up a fight with Congress.

If you track Latin American markets, the fight over Peru pension laws is worth watching. It has become the first big clash between President Keiko Fujimori’s new economic team and the previous Congress — and the outcome could shape how investors read the country’s famous fiscal discipline.

The Legislative Palace, seat of the Congress of Peru in Lima. (Photo: Manuel González Olaechea, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What the fight over Peru pension laws is about

Under President Keiko Fujimori’s new government, Finance Minister Elmer Cuba is preparing formal constitutional challenges — demandas de inconstitucionalidad — at Peru’s Constitutional Court. The targets are four spending laws approved by the previous Congress. These are not technical tweaks; they are major, recurring commitments the new economic team says were enacted without funding.

The four laws are Ley 32581 (teacher pensions), Ley 32561 (military and police pensions), Ley 32563 (bonus and CTS payments for CAS contract workers), and Ley 32424 (a CAFAE incentive for DL 276 regime workers). The two pension laws carry the biggest price tags. The MEF puts the teacher-pension law at roughly S/8 billion a year — about US$2.4 billion — for more than 160,000 retired and former teachers. The military and police pension law is far larger over time: the Fiscal Council and the MEF estimate its cost at around S/46 billion in present value, or about US$13.6 billion — the full future liability, not a single year’s bill.

The government’s argument

Minister Cuba has been blunt. In his own words: “El Congreso no tiene en ninguna parte del mundo desarrollado la iniciativa de gasto. El gasto lo maneja el Ejecutivo.” That translates as: Congress has no spending initiative anywhere in the developed world; the Executive manages spending. It is a direct challenge to the legislature’s role in setting fiscal policy. Cuba has said the government picked the four laws that “pueden mover la aguja” — that can move the needle — on the public accounts.

The MEF’s position is that these laws undermine the fiscal rule Peru has used for years to keep its finances credible. The new Fujimori government leans toward fiscal discipline and has staffed the economic team with pro-market figures. It views the laws as unfunded mandates that would eventually force tax hikes, more debt, or cuts elsewhere.

Why this matters for investors and the region

Peru has long been a poster child for fiscal discipline in Latin America — low debt, a strong central bank, and steady investment. That reputation is now being tested, and the test is structural: who really decides how public money is spent, the Executive or Congress? If the government’s challenges succeed, it reinforces the idea that Peru’s fiscal anchors hold. If they fail, it sets a precedent where the legislature can pass expensive laws without the government’s sign-off — the kind of thing that pressures a country’s credit rating.

Peru still runs one of the lowest public-debt ratios in Latin America — a big reason it holds an investment-grade credit rating that keeps its borrowing costs down. That standing is the asset the MEF says it is defending. A steady run of costly, unfunded laws is exactly the kind of drift that erodes it over time, and rating agencies watch these fights closely.

If you hold Peruvian assets, or regional funds that include them, that is the signal to watch. It also shows how the Fujimori government will handle an opposition-leaning Congress that still holds real institutional power — and whether Lima’s reputation for keeping spending in check survives its first real test of the new term.

What happens next

The Constitutional Court will first decide whether to admit the challenges, then rule on the merits — a process that can take months. No case number or filing date has been reported yet. In the meantime, the politics are heating up: teachers’ unions are already defending Ley 32581 as the correction of a historical injustice and a path to dignified pensions after decades of service. That is a powerful counter-narrative, and it will not be easy for the government to face down.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which four laws is Peru’s MEF challenging? The four laws are Ley 32581 on teacher pensions, Ley 32561 on military and police pensions, Ley 32563 on bonuses and CTS for CAS contract workers, and Ley 32424 on a CAFAE incentive homologation. All were passed by the previous Congress and now face constitutional challenges. How much do the pension laws cost? The MEF puts the teacher-pension law at about S/8 billion a year, roughly US$2.4 billion, for more than 160,000 retired teachers. The military and police pension law is estimated at around S/46 billion in present value, about US$13.6 billion, by the Fiscal Council and the MEF. These figures come from the government and its fiscal watchdog. What does the government want the court to do? The government wants the Constitutional Court to declare the laws unconstitutional, arguing that Congress cannot create spending obligations on its own. The MEF says the laws threaten the fiscal rule and could strain public accounts.

Sources: El Popular; Gestión; La República; Infobae Perú; Peru’s Consejo Fiscal and Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF).

World.title: El Niño Turns Central America’s Dry Corridor Into a Hunger Zone
World.content:
Key Facts Guatemala hunger 3.2 million people — about 17% — face acute food insecurity in July–September 2026, per SESAN.

3.2 million people — about 17% — face acute food insecurity in July–September 2026, per SESAN. Honduras crisis 1.8 million already affected, and up to 2.2 million possible by year-end, per UNAH.

1.8 million already affected, and up to 2.2 million possible by year-end, per UNAH. Global warning A stronger El Niño could add 49 million people to acute hunger worldwide, per the WFP.

A stronger El Niño could add 49 million people to acute hunger worldwide, per the WFP. Regional reach More than 16 million people affected in Latin America and the Caribbean, with Central America the sharpest riser, per the WFP.

More than 16 million people affected in Latin America and the Caribbean, with Central America the sharpest riser, per the WFP. Emergency declared Marcovia, in southern Honduras, cited 15,000 families hit by drought and crop loss.

Marcovia, in southern Honduras, cited 15,000 families hit by drought and crop loss. Livestock losses More than 400 cattle have died in southern Honduras, reports La Prensa.

Central America · Climate

Drought is tightening across Central America’s Dry Corridor, and failed harvests are turning hunger into an everyday reality.

If you follow Latin American markets or live in the region, the El Niño food crisis deserves your attention now. The parched fields of Honduras and Guatemala are already feeding through to grocery bills, migration pressure and regional stability — and the worst of the lean season is still ahead.

El Niño Turns Central America’s Dry Corridor Into a Hunger Zone. (Photo internet reproduction)

What is happening in the Dry Corridor

The Dry Corridor runs through Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua — a strip of land that has always known tough farming. But this El Niño is landing at the worst possible moment, bringing drought, erratic rains and extreme heat just as farmers should be planting maize and beans.

In Guatemala, the food-security secretariat SESAN, using the IPC/CIF phase scale, projects 3.2 million people — about 17% of the population — in acute food insecurity between July and September 2026. In practice that means skipping meals, selling off animals or tools, and eating less to get by.

In Honduras, the crisis is already here. The food-security observatory at UNAH, the national university, estimated on August 6, 2026 that 1.8 million people face a food crisis today, a figure that could climb to 2.2 million by year-end if the rains stay away. These are families farming small hillside plots, dependent on a single harvest to eat for the year.

What the El Niño food crisis looks like on the ground

Talk to farmers in southern Honduras and you hear the same thing. The corn is stunted, the bean plants are withered, the wells are drying up. On August 5, 2026, the municipality of Marcovia in Choluteca declared a state of emergency for more than 15,000 families hit by water shortages and crop losses.

Honduras’s emergency agency COPECO has put 75 municipalities on yellow alert and 49 on green alert — a sign the strain is spreading well beyond one district. La Prensa reported on August 5, 2026 that the drought has already killed more than 400 head of cattle, and warned of higher prices for grains, milk and meat in the months ahead if the rains do not return.

This is not just a bad season. FEWS NET’s El Niño 2026–2027 outlook flags the Dry Corridor as a zone of concern. The region is still recovering from earlier climate shocks, and high fuel and fertilizer prices make it far harder for small farmers to bounce back. They are caught in a trap: no rain to grow food, and no money to buy it.

Why this matters for Latin America and investors

A drought in rural Honduras is not a local footnote. The Dry Corridor is a major source of staple food for the region, so when maize and bean harvests fail, prices climb in markets from Guatemala City to San Pedro Sula. That hits urban families too, and feeds inflation in economies that are already stretched.

There is also a slower consequence: migration. Drought, crop loss, poverty and hunger are well-documented drivers of migration pressure from the region — when people cannot feed their children, they move. That means more strain on borders and more political noise across the hemisphere. For investors, the takeaway is plain: Central American food supply chains are exposed to climate shocks, and prices can spike fast. The WFP warned around August 5–6, 2026 that a strengthening El Niño could push an extra 49 million people worldwide into acute food insecurity, lifting the global total to about 274 million by the end of 2027. For Latin America and the Caribbean, it put the figure at more than 16 million people affected, with Central America projected to see the largest proportional increase. That is not a distant scenario — it is happening now.

Aid agencies are already repositioning. The WFP says it is scaling up preparedness across the region, and Honduras has begun channelling emergency support to the hardest-hit municipalities. But funding for these responses is chronically tight, and the lean season — when last year’s stocks run out before the new harvest — is only beginning. The next rains, or their absence, will decide how deep this crisis runs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which countries are most affected by the El Niño food crisis? Guatemala and Honduras are the hardest hit this cycle, across the Dry Corridor. Guatemala’s SESAN projects 3.2 million people in acute food insecurity between July and September 2026, and UNAH estimates 1.8 million in Honduras, potentially rising to 2.2 million by year-end. How does El Niño cause food shortages? El Niño shifts weather patterns, bringing drought to some areas and heavy rain to others. In the Dry Corridor it means below-average rainfall and higher temperatures, which damage maize and bean harvests. FEWS NET adds that weak recovery from earlier shocks and high fuel and fertilizer prices make the impact worse. What is the global scale of this El Niño event? The WFP estimates that a strengthening El Niño could push an additional 49 million people worldwide into acute food insecurity, bringing the global total to about 274 million by the end of 2027. In Latin America and the Caribbean, it expects more than 16 million people affected, with Central America seeing the largest proportional rise.

Sources: Guatemala’s SESAN (IPC/CIF); OBSAN-UNAH (Honduras); UN World Food Programme; FEWS NET; COPECO; La Prensa (Honduras).

World.title: Why Banxico’s New Bond Tool Is Testing Its Autonomy
World.content:
Mexico · Economy

Key Facts Rate held Banxico kept its benchmark at 6.50% on Aug 6, 2026, in a unanimous vote.

Banxico kept its benchmark at 6.50% on Aug 6, 2026, in a unanimous vote. Inflation low July 2026 inflation fell to a six-year low, though the bank sees the next declines coming more slowly.

July 2026 inflation fell to a six-year low, though the bank sees the next declines coming more slowly. New power From Aug 17, Banxico can buy up to 100 billion pesos (about US$5.8 billion) of Cetes and Bondes F per quarter.

From Aug 17, Banxico can buy up to 100 billion pesos (about US$5.8 billion) of Cetes and Bondes F per quarter. Secondary only The purchases happen in the secondary market to ease temporary liquidity shortages — not to finance the government.

The purchases happen in the secondary market to ease temporary liquidity shortages — not to finance the government. Legal firewall Article 28 of the Constitution and Articles 11 and 12 of the Banxico Law still bar direct government financing.

Article 28 of the Constitution and Articles 11 and 12 of the Banxico Law still bar direct government financing. Board intact Governor Victoria Rodríguez Ceja led the five-member board, with no dissent and no political pressure.

A new emergency tool tests how the market reads Mexico’s central bank independence — but the legal guardrails, specialists say, are still firmly in place.

You may have seen headlines suggesting Mexico’s central bank just cracked open the door to government meddling. That is not what happened. This is a new liquidity tool, and it helps to understand why it does not erode Banxico autonomy. Since 1994, the bank has run independently, and a constitutional ban on directly financing the government still holds. The new power, effective Aug 17, 2026, lets the bank buy up to 100 billion pesos (about US$5.8 billion) of Cetes and Bondes F each quarter — but only on the secondary market, and only to relieve temporary cash shortages. That is a long way from printing money to cover the budget.

The Banco de México headquarters in Mexico City. (Photo: ProtoplasmaKid, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What the new tool means for Banxico autonomy

Here is the short version: Banxico autonomy is not being eroded, according to most specialists who have read the measure. The tool works like the exchange commission’s dollar auctions — used only in specific, stressed moments, not as a daily habit. Luis Gonzalí drew that comparison, noting that months can pass between uses. Barclays analysts stress the bank “cannot flood the system with liquidity,” because the constitutional limits still bind. The market’s nervous reaction, economist Gabriela Siller notes, simply shows that investors pay close attention to what the central bank does — which is healthy, not alarming.

Skeptics exist. Guillermo Barba has argued that once a central bank grants itself a power this large, the real question is no longer whether it will use it, but when. It is a fair point about precedent. But note the context: there is no statement from President Claudia Sheinbaum or the Finance Ministry attacking the bank’s independence — no political pressure, no attempted takeover. The worry is about perception, in a market already watchful after Mexico’s judicial reform. For now, there is no concrete spillover into Banxico’s governance.

Timing is part of why this gets read so closely. Mexico’s overhaul of its courts — including electing judges by popular vote — has left some investors uneasy about the strength of the country’s institutions. In that climate, anything that could blur the line between the central bank and the government draws sharper scrutiny than it would in calmer times. That is exactly why Banxico went out of its way to spell out the limits.

How the intervention actually works

Picture a bank that holds government bonds and suddenly needs cash. Normally it sells them. But in a panic, buyers vanish. Banxico can step in, buy the securities, hand over temporary cash, and sell them back later. That is a classic liquidity operation — not financing, because the government gets no new money. The trade sits between the central bank and market players such as banks, brokerages and pension funds, never with the Treasury. The 100 billion peso (about US$5.8 billion) quarterly cap — up to roughly 400 billion pesos (about US$23 billion) a year — is generous but bounded, and the prohibitions in Article 28 and Articles 11 and 12 stay untouched.

The timing helps explain the caution. July inflation hit a six-year low, yet Banxico expects the decline to slow, which is why it held rates at 6.50%. The new tool simply gives the bank another way to handle short-term market stress without touching rates — a technical upgrade, not a political one.

Why Latin American readers and investors should care

This is bigger than Mexico. Across the region, central banks live or die by credibility. If markets ever decided Banxico had been captured, the peso would weaken, bond yields would jump, and money would leave — and not only from Mexico, as investors re-rate the whole region. So this is a test of whether an independent bank can adopt a new tool without denting its mandate. Peers in Brazil, Colombia and Chile will be watching. If you hold pesos, reais or Chilean pesos, your returns rest on trust in these institutions.

The reassuring part: the safeguards are strong, and the people who follow this daily say autonomy holds. The signal to watch is simple — how often the tool is actually used. Rare, emergency-only use supports independence; frequent use would be the red flag.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does this let the government borrow money from Banxico? No. The law bars direct financing of the government. Purchases happen only in the secondary market, so Banxico buys securities from banks and funds, not from the Treasury, and the government receives no new money. Why is the market concerned if the rules are clear? Investors focus on perception and precedent. They worry that a large new power, even a well-guarded one, could be widened later. Analysts counter that the secondary-market-only scope and the constitutional limits keep that risk small. What should an investor watch to judge Banxico independence? Watch how often and how heavily the tool is used, and whether anyone moves to change Article 28 or the Banxico Law. Occasional use in genuine liquidity emergencies supports autonomy. Sustained or growing use would raise real concerns.

Sources: El Universal; Banco de México; Reuters; Bloomberg; Barclays; INEGI.

World.title: Indonesia Pitches a Mercosur Trade Deal, With Brazil as the Broker
World.content:
Brazil · Trade

Key Facts First step Indonesia proposed a narrow preferential trade agreement (PTA) with Mercosur at the BRICS Trade Ministers’ Meeting in Jaipur, India, on Aug 7, 2026.

Indonesia proposed a narrow preferential trade agreement (PTA) with Mercosur at the BRICS Trade Ministers’ Meeting in Jaipur, India, on Aug 7, 2026. Stalled CEPA The broader Indonesia-Mercosur Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement is stuck over how wide and deep the deal should be.

The broader Indonesia-Mercosur Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement is stuck over how wide and deep the deal should be. Consensus ask Jakarta asked Brazil to bridge differences and build alignment among Mercosur members on the PTA.

Jakarta asked Brazil to bridge differences and build alignment among Mercosur members on the PTA. Open response Brazil’s development, industry, trade and services minister, Márcio Elias Rosa, said Brasília will study the proposal.

Brazil’s development, industry, trade and services minister, Márcio Elias Rosa, said Brasília will study the proposal. Trade heft Indonesia-Brazil trade was about US$7 billion in 2025 and US$3.53 billion in the first half of 2026.

Indonesia-Brazil trade was about US$7 billion in 2025 and US$3.53 billion in the first half of 2026. Asia pivot Mercosur is already advancing deals with the EU and Japan and eyeing one with China as it diversifies away from US trade friction.

Indonesia wants a faster, narrower trade pact with South America’s big bloc — and it is asking Brazil to make it happen.

If you have been watching Mercosur’s busy year, you know the bloc has become the emerging world’s most sought-after trade partner. Now add Indonesia. In early August, Jakarta’s trade minister floated an Indonesia-Mercosur trade deal in slimmed-down form — skip the full agreement for now and do a smaller, quicker one instead. Nothing is signed. But it tells you a lot about where global trade is heading, and where your next opportunity might sit.

Indonesia Pitches a Mercosur Trade Deal, With Brazil as the Broker. (Photo: Internet reproduction)

What Indonesia is proposing

Indonesia’s trade minister, Budi Santoso, used the BRICS Trade Ministers’ Meeting in Jaipur, India, to suggest a fresh path. His pitch was a preferential trade agreement, or PTA — a focused deal that cuts tariffs on a selected list of goods. Think of it as trade’s express lane — faster and easier than a sprawling comprehensive pact.

Why the change of tack? The bigger Indonesia-Mercosur Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, or CEPA, has stalled. The problem is not Jakarta’s appetite — it is friction inside Mercosur over how broad the deal should be. So Indonesia asked Brazil for help. “We hope Brazil can help build consensus among Mercosur members and advance negotiations for the Indonesia-Mercosur PTA,” Santoso said. Brazil’s development, industry, trade and services minister, Márcio Elias Rosa, replied that Brasília is open to more talks and will study the proposal. No timeline was set. This is a proposal, not a deal.

What the Indonesia-Mercosur trade deal would cover

Here is where it gets interesting for commodities. Indonesia is the world’s biggest palm oil producer. Brazil and Argentina are soy oil powers. Those two oils compete head-to-head in global food and biofuel markets, and a PTA would help decide which one gets the tariff edge in the other’s backyard. A deal would likely cover tariffs on goods ranging from vegetable and animal fats to vehicles, electrical machinery, rubber, mineral fuels, sugar, cotton, tobacco and metal ores.

Look at the current picture. In the first half of 2026, Indonesia-Brazil trade reached US$3.53 billion. Indonesia sold Brazil about US$1.17 billion of goods — palm oil, vehicles and rubber — while buying roughly US$2.36 billion of Brazilian farm residues, sugar, cotton and ores. That leaves Jakarta with a deficit of about US$1.19 billion. A PTA is, in part, Indonesia’s attempt to rebalance that ledger by getting more of its products onto Brazilian shelves.

There is a bigger strategic thread here too. Indonesia has spent recent years chasing new markets to cut its reliance on China and the West — from a fresh pact with the EU to joining BRICS. Latin America is one of the last large regions where it has little preferential access. A Mercosur deal, even a narrow one, would plant a flag and give its exporters a foothold before rivals lock in their own terms.

Why Latin American readers should care

This is not just a Jakarta-Brasília affair. It is a window into Mercosur’s strategic pivot. The bloc is already living with the EU-Mercosur agreement, which took provisional effect on May 1, 2026. It launched talks with Japan in June, is eyeing a deal with China, and now Indonesia — a BRICS member since January 2025, with more than 280 million people — wants a foothold. That is a lot of suitors at one dance.

For Brazilian and Argentine agribusiness, the prize is Asian market access at preferential rates. For Indonesian palm oil, South America is a growing market and a hedge. And with the United States raising tariffs on major partners, every new Mercosur deal trims the bloc’s reliance on any single buyer. If you invest or live in the region, watch the farm supply chain: if this advances, expect ripples in vegetable-oil pricing and machinery flows.

What happens next

Do not expect a quick signature. Brazil has to study the proposal, then take it to Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay and Bolivia — a full Mercosur member since 2024. Each has its own farm lobbies and industrial priorities, which is exactly why the CEPA stalled. The PTA route lowers the bar to a smaller menu of goods. Get consensus, and Indonesia is through the door; miss it, and the bigger deal stays parked. Either way, Southeast Asia is signalling that it is serious about Latin America.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Indonesia-Mercosur trade deal signed? No. It is a proposal. Indonesia suggested a PTA at the BRICS meeting in August 2026 as a first step toward a broader agreement. Brazil said it will study the idea. No timeline was set, and formal negotiations have not started. What is the difference between a PTA and a CEPA? A PTA is a narrow agreement that cuts tariffs on specific, selected goods, so it is quicker to negotiate. A CEPA is comprehensive, covering goods, services, investment and trade rules, which makes it far more complex and slower to finalize. Why does Indonesia want a deal with Mercosur? Indonesia wants preferential access for its palm oil, vehicles, rubber and machinery, while narrowing its trade deficit with Brazil. It also wants a foothold in South America as Mercosur signs deals with the EU, Japan and others. For a country of more than 280 million people, early access matters.

Sources: Indonesian Ministry of Trade via ANTARA News; MLex; Brazil’s Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services (MDIC); Nikkei Asia; European Council.

01 The session in one read

Copper futures, via the CPER tracking fund, settled at US$40.18 on Monday, a 0.70% rise that animated the largest mining listings in the Americas. The movement was neither frantic nor speculative; it was a methodical climb built on solid, if unglamorous, industrial consumption.

The two giants of the Andean copper belt moved in lockstep. Southern Copper, deeply embedded in Peru’s southern mining corridor and Mexico’s Sonora state, advanced 0.53% to US$200.11. Freeport-McMoRan, whose Cerro Verde operation in Peru ranks among the world’s biggest concentrating sites, rose 1.28% to US$70.51.

Assessment — Demand persistence, not a spike HIGH The session lacked a single explosive catalyst, which is precisely why the gains matter. Prices advanced because everyday demand from manufacturers and infrastructure builders remains resilient, not because of a temporary supply scare. This persistent bid, anchored in electrification and Chinese factory activity, rewarded patient holders of miners like Freeport-McMoRan and Southern Copper. The variable to watch is any shift in China’s fiscal support for grid spending, as that flow of orders is the quiet engine beneath the copper market right now.

02 The board

The trio of copper proxies flashed uniformly green on Monday. The CPER fund, designed to mirror futures contracts rather than physical metal, printed US$40.18 at the settlement. The gain of 0.70% set the pace for mining equities, which typically amplify the commodity’s moves.

Southern Copper’s US$200.11 close was the more muted of the two, its 0.53% gain trailing Freeport-McMoRan’s 1.28% rise to US$70.51. Both stocks sit on vast proven and probable copper reserves across Chile and Peru, making their daily swings a reliable barometer of investor conviction in the industrial metal’s trajectory.

03 What moved it

The session’s primary driver was the enduring pull of Chinese demand. Order books for copper-intensive goods, from electric wiring to transformers, remained full as state-backed infrastructure programs kept consumption steady. This wasn’t a speculative frenzy triggered by a single policy announcement, but rather the hum of regular procurement.

Layered on top was the energy transition’s insatiable appetite for copper. Wind turbines, solar farms, and a growing fleet of electric vehicles require multiples more of the metal than their fossil-fuel equivalents. Monday’s incremental price rise captured that slow-building structural deficit, which continues to absorb supply even when other commodities face headwinds.

04 The Latin American read

For Chile and Peru, Monday’s equity board translated a quiet day in the pits into measurable national wealth. Chile, the world’s top copper producer, sees its fiscal resources tied directly to the metal’s fortunes, and a rising CPER and Southern Copper share price feeds directly into the outlook for Santiago’s spending plans.

Peru, the number-three supplier globally, felt the session through Southern Copper and Freeport-McMoRan’s extensive local operations. The 0.53% gain in Southern Copper, a company with immense reserves in Peru’s Arequipa and Moquegua regions, lifted the entire mining-weighted Lima exchange in after-market sentiment, reinforcing the country’s deep economic link to the red metal.

05 The names to watch

Southern Copper, now trading at US$200.11 after a 0.53% daily climb, remains the purest large-cap play on Andean copper. Its low-cost production profile across Peru and Mexico makes its share price acutely responsive to even modest futures advances.

Freeport-McMoRan, at US$70.51, adds a global dimension with large-scale leaching and milling operations in South America and North America. Its 1.28% gain reflects not just copper’s direction but also confidence in stable operational permits and disciplined capital spending across its Cerro Verde and Grasberg interests.

06 The outlook

Copper’s ability to rise without a crisis catalyst signals a market that is structurally tight. With Chinese grid investment pressuring daily supply and no major mine ramp-up imminent in Chile or Peru, the path of least resistance for CPER and its associated miners appears gently upward, barring a sudden macroeconomic shock.

07 What to watch

Chinese grid-ordering data: Any uptick or downtick in China’s State Grid procurement will move copper directly, as it remains the single largest institutional buyer of refined copper wire and cable.

Any uptick or downtick in China’s State Grid procurement will move copper directly, as it remains the single largest institutional buyer of refined copper wire and cable. Peruvian community negotiations: Southern Copper’s projects in Arequipa and Moquegua frequently face community dialogue; a disruption would tighten the supply picture and could send Freeport-McMoRan’s shares higher on scarcity.

Southern Copper’s projects in Arequipa and Moquegua frequently face community dialogue; a disruption would tighten the supply picture and could send Freeport-McMoRan’s shares higher on scarcity. Energy transition bill of materials: Quarterly updates from wind, solar and EV manufacturers on copper content per unit will signal whether structural demand is still accelerating or plateauing.

Quarterly updates from wind, solar and EV manufacturers on copper content per unit will signal whether structural demand is still accelerating or plateauing. Chilean constitutional mining debate: Any revival of royalty or nationalisation discussions in Santiago would immediately affect Southern Copper’s risk premium and alter the regional investment case for copper majors.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did copper rise on Monday?

The CPER fund gained 0.70% to US$40.18 because steady Chinese industrial buying and ongoing energy-transition orders kept demand firm, lifting futures and mining shares in tandem.

How did Southern Copper perform?

Southern Copper added 0.53% to US$200.11 on Monday, trailing Freeport-McMoRan among major copper miners for the session, driven by its deep exposure to Peruvian and Mexican production.

What is CPER?

CPER is an exchange-traded fund that tracks copper futures rather than the spot price of physical copper; its Monday settlement was US$40.18, reflecting a 0.70% daily increase in the futures market.

Are Chile and Peru still the top copper producers?

Yes, Chile is the world’s number-one copper producer and Peru ranks third, behind the Democratic Republic of the Congo; together they supply a large portion of the global concentrate, making Monday’s share moves in Southern Copper and Freeport-McMoRan particularly relevant for Latin American investors.
