World.title: Young women collapse one after another at Budapest concert: police investigate as victims recount same story
World.content:
Police have launched an investigation into suspected drug possession following a series of medical incidents during DJ Balázs Sebestyén’s show (DJ OTI), Telex reported on Monday, citing the Budapest Police Headquarters. Several women fell ill during Saturday’s concert, amid media reports that GHB – known in Hungary as “gina” – may have been slipped into their drinks. When combined with alcohol, the drug can cause paralysis of the central nervous system.

Young women collapsed one after another at Budapest concert

In response to questions from the newspaper, Budapest police said investigators had already interviewed several witnesses and were seeking to establish the full circumstances of what happened. One young man posted on Sunday that his sister may have been drugged without her knowledge during the party. Shortly afterwards, a 39-year-old woman described in a video how she had collapsed almost immediately after drinking from her glass, MTI wrote.

The organisers of the Sziget Festival also responded to the reports on Sunday evening. They said that the DJ OTI production was not part of the programme of the Sziget Festival. They added that they were “deeply outraged” by the accounts circulating on social media and urged anyone affected by a similar incident to contact the police. The organisers added that they would assist the investigation.

Sziget Festival opens its gates today. Photo: Facebook/Sziget Festival Official

They also said their catering outlets had worked for years with the same tried-and-tested, reliable subcontractors, who served festival-goers safely and to a high standard.

Treated as drug users in the detox unit

In his post, the participant of DJ OTI’s concert said that while he was waiting at the on-site detox unit, at least 18 young people were taken there in connection with similar incidents. He condemned the way both his sister and he were treated, saying they had been made to feel as though they were responsible for what had happened.

Hungary’s National Ambulance Service responded to criticism on social media by saying it took seriously concerns about both patient care and communication, and would therefore review the circumstances surrounding its operation.

Illustration. Photo: Daily News Hungary

The service said that, alongside professional medical care, it was essential for its staff to treat every patient and relative appropriately and with empathy. “We believe it is important to learn from such feedback, identify the causes of any potential mistakes or shortcomings, and improve our procedures wherever necessary,” it said.

Ambulance arrived after two hours

We also reported on the case yesterday. Enikő, the 39-year-old woman mentioned above, said she had asked someone to bring her a drink from the VIP area because the queue was so long.

She then collapsed, something she said could not have been caused by alcohol. A young doctor and his wife tried to keep her conscious. Had her husband and the couple not been there, “anything could have happened” to her, she said. According to Enikő, the ambulance did not arrive for another two hours.

There were a lot of people at Balázs Sebestény’s Budapest concert the day before yesterday. The venue was the same as Sziget Festival’s. Photo: Facebook/DJ OTI

If you missed: Georgian tourist attempted to rape Hungarian teenager – but Chinese neighbours stepped in just in time

Several people on social media suspected that GHB may have been added to the women’s drinks, although this has not yet been confirmed. GHB is a synthetic drug, meaning it can only be produced in a laboratory. It is a colourless, odourless liquid and is known as a “rape drug” because of its association with sexual assault. It is often added to the drinks of young women, but its use carries serious risks: it can cause respiratory failure and, in the worst cases, death, Blikk reported.

Source: Pixnio.com

The drug can be detected in the blood for only four to five hours and in urine for between eight and 12 hours. Specialised, expensive toxicology tests can, however, detect it in hair months later.

If there is even a suspicion that someone has been given GHB, an ambulance should be called immediately and the person taken to a safe place and placed in the recovery position.

World.title: Spanish fashion group Tendam brings Cortefiel brand to Romania with store in Rivus Cluj-Napoca
World.content:
Spanish fashion group Tendam will bring three of its brands to Rivus Cluj-Napoca, the real estate project currently under development.

Cortefiel, the fashion group’s original brand, will open its first store in the country in Cluj. The other two units will operate under the Springfield and Women'secret brands. The three brands will take up a total area upwards of 1,000 sqm, Rivus said.

Tendam recently opened two stores under the Springfield and Women'secret brands in Iulius Town Timișoara.

Tendam, Spain’s second-largest apparel group by market share, has been majority-owned by the Abu Dhabi-based investment holding company Multiply Group since last year. It operates more than 1,800 points of sale and runs digital loyalty programs in over 80 markets, including Spain, Portugal, France, the UAE, and Latin America. The company manages 13 fashion brands: Women'secret, Springfield, Springfield Kids, Cortefiel, Pedro del Hierro, Hoss Intropia, Slowlove, High Spirits, Dash and Stars, OOTO, HI&BYE, Milano and Fifty.

Rivus Cluj-Napoca is a EUR 550 million investment by Iulius and Atterbury Europe. Spanning 14 hectares, the complex will integrate a diverse mix of uses: cultural, educational, sports, entertainment, events, park, shopping, and office. Its leasable retail area amounts to 142,000 sqm, with more than 70% already pre-leased, according to the developers.

The project is supported by a EUR 400 million syndicated green loan, the largest of its kind granted to a new real estate development in Romania. The financing is tied to meeting international sustainability standards, including LEED Platinum and EDGE Advanced certifications.

(Photo: Rivus Cluj Napoca)

World.title: Bucharest Court of Appeals gives reasoning in Bihor unauthorized care homes case
World.content:
The Bucharest Court of Appeal rejected the accusations of human trafficking and organized criminal group made against Viorel Pașca, the owner of an authorized care homes network in Bihor County, western Romania, when it ruled against his detention back in July.

The information emerged from the reasoning of the judge, now made public, who decided on July 16 that Viorel Pașca and his family members should be investigated while at liberty, an opinion contrary to that of the other magistrate from the Bucharest Tribunal who considered that “there are reasonable suspicions” against Pașca.

“At least at first glance”, the manner in which the injured persons were treated in Pașca’s nursing homes “does not present characteristic elements of keeping persons in a state of slavery or subjecting them to procedures similar to deprivation of liberty or servitude,” the Court of Appeals judge said, according to Digi24.

DIICOT prosecutors had said that the victims were treated improperly, and that money intended for their care did not serve the stated purpose.

However, the judge rejected DIICOT’s accusations. The sums of money were not appropriated by Pașca and his family, according to the evidence presented.

The Bucharest Court of Appeal also maintained that “the accommodated persons benefited from basic medical assistance.” Those in the care homes had “periodic medical consultations, including psychiatric specialist consultations, from prescribed and monitored treatments, from recreational activities and from assistance in carrying out current activities.”

The judge further mentioned that “persons with mental illnesses were involved in various activities carried out within the community and benefited from bodily hygiene services - haircuts, washing, shaving, as well as clean clothing and linen.”

Among deficiencies, the Court noted the fact that the persons dealing with the care of the sick and the administration of medicines had an extremely low educational level. Some did not have the ability to read and write.

Similarly, several accommodated persons did not benefit “in all situations” from “the medical treatment corresponding to the illnesses they suffered from.” Moreover, some of the patients contributed to the administration of medicines. The staff dealing with the care of the elderly was insufficient;

However, these shortcomings, the judge of the Bucharest Court of Appeal maintained, are due to “the lack of financial resources, and not at all to the fact that the defendants appropriated the money from which the patients benefited from the received donations.”

At the same time, the judge further said that the aid received from the state by vulnerable persons (such as a pension or any other form of social assistance) would not have allowed them to live in better conditions than those ensured by Viorel Pașca’s family.

The Bihor illegal care homes case broke at the end of June, uncovering similarities with another, more serious case from 2023. Unlike the latter, however, the situation of the care homes in Bihor is not as clear, leading many to argue that Viorel Pașca and his association were doing their best with the available resources, taking care of patients who had been abandoned by state institutions.

Ever since then, Viorel Paşca defended the activity of his association, which housed vulnerable people despite the fact that it lacked a license to do so.

World.title: Bucharest City Hall: Underground utility infrastructure works complicate tram track upgrades
World.content:
More than 70 kilometers of underground utility networks are being upgraded alongside the works on approximately 50 kilometers of tram tracks, the Bucharest City Hall said.

According to the institution, difficulties arise “as the actual location of pipes and other infrastructure does not always match the blueprints.”

The City Hall said this was the reason why, at times, there is no activity on already-opened construction site segments.

“When it comes to modernizing the tram tracks, we have all the documentation, so things are relatively straightforward and predictable. The complexity and unpredictability of the work come from the underground networks,” Bucharest mayor Ciprian Ciucu explained, quoted by Mediafax.

In some cases, new designs and permits are required, or pipes have to be resized or rerouted. Work may be halted in certain sections for weeks or even months, the City Hall said.

Before construction begins, a “network coordination plan” is drawn up and approved by the operators of the underground infrastructure, including Apa Nova, Distrigaz and Termoenergetica. The document is intended to show where the pipes are located. Problems arise once the old tracks are removed and excavation begins.

“The plans on paper do not match the reality on the ground. Once the old track is dismantled and the excavators start digging, we discover that pipes we thought were in one place are several meters away, while others emerge from places where we did not expect them,” Ciucu said.

At times, the construction work has uncovered archaeological remains that need to be assessed by the Ministry of Culture. Such situations force the temporary halt of work and the search for alternative technical solutions. Weather conditions can also lead to temporary work stoppages.

Bucharest is currently working on upgrading 50 kilometers of tram tracks. A EUR 266 million loan tranche from the European Investment Bank (EIB) backs the effort, which also includes the introduction of new vehicles and upgrading depots.

(Photo: Primăria Municipiului Bucureşti Facebook Page)

World.title: Roughly 5,000 trees cut down illegally in Romania’s Brașov County, minister says
World.content:
Interim environment minister Diana Buzoianu said on Monday, August 10, that one of the largest areas of illegal tree cutting in Romania was in Brașov County. Roughly 5,000 trees were cut without proper authorizations in the area.

The minister said she will travel to the area in question and noted that several such locations were uncovered after checks carried out within the Forest Guard.

"Everyone was satisfied. The phenomenon of illegal logging seemed no longer to exist. That was the story that was being sold to me. This phenomenon continues to exist, and I am glad that the authorities are finally taking the necessary measures to increase the number of cases they discover,” the minister said, cited by News.ro.

In March, Diana Buzoianu stated that she was requesting periodic reports from the Forest Guard regarding the situation of illegal logging and that in December inspections had increased exponentially and the largest number of damages had been identified.

"In December, more damages and a larger quantity of illegally cut timber were identified. About 30% of the damages identified in the entire year 2025. So, from the moment we changed the leadership of the Forest Guard, both the number of inspections and the results in the field increased exponentially," environment minister Diana Buzoianu stated.

Romania has been plagued by illegal logging for decades. Earlier this year, inspectors found that employees of the forest authority Romsilva had clear-cut several hectares of the famous Hoia-Baciu forest near Cluj-Napoca.

World.title: Brazil is by far Romania’s main Mercosur trading partner, INS says
Full shutdown of Romania’s Cernavoda NPP appears imminent
World.content:
Romania’s Cernavoda nuclear power plant is just 3 cm above the minimum water level required for operation, after the Danube level fell sharply on August 10 despite emergency works aimed at diverting additional water towards the plant. Figures indicate that the shutdown of the second of two Cernavoda reactors is imminent.

The National Administration of Romanian Waters said on August 10 that the Danube level at Cernavoda had fallen to -227 cm, compared with the minimum operating level of -230 cm, Agerpres reported. The development leaves little margin for the continued operation of the reactor, expected to last for no more than a couple of days.

The latest decline came after the water level had temporarily increased following the sinking of barges loaded with rocks in the Danube as part of an operation designed to redirect more water towards the arm supplying Cernavoda. A 4 cm increase had been reported over the weekend, but the level subsequently fell by 5 cm, according to Antena 3.

"At Cernavodă, the Danube level decreased by 5 cm compared to the previous day, reaching the value of -227 cm (compared to -222 cm as recorded on August 9)," the National Administration of Romanian Waters said.

The authority forecast that the Danube level at Cernavoda would continue declining by around 2 cm per day through August 14. The rate is expected to slow to 1 cm per day thereafter, with the level forecast to stabilize around -236 cm on August 16.

The forecast would take the water level well below the technical threshold required for the plant's second reactor. Cernavoda has already been operating with one of its two reactors shut down, leaving 680 MW of nuclear capacity unavailable.

The situation has increased pressure on Romania's electricity system during a period of high summer demand and exceptionally low Danube flows. The government has prepared a mechanism allowing Transelectrica to disconnect certain large industrial consumers with 24 hours' notice if available generation cannot cover projected demand.

Household consumers and facilities whose operations cannot be interrupted, including hospitals and certain energy infrastructure, are excluded from the mechanism.

The Romanian authorities' efforts on the Danube were intended to extend the operating period of the remaining reactor, but the latest hydrological data indicate that the margin is narrowing rapidly.

World.title: Romania’s foreign trade reverses trend and widens by 4.4% y/y in Q2
World.content:
Romania’s foreign trade deficit (goods) increased by 4.4% y/y to EUR 8.66 billion in the second quarter of the year (Q2), after it had posted negative annual growth rates for the previous four quarters, data from the Statistics Office (INS) show.

For the first half of the year, the trade gap still contracted by 2% to EUR 16.5 billion thanks to the 8.2% y/y contraction in Q1.

Both exports and imports rose faster in Q2, by 4.9% y/y (to EUR 25.2 billion) and 4.7% y/y (to EUR 33.9 billion), respectively in Q2, as a result of higher nominal prices driven by energy prices. The imports visibly shifted from a benign trajectory of nominal stabilization (-1.4% y/y in Q1) towards positive growth rates in contrast to the shrinking domestic demand. This was, most likely, an effect of higher nominal prices, although the stabilization of economic activity (in construction, rather than industry) may have had an impact on the imports as well.

A large part of the swing from a shrinking trade deficit in Q1 to a widening trade gap in Q2 was generated by the trade in mineral fuels (crude oil mainly): while Romania imported less crude oil in Q1 due to outages of its refineries, the country resumed imports in Q2 when the price of crude oil and petroleum products further rose.

Romania is a net importer of petroleum products, and this was visible in the trade balance during Q2. The imports of mineral fuels (crude oil and petroleum products) contracted by 14.2% y/y in Q1 but widened by 11.7% y/y in Q2.

Despite the deterioration in the country’s trade gap during Q2, Romania’s trade deficit in the rolling 12-month period decreased to an estimated 8.4% in June 2026 (subject to revision after Q2 GDP data is released), from 9.6% of GDP in June 2025.

World.title: Romania’s central bank keeps 6.5% monetary rate, warns of inflationary risks
World.content:
In line with expectations, the National Bank of Romania (BNR) on August 10 decided to keep the key policy rate unchanged at 6.50%.

BNR reiterated expectations for headline inflation to drop sharply during Q3 from double-digit rates in Q2, but it also mentions “notable uncertainties and risks” generated by the future evolution of electricity and food prices, amid this year's severe drought, as well as from the trajectory of crude oil prices.

Under the official projections for the inflation trajectory, rather confirmed by independent analysts, BNR is not expected to change the monetary policy over the coming quarters, Erste Group says.

There were no indications of a potential upward revision to the inflation forecast compared with the May projections, Erste Group says in a research note.

BNR will publish the updated quarterly Inflation Report on August 13. Under the May 2026 Report, inflation is expected at 5.7% y/y in September, 5.5% at the end of this year (versus 5.9% y/y projected by Erste) and 2.9% y/y one year later.

Great uncertainties remain associated, including in the current domestic political situation, with the measures potentially adopted in the future to continue budgetary consolidation beyond the current year in accordance with the Medium-Term Budgetary-Structural Plan agreed with the EC and the excessive deficit procedure, BNR added in its August 10 monetary decision release.

BNR also notes that the latest data indicate a slight recovery in economic activity during Q2-Q3 2026, driven mainly by improved performance in Q2 compared with the previous year. Major components of domestic demand showed similar improvements, although developments across key economic sectors remained mixed.

World.title: Turkish Parliament Overwhelmingly Approves PKK Disarmament Law
World.content:
Turkey’s parliament approved the much-heralded framework law that provides a legal basis for disarming the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party, PKK, on Monday regulating the judicial procedures for people linked to it and marking the most comprehensive legislative step yet to end the four-decade-long conflict.

“Brotherhood will grow even stronger; therefore, once the terrorist organisation seeking to come between us is eliminated, Turkey will become even stronger,” Abdulhamit Gul, Parliamentary Deputy Group Leader of the ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, told reporters after the vote.

The “Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration” passed easily, with 467 votes in favour. 88 MPs against and six abstentions.

Support came from the ruling AKP, its nationalist ally, the Nationalist Movement Party, MHP, the pro-Kurdish DEM Party, the pro-Kurdish and Islamist HUDA PAR, some MPs from the opposition Republican People’s Party, CHP, some members of the New Path parliamentary group and several independents.

The new law lays out the legal framework for the post-disarmament process, including temporary judicial provisions for eligible people convicted of, or investigated over, PKK-related offences.

It includes mechanisms such as supervised release, sentence postponement and judicial supervision under specified conditions following the organisation’s dissolution and disarmament.

The law stipulates that its provisions take effect only after Turkey’s National Security Council, MGK, has determined that the PKK and its affiliated structures have fully disbanded and surrendered all weapons.

The opposition right wing Good Party rejected the bill entirely. “[The law] is for paving the way for [President Recep Tayyip] Erdogan to remain president for life.” Musavat Dervisoglu, its leader, said in parliament.

The new main opposition New Party did not adopt a unified decision. Party leader Ozgur Ozel allowed his MPs a free vote, and 54 of its 91 MPs voted against the law.

“I am not against peace. I want terrorism to end, the guns to fall silent, and the Kurdish issue to be resolved through democratic and peaceful means,” New Party MP Mahmut Tanal said in a written statement before the vote. However, he said he would vote “no” because he did not trust the government, stressing its harsh crackdown on the opposition and other critics.

Ozel announced that the senior party leadership had voted in favour.

The legislation follows political developments that began earlier. In February 2025, jailed PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan called on the group to lay down its arms. His appeal followed an unexpected peace initiative by Devlet Bahceli, leader of the MHP, a key ally of Erdogan’s AKP.

The initiative led to the establishment of a parliamentary commission and regular visits to Ocalan by a delegation from the pro-Kurdish DEM Party. The new framework law is regarded as the closest Turkey has come to establishing a comprehensive legal basis for ending the decades-long conflict.

More than 40,000 people have been killed since fighting between the PKK and Turkish security forces began after Ocalan founded the group in 1984.

World.title: Why Emigrants Prefer Democracies and Leave Illiberal States Behind
World.content:
Several years ago, in Gorazde in eastern Bosnia, I had a discussion with a young man who had a job and in general was in a good position in his hometown. He told me he had recently visited a cousin in Sweden, and that, while he had a decent life, he suspected he might emigrate there anyway, to start over.

He noted that it felt good to be able to walk down the street in that country, or be able to turn on the TV, and not see the same politicians he was not able to escape when in Bosnia.

This anecdote would fit well in Justin Gest’s new book, Democratic Drain: Global Migration and the Struggle for Democracy, which explores the motivations for, and impact of, the outflow of people from less democratic societies to more democratic – and more successful – destinations.

World.title: Nowhere To Go: Czechia’s Housing Crisis Keeps Women in Abusive Relationships
World.content:
Problems in border areas and where regions meet

An analysis of availability found that the situation is worst in specialised shelters, where 90 per cent of the recommended capacity is lacking. According to available data from the aforementioned report, there are only three highly specialised shelters in the country, all of which are located in Prague and the South Moravian Region. For residents of other regions, these services are to a large degree inaccessible.

If we assume that every social housing service is capable of caring for victims of domestic violence, the shortage amounts to at least 681 beds. But if we count only those that specialise in victims of domestic violence, the figure is about 3,000.

“Since the beginning of this year, we’ve had to turn away at least 15 women from our shelter. In the crisis apartment, where women can stay for a maximum of one week, we’ve had to turn away nine. And we’re not even halfway through the year yet,” says Janouskova, director of the non-profit Acorus.

If we were to take into account all shelters that serve victims of domestic violence as one of their target groups, we would find that there are significant regional differences here as well.

While assistance is formally available throughout the Czech Republic, a closer examination clearly reveals problematic areas. The situation is worst along the borders with neighbouring countries and at the boundaries between individual regions; care is least accessible where the Olomouc and Moravian-Silesian regions meet, as well as on the border between the Liberec and Hradec Králové regions.

Specialised crisis assistance is completely lacking in five regions, while experts have identified significant gaps in the availability of intervention centres in Vysocina and in the South Moravian and Hradec Kralove regions.

“We have repeatedly drawn attention to the need for accessible housing. I believe that a systemic framework should be established to ensure that apartments are available to address domestic violence, whether at the municipal or regional level,” says Lucie Paprsteinova, director of the Bily kruh intervention centre in Ostrava.

Paprsteinova’s remarks are corroborated by the minutes of meetings of the committees on the prevention of domestic violence, where the issue of housing was addressed at most meetings. The most discussed topic was securing stable funding for residential services.

Organisations that operate these services are struggling to survive amid financial uncertainty. While in Western Europe, institutional funding for shelters is provided directly by the state and regional governments, in the Czech Republic these institutions depend on available grants.

“Funding is provided on an annual basis. The uncertainty lies in the fact that the grant approval process is rather lengthy, and every year you have to wait several months to find out how much you will actually receive,” says Janouskova, noting that such a system does not allow for long-term funding and planning. “The fact that it’s not possible to expand capacity is also due to the fact that you don’t know how much funding you will get – and there isn’t enough of it.”

The UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) has repeatedly drawn attention to the funding situation and strongly urged the Czech Republic to ensure long-term and sustainable support for these services.

In a statement, the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs said it viewed the CEDAW Committee’s recommendations as an important impetus. “We have long supported the funding of specialised social services, and we are currently taking steps to boost the financial stability of social services in general, which will also benefit victims of domestic and gender-based violence,” the ministry said.

This article is part of a five-part series produced in collaboration between data journalists from Czech Radio and researchers from the Institute of Sociology and Charles University. Their shared goal was to identify barriers in the system of support for victims of domestic violence.

Translated from the Czech original by Ian Willoughby

The production of this investigation was supported by a grant from the Journalism Science Alliance.

World.title: Montenegro Faces Economic Test After Decision to Impose Visas for Russians, Turks
World.content:
As Montenegro enters the final phase of its European Union accession process, the tourism-dependent country could face one of its first significant economic tests when it introduces visas for citizens of Russia, Belarus, Turkey, China and Saudi Arabia.

The government says the measure, to be introduced in November, will bring Montenegro’s visa policy into line with that of the EU. It will fulfil one of the final requirements in Chapter 24 of the accession negotiations, covering justice, freedom and security - but it has also angered Russia, which complained that it will damage relations between Podgorica and Moscow.

According to official tourism statistics, Montenegro recorded 2.73 million tourist arrivals and 15.37 million overnight stays in 2025. Foreign visitors accounted for 95.8 per cent of overnight stays. After Serbia, tourists from Russia account for the second biggest proportion – 16.4 per cent – of overnight stays in Montenegro, followed by Bosnia and Herzegovina, Germany and then Turkey at 4.3 per cent.

World.title: NATO Peacekeepers’ ‘Transition’ at Flashpoint Bridge Alarms Kosovo Serb Party
World.content:
A Kosovo Police patrol car on the Iber bridge in Mitrovica, August 10, 2026. Photo: BIRN/Florinda Kelmendi.

The NATO-led peacekeeping mission in Kosovo, KFOR, said on Monday that it had begun a gradual transition away from its permanent presence on the main bridge in the ethnically divided town of Mitrovica, citing “an improved security situation in Kosovo”.

The town has been split into a northern, Serb-run half and a southern, Kosovo Albanian-run half, since the end of the Kosovo war in 1999, sparking numerous incidents since then.

“In line with the improved security situation in Kosovo, this is part of the process for optimising KFOR’s posture,” KFOR told BIRN on Monday.

“This process will be gradual, conditions based, and is being closely coordinated with all relevant stakeholders, including representatives of the Institutions in Kosovo and of international organisations, as well as with representatives of the Kosovo Police and the EU Rule-of-Law Mission in Kosovo (EULEX),” it added.

However, after a Kosovo Police vehicle appeared on Monday on the bridge, Srpska Lista, the Belgrade-backed Kosovo Serb party, said it strongly opposed the withdrawal of KFOR members from the bridge and called for an urgent meeting with KFOR commander Ozkan Ulutas.

“Given the extremely complex political and security situation, as well as the fact that the area around the main bridge has for decades been a site of serious tensions and conflicts, we believe that any decision that could affect security at this sensitive location must be made with the utmost care and with full consideration for the concerns of citizens,” Srpska Lista said.

According to Srpska Lista, Kosovo Police “have failed to build the trust of the Serbian people through their actions.

“Their conduct in numerous situations, including their support for actions that we consider unlawful and directed against the Serbian people and their institutions, has further deepened mistrust and the sense of insecurity among Serbs,” the statement said.

Apart from the main bridge over the Iber/Ibar in Mitrovica, Kosovo’s government has opened two additional bridges connecting the southern and northern, Serb-run, parts of the city.

Earlier on Monday, meanwhile, KFOR announced that it has begun a “gradual integration of Kosovo Police personnel into KFOR’s security architecture” at the Decani Monastery in western Kosovo, an important site for Serbian Orthodox believers. The mission said the move was part of a “broader process to optimise its security posture and will be implemented gradually and based on conditions on the ground”.

KFOR noted that it “remains the first responder responsible for the Monastery site’s protection and will maintain a visible presence in south and north Mitrovica and in northern Kosovo”.

The monastery, a UNESCO World Heritage site, has been under KFOR protection since the end of the war in Kosovo in 1999. The mission said it would maintain close cooperation with the Serbian Orthodox Church, Kosovo institutions, international organisations and the Serbian Armed Forces, in order “to safeguard mutual transparency, cooperation and trust, and to avoid misunderstandings”.

“KFOR’s commitment to the security of the Visoki Decani Monastery and to the safety of all local communities is steadfast,” the mission said.

World.title: Kosovo Protests as Serbia Mulls Changing River’s Course
World.content:
Ujman/Gazivoda lake in northern Kosovo accumulates water from the Iber/Ibar river. Photo: BIRN/Denis Sllovinja.

Kosovo’s Acting President, Albulena Haxhiu, protested on Monday after the Serbian President announced that Belgrade may change the course of the Iber/Ibar river. Deeming the plan a “serious concern”, Haxhiu said the issue should be addressed with the international community.

“As you know, the Iber Lepenc and Ujman [Gazivoda] lake are part of a strategic system for the water supply, energy, agriculture and the lives of hundreds of thousands of citizens of Kosovo,” Haxhiu told the Conference of Ambassadors in Pristina.

“A unilateral intervention in transboundary water flows would have consequences far beyond a technical issue, as it would affect the water, energy, environmental and human security of our republic,” she added.

Haxhiu spoke out the day after President Aleksandar Vucic of Serbia hinted at the initiative in what he described as justified retaliation against the Kosovo government’s policies towards Serbs in Kosovo.

“Since they are harassing our people so much, let’s see, we have various reasons for changing the course of the Ibar, so we’ll see what the Albanians will do and how they will behave,” Vucic said.

On Monday, Vucic doubled down on the statement, adding that he was simply “addressing the waterways within the territory of the Republic of Serbia, in accordance with domestic law”. Serbia regards Kosovo as part of its territory and refuses to recognise its independence.

Vucic insisted that he was not threatening anyone. “We will simply deal with our own problems. We have our own interests, and we are taking care of our own interests,” he said.

This is not the first time Vucic has mentioned the idea of moving the course of the Ibar, which originates in Montenegro, passes through the south-western tip of Serbia and then flows through northern Kosovo and then back into Serbia.

After an explosion on the Ibar-Lepenac canal, which supplies several towns through Lake Ujman/Gazivode, in November 2024, Vucic said that the idea of changing the course of the Ibar had existed since 1985. “We can divert the course of the Ibar, and they would be left without Gazivode. Then there would be no lake anymore,” Vucic said at the time.

He added that he had always opposed the idea. “I did not want us to use nature for political purposes. After all, we were supplying them with electricity,” he said.

On Sunday, Kosovo’s Minister of Environment, Fitore Pacolli, called Vucic’s statements unacceptable.

“According to the Helsinki Convention, states have an obligation to cooperate for the fair and rational use of transboundary waters, to prevent transboundary damage and to protect aquatic ecosystems. Water resources cannot be used as an instrument of threat, pressure or destabilisation against another state,” Pacolli said.

World.title: Zelensky’s Belgrade Visit Tests Serbia’s EU-Russia Balancing Act
World.content:
Serbia and Ukraine have maintained a more functional relationship since Russia’s full-scale invasion than Serbia’s domestic media environment might suggest. From the beginning of the war, Belgrade has formally supported Ukraine’s territorial integrity while refusing to impose sanctions on the Kremlin.

Serbia has backed UN resolutions affirming Ukrainian sovereignty, accepted Ukrainian refugees and provided financial, humanitarian and energy assistance. Kyiv, meanwhile, has not recognised Kosovo’s independence, enabling both governments to emphasise reciprocal respect for territorial integrity. Political contacts have steadily intensified. This has included meetings between Vucic and Zelensky on the margins of international summits, visits by senior Ukrainian officials such as Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba’s trip to Belgrade in 2024, and Vucic’s two visits to Ukraine in just over a year.

Yet Serbia’s foreign policy abroad and its political communication at home tell different stories. While the government formally describes EU membership as a strategic objective, much of the pro-government media ecosystem continues to cultivate anti-Western, anti-EU and pro-Russian narratives.

A 2026 Belgrade Centre for Security Policy study found that the narrative presenting Ukraine as a proxy in a wider Russia-West war was dominant in the Serbian pro-government press between early 2022 and mid-2025. Echoing Kremlin rhetoric, pro-government media portrayed Zelensky as Ukraine’s illegitimate president, while repeatedly depicting the country as subordinate to NATO and the West. Corruption scandals involving Zelensky’s inner circle have likewise been amplified by tabloids to portray the Ukrainian leadership as compromised.

The ruling party also echoed “colour revolution” rhetoric – that Serbia is being subjected to foreign subversion – through loyal media outlets, to delegitimise and justify the crackdown on mass protests against corruption, growing autocracy and political repression. There have been repeated warnings that the authorities would not allow another “Euromaidan in Belgrade”.

Zelensky’s visit creates a domestic communications challenge for Serbia’s president, particularly with his pro-Russian electoral base. The same media ecosystem that has spent years cultivating suspicion of Ukraine and hostility towards the West must now explain why Zelensky is being formally welcomed in Belgrade.

For tabloids such as Informer, the crucial message is not what the visit changes, but what it does not. Closer ties with Ukraine, and Zelensky’s visit to Belgrade, do not necessarily signal a shift in Serbia’s policy toward Russia, nor do they imply the introduction of sanctions. Vucic has already stated that Serbia defined its sanctions policy years ago and that this position will remain unchanged.

That is also a reason not to read too much into the visit. Just weeks earlier, Vucic was the only leader at a Ukraine-South East Europe summit in Kyiv who refused to sign the joint declaration calling for continued support for Ukraine and greater pressure on Russia. He also did not attend a ceremony honouring Ukrainians killed in Russia’s aggression. At the same time, Serbia is seeking to deepen economic ties with Kyiv to advance its bid for membership in the World Trade Organization, while continuing arms exports, exploring possible security and defence cooperation, and publicly reaffirming its support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity.

This is not necessarily a contradiction, but rather the essence of Vucic’s foreign policy: cultivating relationships with competing powers while avoiding commitments that would foreclose other options.

Zelensky’s visit therefore demonstrates to Moscow that Serbia is not exclusively Russia’s partner, while signalling to Brussels and Washington that Belgrade wants to remain geopolitically useful. But unless it is followed by sanctions, substantially greater alignment with EU foreign policy or a structural reduction of Serbia’s dependence on Russia, the visit looks less like a Serbian pivot to the West than another attempt by Vucic to continue his balancing act.

Maja Bjelos is a senior researcher at the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy.

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: eVisitor Just Recorded the Best July in Croatia in the Past Two Years
World.content:
August the 11th, 2026 – The widely praised eVisitor system just recorded the best July in Croatia in the past two years, with enviable numbers of both arrivals and overnight stays.

According to the latest data from the eVisitor system, which records tourist traffic achieved in commercial and non-commercial facilities as well as nautical charter (eCrew system), Croatia recorded 12.4 million arrivals and 59.1 million overnight stays in the period from January to the end of July. Poslovni reports that when compared to the same period last year, this represents growth of 1 percent in arrivals and in overnight stays. Of that total, 56.1 million overnight stays were achieved on the Adriatic, a rise of 0.5 percent compared to last year, while the continent, including the city of Zagreb, recorded more than 3 million overnight stays, which is 1 percent more than last year.

4.7 million arrivals and 29.6 million overnight stays

eVisitor data also show that during July this year Croatia recorded an extremely impressive 4.7 million arrivals and 29.6 million overnight stays, which compared to July last year represents growth of 2.5 percent in arrivals and 1 percent in overnight stays.

In the seventh month the largest number of guests came from the markets of Germany, Slovenia, Croatia, Poland, the Czech Republic, Austria, Hungary and others. By counties, the most tourists were counted in Istria, Split-Dalmatia County and Kvarner, while among individual destinations the most visited were Rovinj, Vir, Poreč, Medulin and Dubrovnik.

“We’re more than satisfied with the tourist results achieved throughout the first seven months of this year, and especially with the fact that in July we achieved the best result in the last two years. This confirms that Croatian tourism continues to maintain its competitiveness and resilience and that, despite changes in the market, we are succeeding in maintaining positive trends. It is particularly pleasing that we are also recording good results in financial indicators. In July the value of fiscalised invoices rose by 18 percent, while the number of issued invoices was 8 percent higher compared to the same month last year. We are also recording growth in road, air and maritime traffic, and all these results confirm that we have responded well to market circumstances – both through quality promotion of Croatia and through timely adjustment of the offer.

I’d like to sincerely thank the entire tourism sector for the effort invested, and especially accommodation providers who responded to our appeals and with their special offers additionally contributed to the competitiveness of our offer. Ahead of us is still a good part of August after which we will make a complete overview of this main part of the tourist year. Croatian tourism is once again confirming its strength this year, and the results achieved show that we are on the right path and that together we are successfully responding to changes and challenges,” said Tonči Glavina, Minister of Tourism and Sport.

the situation on a county by county basis

When Croatia’s tourist results are segmented by counties, in the first seven months the most overnight stays were achieved in Istria (16.7 million overnight stays), Split-Dalmatia County (11.1 million overnight stays) and Kvarner (9.7 million overnight stays), while by destinations the leaders were Dubrovnik, Rovinj, Poreč, Split and Umag.

“The course and results of the tourist year so far show that Croatia still has a very strong position on the global tourism market, despite all the demanding circumstances. What we particularly read from this year’s tourist movements is a change in the way guests make decisions about their travels. Last-minute reservations play an important role, and when choosing a destination the best value for money is increasingly sought, along with safety and easy accessibility.

croatia’s enviable geographical position as a massive aid

In this context Croatia has a series of advantages: from proximity to our most important source markets and good transport connections to the diversity of the offer that enables different types of holidays. The results achieved therefore give us additional wind in our sails for the continuation of the tourist year, all the more so as the period of Ferragosto is ahead of us, traditionally very important for the travel of Italian guests. In addition to the main summer months, we are also recording excellent announcements for the post-season, for which promotional activities start in mid-August, especially on the markets of Poland and the United Kingdom,” said Kristjan Staničić, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board.

Viewed by markets, during the first seven months the most overnight stays were achieved by guests from the markets of Germany (10.3 million overnight stays), Croatia (7.6 million overnight stays), Slovenia (6.7 million overnight stays), Austria (4.3 million overnight stays), Poland (3.9 million overnight stays), the Czech Republic (3 million overnight stays), the UK (2.2 million overnight stays), Hungary (2.1 million overnight stays) and others.

World.title: Croatian Public Debt Rises by 4.6 Billion Euros in a Single Year
World.content:
August the 11th, 2026 – Croatian public debt has increased by 4.6 billion euros in a single year, with long-term borrowing dominating the entire picture.

As Poslovni/Ana Blaskovic writes, Croatian public debt stood at a whopping 55 billion euros back at the end of April, which is 4.6 billion euros or 9 percent higher than in the same period last year, according to the latest data from the Croatian National Bank (HNB). Compared to the end of last year, the debt increased by 2.7 billion euros, or 5.2 percent, while on a monthly basis a slight decrease of 148 million euros was recorded.

The largest sum of the increase comes from stronger borrowing by the central government, whose debt reached 54 billion euros. This means the central government accounts for more than 98 percent of Croatia’s total public debt. At the same time, local government units, municipalities, cities and counties, are borrowing more and more. Their obligations have been rising for 15 consecutive months, and at double-digit rates.

the domination of long-term borrowing

Back in April, the annual growth rate stood at 21.4 percent, after 20 percent in March. In contrast, social security funds continued to reduce their debt level, which was 32.2 percent lower on an annual basis.

The structure of borrowing shows that long-term instruments still prevail. About 65 percent of the non-consolidated debt relates to bonds, while the rest consists of loans, deposits and short-term securities. Notably, the Ministry of Finance has significantly increased the issuance of treasury bills, which is why domestic debt in the short-term securities segment rose by 45.5 percent year-on-year, Raiffeisen analysts note.

Croatia continues to finance itself mostly on the domestic market. At the end of April, domestic investors held 68.6 percent of the public debt, while the share of foreign creditors was 31.4 percent. After Eurozone accession, the share of the domestic component stabilised around 70 percent, reflecting a multi-year trend of strengthening domestic sources of state financing.

the public invests 4.9 billion euros in a year

HNB data also show growth in investments from the general public in government securities. Household investments increased from 3.9 billion euros to 4.9 billion euros in one single year, while financial companies raised their exposure to state debt from 31.1 billion euros to 32.6 billion euros. Despite the rise in nominal debt, Croatia remains below the Maastricht threshold. At the end of the first quarter, the public debt-to-GDP ratio stood at 58.4 percent, 0.2 percentage points higher than a year earlier.

Raiffeisen analyst Petar Bejuk assesses that domestic fiscal indicators remain more favourable than the wider Eurozone average, primarily thanks to strong nominal economic growth. For the full year, he expects the public debt ratio to stay below 60 percent of GDP, noting that fiscal policy should preserve enough room to respond to possible future risks.

World.title: Ancient Greek Treasure Over 2,000 Years Old Found in Attic in Trogir
World.content:
August the 11th, 2026 – An ancient Greek treasure over 2,000 years old was discovered by change in an attic in Trogir. Meet the Trogir Kairos.

Have you heard of the Trogir Kairos? It is a beautiful ancient Greek marble relief from the 4th or 3rd century BC depicting the god Kairos. The work is considered an exceptional artistic achievement and one of the rare surviving sculptural representations of this Greek deity.

this fascinating relief ended up in an attic in trogir, but how?!

Even today, almost 100 after its discovery, debates continue about its journey and just how it ended up sitting in an attic in a Dalmatian coastal town. Poslovni reports that the ancient artwork, created by Lysippos, one of the greatest sculptors of antiquity, was found in the attic of a house belonging to a prominent Trogir family. According to multiple experts, it was brought from Greece up to nearby Croatia during the Renaissance period. Whether those who brought it knew its true value remains an open question and will never be answered.

The precious relief was discovered in the attic of a house that once belonged to the Statilić (Statileo) family, which produced several notable figures — diplomats, artists connected to the Hungarian-Croatian court, and world travellers. Historians therefore believe that one of the family members found the relief while travelling and brought it back to Trogir. It was discovered there in 1928 by the Trogir art historian Don Ivan Delalle.

who is the greek god kairos?

In Greek mythology, Kairos was the youngest son of Zeus, known as the god of the fleeting, brief moment. According to the myth, Kairos, who symbolises the right and decisive moment, must be seized by the lock of hair on his forehead before he flies away. The young god, depicted by Lysippos with wings on his feet and back, barely ever touches the ground, conveying his sheer speed. He reminds mere mortals that the right moment passes quickly and that opportunities do not return.

Kairos has no hair on the back of his head, symbolising the transience of chances: once he has passed by, he can no longer be grasped, and a missed moment cannot ever be recovered. This utterly remarkable relief from Trogir is regarded as one of the best-preserved and rarest depictions of the Greek god Kairos in the entire world.

World.title: Omiš Returns to its Pirate Past With a Real Spectacle at Sea!
World.content:
August the 11th, 2026 – Located in the very heart of central Dalmatia, Omiš is closely connected to the world of the pirate, and the 18th of August promises an absolute spectacle at sea.

If you’ve ever been to Dalmatia (and particularly if you’ve sailed along the heavily indented coastline and islands), you may have asked how the country fared back during the days when marauding pirates ruled the Adriatic. Turning the pages of the history book (a long way) back, we find ourselves in an era where piracy wasn’t nearly as frowned upon as it is today. Back then, it was a legitimate business that only the brave dared try their hand (or sword) at.

Along the heavily indented, cove-ridden rocks of the Dalmatian coast, the tradition of piracy goes back even further. It was noted way back during the reign of the various Illyrian tribes that used to live there before the ethnic Croatians arrived.

a hard lesson for venice…

Across the Adriatic Sea, the mighty and somewhat problematic Venetian Empire was very wary of the pirates from Croatia’s Neretva basin. Dominating Adriatic trade, Venice stacked up its enemies and had good reason to keep looking over its proverbial shoulder.

Indeed, back in 887 AD, a battle near Makarska between the Venetians and the so-called Narentine pirates took place, and during which Venetian Duke Pietro Candiano lost his life and his fleet was sunk to the watery depths below. After this event, the Venetians likely paid dearly for the freedom to travel and trade without encountering problems in the Croatian part of the Adriatic.

That relative ease didn’t last long, as the Omiš pirates (or gusari, if you want to truly go local) began disrupting it. That time period coincided with the rising prominence of the Kačić dynasty during the 12th century. This family didn’t have a tree. It was more like a forest. They were dukes and widely known for their ruthlessness and ruled over a large part of southern and central Dalmatia. Although they were officially the subjects of the Hungarian-Croatian king, they enjoyed plenty of autonomy. They opted to use that by organising professional piracy within their dominion.

keeping up with the Kačić family

This fearsome dynasty controlled the majority of the maritime traffic along the eastern Adriatic coast, and both Venetian and Ragusan (Dubrovnik) merchants had to pay up if they wanted to ensure their safe passage through that part of the sea. Just how far they were willing to go in their efforts to fully control that traffic is best explained by the fact that they were accused of attacking the vessels which took the Crusaders to the Palestine, and that even the Pope Honorius III started a war with the pirates, which he lost.

Every peace agreed upon with the Kačić family and Omiš pirates was short-lived, and it took almost two centuries to defeat them and establish safer passage along the Adriatic coast. The Kačić dynasty was eventually defeated and expelled from Omiš after the Venetians finally got the upper hand in 1287. Piracy lingered on, but it eventually weakened. By the time 1444 rolled around, Omiš ended up entirely occupied by the Venetians, and that marked the end of the tradition of piracy once and for all.

Thankfully, you can now freely sail in Dalmatia without any fear of being plundered, pillaged, or forced to pay for your safe passage, but it wasn’t always so peaceful!

Omiš takes us back to its pirate past on august the 18th

Now we’ve delved into the history of just why pirates are so significant to this part of the Dalmatian coast, we can look at what’s to come. After a six year break, Omiš is finally bringing back its beloved Pirate Battle. If you were to ask most people, they’d argue that it’s by far the Adriatic’s most spectacular historical reenactment, and it couldn’t possibly take place in a more apt location. On Tuesday the 18th of August, the Port of Omiš will shed all signs of modernity and totally transform into an authentic thirteenth-century battlefield.

Old vessels will cut across the water, cannons will drown out the summertime cicadas, swords will be drawn and fireworks will light up the blackness of the night sky above the Cetina canyon’s imposing rock faces. This is so much more than a show by the sea, it’s a living, accurate recreation of the moment when the fearless pirates of Omiš outsmarted the powerful and problematic Venice and cemented their rightful place in Dalmatian and indeed wider Croatian legend.

spectators will watch an ancient pirate battle from a modern setting

The last Pirate Battle took place in 2019, just before the coronavirus pandemic struck. An extremely extensive 15 million euro reconstruction of the Port of Omiš began soon after, forcing the event into a temporary pause. Now, the brand-new pier and seafront promenade are finally complete, offering the perfect stage for one of Croatia’s most atmospheric summer spectacles. You’ll be able to watch this ancient battle from a modern waterfront, witnessing heritage and history blend with modern Omiš in perfect harmony.

The newly renovated port and accompanying waterfront can comfortably host 10,000+ spectators, meaning that you’re guaranteed to find a spot from which you can enjoy the re-enactment and the rest of this marvellous event.

Around 150 costumed participants will take part in the upcoming event, with the local KPU Omiški gusari (Omiš Pirates Association) at the helm (no pun intended). They’ll be joined by allied historical groups from across the rest of Croatia: Kumpanija Vela Luka, the Dubrovački trombunjeri, the Klis Uskoks, Društvo Poljičana Sveti Jure – Priko, Bakar Town Guard 1848 and the Požega Town Guard. The event is being entirely organised by the Omiš Tourist Board, with great care paid both to historical accuracy and as a big “welcome back” to a much loved event.

what we can expect on the evening

The programme is set to begin early so that families with children and history lovers can soak up every moment.

18:30 – Activities for children on the waterfront will take place.

19:15 – A grand parade of all of the historical troops through the ancient streets of Omiš will delight all those gathered.

20:15 – The main event will begin, with the Pirate Battle itself in taking place in the ultra-modern, new port.

celebrations across the town

Immediately after that, the celebrations will continue with a performance by Kumpanija Vela Luka, ceremonial cannon fire from the famous Dubrovački trombunjeri (21:10), a dramatic fire show and an incredible fireworks display that will light up the entire harbour and the surrounding tall cliffs which make this town is instantly recognisable (21:40). Once those cannons eventually do fall silent, the celebrations will move to the Croatian Veterans’ Park. Organised by KPU Omiški gusari, the after-party features local food and drink, demonstrations of traditional crafts and a live concert by the popular band Vigor (21:50).

We can say with confidence that this is certainly the perfect way to bring an unforgettable Omiš summer evening to a close.

here’s a look at 2019’s event to get you prepared!

Should you need further information, look no further than here, and make sure to follow along on Instagram for more fantastic images and videos.

World.title: Zagreb Under the Surface – Explore the City Below the City
World.content:
August the 11th, 2026 – Zagreb might not have a metro network, but there’s a world under those tram tracks. Here’s how to explore the city below the city.

One of Zagreb’s most fascinating attractions lies out of sight, far from everything that has transformed the once overlooked Croatian capital into a hit city break. Underneath the streets lie a network of tunnels, shelters and passages, all hidden beneath the historic centre. The most famous and accessible of these is the weird and wonderful Grič Tunnel. Few realise however that this tunnel forms only one bit of a far more expansive underground saga, encompassing the horrors of war to a modern, swanky cultural space.

These odd and fascinating subterranean areas offer a different way to experience the capital. They provide a lot of relief with their much cooler temperatures in summer, as well as a handy shortcut through the heart of the city.

Grič – from protection from allied bombing to a quirky underground exhibition space

The Grič Tunnel is an underground artery stretching for approximately 350 metres deep beneath the historic Grič (Gradec) neighbourhood of Upper Town (or Gornji grad, if you want to go local). It connects the very old Mesnička Street on the west with Radićeva Street on the east, with southern exits leading towards Ilica and Tomićeva Street, including two that open into the Art Park near the funicular.

Construction began in 1943 during WWII, when Zagreb’s authorities at the time ordered the proper construction of a public air-raid shelter under the Upper Town hill in response to the threat of Allied bombing. Croatia, then the so-called Independent State of Croatia, was in a very precarious position politically, and found itself in serious danger from attack. Despite the end of that terrible war finally arriving in 1945, construction actually continued all the way until that year. It was projected and designed both as a protective space and a potential promenade or traffic corridor should it be needed. It fell into more or less total disuse after the end of WWII, serving at times as storage, occasional shelter, or simply remaining closed to the public entirely.

It became useful again as Croatia was fighting for its independence during the 1990s, acting as a shelter for civilians. In 1993, it even hosted the legendary Under City Rave, one of the first major rave parties in all of Croatia and an event that even drew attention from no less than MTV. Decades of neglect followed, with the city eventually deciding to renovate and open the tunnel to the public once again in July 2016. It now operates daily (typically 09:00–21:00) as a free pedestrian passage used daily by locals and visitors alike, as well as an occasional cultural event and/or exhibition space.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

When it isn’t playing host to an art exhibition or an event, the tunnel’s thick concrete walls and dim lighting instantly reveal its original wartime purpose. In fact, even the original wartime signage remains there. The constantly cool temperature makes it a welcome escape from the scorching Croatian summer heat or indeed the tiresome winter rain that plagues Zagreb when the temperatures drop. During the much loved Advent in Zagreb, it is decorated with lights, installations and seasonal programmes, transforming this wartime structure into one of Zagreb’s more unexpected and highly unusual festive venues.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

If you fancy a stroll through this wartime tunnel, the entrances are easy to find. Either head to Mesnička Street, the courtyard at Radićeva 19, Art Park (at which there are two entrance points), and of course – Ilica. Many people choose to combine the tunnel with a loop through Upper Town, emerging near Strossmayer Promenade, Lotrščak Tower or the historic St. Mark’s Square.

this tunnel wasn’t built in isolation…

Julien Duval/TZGZ

While it’s true that the fascinating Grič Tunnel is the only totally public section of Zagreb’s wartime underground, it wasn’t constructed in isolation. Between 1943 and 1945, various other secret tunnels and shelters were excavated under Upper Town, intended both for civilian protection and official use. One parallel passage connects the area around Tkalčićeva Street with the famous Dubravkin put near Tuškanac. Others were connected to government buildings of the period. Most of them are now closed or restricted, their echoes of an uncomfortable past silenced with them.

Sime Modric/TZGZ

If you want to head outside of the city itself and spend some time in nature, then Medvednica is your best bet. While the panoramic views, nature and the chance to see all kinds of wildlife are all lures, there are wartime bunkers and tunnels on the northern slopes towards Medvednica, as well. That goes without mentioning the natural cave systems…

These include those located around the former Villa Rebar area. It does have to be stated that generally speaking, these tunnels aren’t open for casual tourism and some carry local legends of longer connecting systems. Stories of older, pre-20th-century passages, sometimes linked to medieval cellars, church treasuries or strange 19th-century-era freemasonry, circulate. There’s been no proof that this is what they were for, but what would a weird tunnel be, without a weird legend to go with it?

zagreb is a city of layers, both above and below the ground

Samir Ceric Kovacevic/TZGZ

I’ve often said that Zagreb is a bit like an onion. In fact, I used that exact expression when describing the city’s architecture. It spans very old, Austro-Hungarian, socialist, brutalist, and ultra-modern. These styles are all contrasting, yet they somehow blend together effortlessly.

The same can be said about layers of history that form the underground world, deep beneath the plodding of shoes and the noise of tram tracks. Zagreb’s darker periods lie beneath the pavement. WWII ghosts can still be felt, and all the consequences that came with being an Axis country remain within the walls of these tunnels. Whether you fancy a stroll for the sake of it, or intend to visit to see an exhibition or an event, they’re absolutely worth seeing.

Interested in going even deeper, as it were? Look no further!

World.title: The Green Heart of Zagreb: Exploring the Croatian Capital’s Parks
World.content:
August the 10th, 2026 – Zagreb is one of the most heavily forested EU capitals, and the green heart of Zagreb acts as the lungs of the urban side’s beating heart.

Zagreb, much like Croatia as a whole, is very widely praised for its cafe culture, but you don’t need to be sitting in a busy city street to enjoy that coffee. Less celebrated, but equally defining, is just how green the city feels. Parks, gardens, lakes and densely forested hills weave through and around the capital, giving it (as touched on above) one of the highest concentrations of green space among EU cities.

For visitors, this means you can move from a museum, restaurant or old square to a lush, green meadow or park in mere minutes. Croatia is full of natural beauty, but when it comes to cities, these spaces are not an afterthought or somewhere forgotten by builders, they’re an absolutely central to the city’s identity and daily life.

The Green Horseshoe: Nature Woven into the City Centre

Sanjin Kastelan/TZGZ

Turning the clock back to the late 19th century, celebrated urban planner Milan Lenuci designed a U-shaped sequence of parks and squares that still frames the Lower Town (Donji grad). Known locally as Lenuci’s Green Horseshoe (or, if you want to get even more local: Zelena potkova), it connects promenades, blooming flower beds, monuments and grand public buildings into a continuous green corridor stretching for roughly 1.2 miles.

Zrinjevac is arguably the most atmospheric part of all. Just a short walk from the hustle and bustle of Ban Jelačić Square, an oasis awaits. It features towering mature plane trees, flower beds, fountains and a distinctive cast-iron music pavilion. During the summer, the pavilion hosts open-air concerts and free dance evenings; locals and visitors gather for waltz, swing or salsa under the trees. The scorching Croatian summer heat is calmed by the trees and thick plant life. The sequence continues near Strossmayer Square and King Tomislav Square, all the way to the main railway station (Glavni kolodvor), with statues, shaded walkways and seasonal colour. During the much cooler winter, Tomislav Square transforms into a ice rink; while swapping out its winter attire to serve as an open stage for classical concerts in summer.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

These central parks reward unhurried wandering. They are places to sit with a coffee, watch the city pass by, or simply appreciate how thoughtfully nature was integrated into Zagreb’s 19th-century expansion.

zagreb’s botanical garden

Marko Vrdoljak/TZGZ

At the southwestern end of the Green Horseshoe sits the Zagreb Botanical Garden (Botanički vrt). It was formally established back in 1889 by Professor Antun Heinz of the University of Zagreb, and opened to the public in 1891. Spanning about five hectares, it is both a scientific institution and a public garden of real charm.

The layout mixes English landscape style, long, winding paths, irregular plantings and a substantial arboretum with a more formal French-style parterre of flower beds. Collections include native Croatian flora, alpine and Mediterranean plants, aquatic species, conifers, and exotic trees and shrubs from all around the world. Estimates of the plant holdings range from several thousand to over 10,000 taxa, including many protected and endemic species. Small lakes with bridges, a rock garden and historic glasshouses (including a house for the giant Amazonian water lily Victoria amazonica) add to the allure.

Boska i Kreso/TZGZ

The garden is compact enough to explore in an hour or two yet rich enough to reward slower visits. It’s open seasonally (typically from April to early November, with limited winter opening in particularly calm, good weather) and charges a modest entrance fee. Located a short walk from the main train station, it is one of the easiest major green spaces to reach.

the legendary (and gorgeous) park maksimir

Julien Duval/TZGZ

East of the city centre lies Maksimir, the city’s largest, most famous, and most beloved park of all. Founded on the initiative of Bishop Maksimilijan Vrhovac and opened to the public back in 1794, it was the first large public park in all of southeastern Europe at the time. Spanning roughly 316 hectares (about 780 acres or so), it is comparable in scale to some of the grand European landscape parks and remains a protected monument of garden architecture and cultural heritage.

Originally conceived with baroque elements and later reshaped in the English Romantic style under Bishop Juraj Haulik, Maksimir combines broad meadows, mature oak and hornbeam woodland, five artificial lakes, streams, pavilions and long tree-lined avenues. Historic structures like the Swiss House, the Echo Pavilion and lookout points still stand. Wildlife of all kinds absolutely thrives here, with the park a well known habitat for birds, including rarer species.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

Within the park sits Zagreb Zoo, one of the oldest in the region (opened 1925), home to lions and all kinds of other animals you (thankfully) wouldn’t bump into in a cafe.

Families come for the playgrounds and lakeside walks; runners and walkers use the extensive paths; picnickers claim the grass on weekends. Trams (lines 4, 7, 11 and 12 among others) make it straightforward to reach. Maksimir feels both historic and lived-in. It’s a genuine city park that has adapted to changing fashions while retaining its charming, grand 18th- and 19th-century character.

the city of lakes – meet bundek and jarun

Julien Duval/TZGZ

South of the centre, the winding Sava River corridor offers a different kind of green space with a distinctly more recreational and watery character.

Bundek Park in Novi Zagreb sits between the Liberty (Most slobode) and Youth (Most mladosti) bridges. It centres on two expansive lakes surrounded by walking and cycling paths, meadows, playgrounds, sports courts and barbecue areas. Significantly renovated back during the mid-2000s, it has become a beloved for families, picnics and summer swimming (with lifeguards on the larger lake during the hotter season). An open-air stage hosts events, including the Pop Up by the Lake festival. Its proximity to the city centre (a short bus ride from the main station) and relaxed atmosphere make it especially popular with locals.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

Jarun sits further west and is often called Zagreb’s very own “sea”. This large artificial lake is ringed by paths popular with cyclists, runners and more. Islands, beaches, cafes, outdoor gym equipment and sports facilities give it a lively, active character. During the summer, it is a major venue for outdoor living; it also hosts the INmusic festival. Trams 5 and 17 serve the area. Where Bundek feels more intimate and family-oriented, Jarun offers scale and a truly energetic feel. Together, the two lakes give Zagreb something very few inland capitals possess: genuine waterside recreation within easy reach of the busy urban core.

bear mountain – medvednica has always had zagreb’s back (quite literally)

Julien Duval/TZGZ

Just north of Zagreb rises Medvednica, a densely forested mountain and protected nature park that functions as the city’s great outdoor backyard. Its highest peak, Sljeme, stands at 1,033 metres. The park is home to dozens of marked hiking trails of varying difficulty, mountain lodges serving traditional food, the medieval fortress of Medvedgrad, the Veternica cave, and viewpoints that look back over the entire city.

Miroslav Zadravec/TZGZ

Popular routes include the gradual Leustek trail and the steeper Bikčević trail toward the summit or lodges such as Puntijarka. Medvedgrad itself is a rewarding shorter destination, combining history with panoramic views. In winter the upper reaches attract skiers and sledgers; year-round the forest offers cool shade and clean air. Public transport (tram to Mihaljevac followed by bus, or the Sljeme cable car) and road access make it straightforward for visitors without a car. Few European capitals can claim a proper mountain nature park so close to the centre. For many Zagreb residents, “going to Sljeme” remains a ritual escape.

Though named after the populations of brown bears that once called it home (in Croatia, bear is medvjed), you won’t find them there now. As Zagreb expanded and grew, the bears retreated to more remote areas. If you do want to see them – head to Lika!

honestly, you can’t even name them all…

Julien Duval/TZGZ

Beyond these major sites, Zagreb is sprinkled with additional green spaces. Ribnjak Park near the cathedral offers a more intimate central oasis. Tuškanac and Cmrok on the northern slopes provide wooded walks and, in winter, popular sledging slopes. Mirogoj Cemetery, designed by Herman Bollé, is as much a landscaped park and open-air architectural gallery as a burial ground, with arcades, monuments and mature trees.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

Most city parks are free to enter, but the Botanical Garden and Zagreb Zoo charge modest fees. Public transport (trams and buses) reaches nearly all the major sites efficiently; walking and cycling are excellent options for the central Green Horseshoe and the lakeside paths. Spring brings blossom and milder temperatures; summer is ideal for the lakes and shaded trails; autumn colours are spectacular in Maksimir and on Medvednica; winter has its own quiet beauty, especially after snow has fallen.

zagreb gets hot, but it would be far hotter without these green spaces

Julien Duval/TZGZ

The above photo likely doesn’t stir up mental images of sunscreen and t-shirts, but we won’t sugarcoat it – Croatia is extremely hot in summer. Zagreb, far from the sea breeze, can become absolutely stifling. This is where the functionality of these green spaces come to the fore. Zagreb’s green network is not merely decorative. It cools the city down, supports biodiversity, provides everyday recreation for residents and offers visitors an immediate sense of the city’s character.

Sanjin Kastelan/TZGZ

You can step out of a cafe on the main square and be under the protective shade of tall plane trees within minutes, or leave the centre and be hiking forest trails and bumping into deer an hour later. That accessibility is rare and worth experiencing deliberately when in Zagreb. Everyone can become sick of the sound, pace and stress of the city, but you can’t always escape it as easily as you can here.

Whether you prefer the grandeur and elegance of Zrinjevac, Maksimir’s sprawling trails and numerous lakes, the energy of Bundek and Jarun, Medvednica or anywhere else, Zagreb’s green spaces should enjoy much more attention than they get.

World.title: Big Changes Coming for Drivers in Croatia in Autumn
World.content:
August the 10th, 2026 – Big changes are on the horizon for drivers in Croatia this autumn, more specifically as of October the 1st.

The beginning of the roll out of this change has in fact already begun. As of the 1st of July this year, drivers in Croatia are no longer able to use their previous top up SMART cards. However, they’ve still been able to spend the existing balance on them and will be able to continue doing so until the end of September.

After October the 1st, the SMART card will cease to function entirely as a means of payment on the motorways managed by HAC (Croatian Motorways), as reported by Poslovni.

an overhaul of a system used for years

For drivers in Croatia who still have a remaining amount on the card, there are two possibilities available to them. Those who wish to continue using electronic toll collection can transfer the money from their SMART prepaid account to an ENC prepaid account. In the process of doing that, they can exchange their SMART card for an ENC device at Croatian Motorways sales offices.

The second option is intended for those who do not wish to switch to ENC. They can request the closure of the SMART prepaid account and a refund of the available money. The request can be sent to HAC by e-mail or submitted in person at one of their sales offices.

Some drivers have been using the SMART system for years, especially on the motorways previously managed by Autocesta Rijeka – Zagreb, so it’s fairly understandable that some cards are still sitting in cars. Precisely these users should pay attention to the deadline, because after 30 September they will no longer be able to spend the remaining balance in the usual way.

massive changes are afoot for the toll collection system

The change comes at a time of major interventions in the Croatian toll collection system and increasing reliance on electronic payment. For the SMART card user themselves, however, the most important question is much simpler – whether there is still money on the account and what to do with it before the card ceases to be valid.

That is why it is not a bad idea to check the balance already now, especially if you use the SMART card only occasionally. Until the 1st of October, it can still be used for payment, but topping up is no longer possible. After that date the options remain transferring the funds to ENC or getting a monetary refund.
