World.title: Armenian Catholicos Garegin II attends first hearing in criminal trial
World.content:
Catholicos of All Armenians appears in court

A court in Armenia‘s Armavir region has begun hearing the criminal case against the Catholicos of All Armenians and six bishops who serve on the Supreme Spiritual Council. Garegin II attended the hearing in person.

Clergy members and politicians gathered outside the courthouse. Lawmakers from the opposition Armenia Alliance and I Have Honour Alliance left parliament during the afternoon and travelled to Etchmiadzin to show their support for the Catholicos. Dozens of worshippers also gathered outside, periodically chanting “Your Holiness” and singing traditional Armenian church hymns (sharakans).

Prosecutors accuse the Catholicos and the senior clergy of obstructing the enforcement of a court ruling.

Garegin II removed Bishop Gevorg Saroyan, head of the Masyatsotn Diocese, from his post. Saroyan is one of the senior clerics who joined Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan’s campaign to “reform the Church”. The bishop challenged his dismissal in court. The court ordered his temporary reinstatement as head of the diocese until it reaches a final decision in the case. However, before the court could rule on the merits, the Supreme Spiritual Council, led by the Catholicos, also defrocked him. The council argued that the courts have no jurisdiction over the Church’s internal affairs.

Lawyer Ara Zohrabyan says the Catholicos faces criminal prosecution for carrying out his “ecclesiastical and canonical duties”.

He argues that state interference in the Catholicos’s decisions violates the principle of Church autonomy, the constitutional relationship between the state and the Church, and freedom of religion.

“In this criminal case, the court will examine not only the charges against specific individuals, but also another fundamental question: whether the secular authorities can interfere in the internal life of the Church and criminalise the exercise of the canonical authority of the Catholicos of All Armenians,” the lawyer said.

The trial comes after tensions between the government and the Church steadily escalated.

About a year ago, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan called for the Catholicos to step down. He first argued that Garegin II could not lead the Church because he had broken his vow of celibacy and had a daughter. He later accused the Catholicos of having links to foreign intelligence services. The ruling Civil Contract party has also included the removal of the “de facto head of the Church” in its election manifesto.

Members of the ruling party accuse the Church of interfering in Armenia’s domestic and foreign policy. The parliamentary opposition rejects that claim. Opposition lawmakers argue that it is the government that is unlawfully interfering in the Church’s affairs.

First hearing ends after 30 minutes as judge recuses himself

Shortly after the hearing began, Judge Hakob Manukyan announced that part of the proceedings would take place behind closed doors because they would involve “personal information”. He said the information concerned both himself and the Catholicos’s lawyer.

“A few minutes later, lawyer Ara Zohrabyan told journalists: “The judge has recused himself. He has withdrawn from hearing this case.”

According to Zohrabyan, the judge said he had once granted him his licence to practise law, which could “raise doubts about his impartiality”. Zohrabyan said he did not believe this constituted valid grounds for recusal.

“However, he refused to take part in this disgraceful trial. The very fact that the Catholicos is standing trial is deeply troubling. The case will now go to another judge.”

After the hearing, the Catholicos of All Armenians and his supporters headed to the cathedral to attend a church service and pray together.

Garegin II: “The authorities are trying to bring the Church under their control”

After the service, the Catholicos addressed those gathered outside the cathedral. He said the authorities were taking steps to undermine the Church’s authority, restrict its autonomy and bring it under their control.

“The authorities are persecuting the Church and the clergy. They have arrested and restricted the freedom of a number of clergymen, benefactors and other patriotic individuals through unlawful and fabricated criminal cases,” he said.

The Catholicos dismissed the charges against himself and the six clergymen as groundless.

“We remain steadfast in our faith and determination to defend our rights, which are guaranteed both by our country’s Constitution and by the fundamental principles of international law.”

Opposition declares a “day of shame”

Marianna Gakhramanyan, an MP from the opposition I Have Honour Alliance, said:

“Today is a day of shame. The Catholicos of All Armenians, our spiritual father and the head of our Church, is standing trial in Etchmiadzin. It is shameful and unprecedented. This is an attack not only on the independence of the Armenian Apostolic Church but also on Armenia’s Constitution, which clearly states that the political authorities have no right to interfere in the affairs of the Church and that the Church is separate from the state.”

“Who is defending the Church – us or you?” asks ruling party MP

Commenting on opposition lawmakers who came to support the Catholicos, Civil Contract MP Artur Hovhannisyan said:

“The Church has begun interfering in Armenia’s domestic and foreign policy.”

He also referred to the allegations that the Catholicos had violated his vow of celibacy:

“We are the ones standing with the Church. We are the ones defending the Church. You are defending clergymen who broke their vow of celibacy, who engage in politics and use religion and the Church to protect themselves from the consequences of breaking that vow and taking part in politics. Anyone who has broken the vow of celibacy should leave the Church.”

The ruling Civil Contract party’s election manifesto also outlines plans to reform the Church. Under the proposal, the “de facto head of the Church”, as Pashinyan’s team refers to the Catholicos, should leave office. The plan calls for the election of a locum tenens, the adoption of a new Church charter containing “mechanisms to preserve centuries-old traditions”, and, ultimately, the election of a new Catholicos.

Comment

Political analyst Tigran Grigoryan told Reuters:

“Pashinyan has come to see the Church as a political threat and as an institution capable of supporting the opposition and various political parties in their efforts to gain power.

“The case against the clergy fits into a broader pattern of selective justice pursued by Pashinyan’s government, under which leading opposition figures have been arrested and some of their property has been confiscated by the state.”

Catholicos of All Armenians appears in court

World.title: Sussan Ley took America's 'road to nowhere', it helped her find herself again
World.content:
After 276 days as the first female leader of the Coalition, Sussan Ley was axed as Opposition leader. It led to a life-changing and eye-opening experience as she found solitude, her voice and an empathy for the downtrodden of middle America while on its 'road to nowhere'.

Here, on a series of Greyhound buses, Ms Ley saw the United States. She saw a dispassionate and divided nation but one that cannot be compared to Australia.

"I think we make a mistake if we try to draw parallels," Ms Ley told 7.30 in her first interview since exiting politics.

"And if you go to the US and feel that there are immediate parallels, well, the first thing that hits you is that there actually are not."

While Ms Ley was away and out of the spotlight, the rise of One Nation has continued.

The party has soared in opinion polls and its leader Pauline Hanson has captured plenty of attention and coverage.

Senator Hanson's meeting with convicted criminal and far-right activist Tommy Robinson courted controversy but it has been her comments about wanting to make Australia a monocultural society that have drawn much discussion.

One Nation and its leader Pauline Hanson have enjoyed a rise in the polls. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Ms Ley said her visit to the US only strengthened her view of the success of multiculturalism in Australia.

"I am a huge supporter of the Australian multicultural project for the simple reason that we have been able to achieve multicultural Australia not by erasing people's differences but by giving them space to belong," Ms Ley told 7.30.

"I think this is something we should all be incredibly proud of.

"I'm not a political commentator for the US, but I didn't see communities melting together like I see here.

"In fact, I saw different communities from different backgrounds sitting very uncomfortably alongside each other."

Prisoners, nuns and homeless travel companions

Asked if that meant that One Nation had got it wrong Ms Ley was noncommittal but said what she also saw in the US was a clear disconnect between the elite political class and those she travelled with.

Sussan Ley was on a journey to find her own voice after her political career ended. (Supplied: Sussan Ley)

As she travelled on those Greyhound buses — with " a lot of sketchy and strange characters" — on a journey she had dreamt up more than two decades ago, Ms Ley said she found the true US.

It was a surprising reckoning.

"I always felt that to the views of America that tourists had, that the media had, that we hear so much in the Zeitgeist, the view from Disneyland, the Statue of Liberty, Yosemite, Vegas, were just not the real America.

" I wanted to see that ... and I did. And what I saw was incredible and surprising. "

While the trip Ms Ley undertook was hardly the glitz and glamour of driving Pacific Coast Highway or Route 66 it removed some of the romanticism that usually surrounds the notion of the great American road trip.

The Greyhound bus has long been a cheaper option for the masses but what Ms Ley saw and heard revealed more about modern day USA.

Travelling through the middle of America on a Greyhound bus had been a bucket list item for Sussan Ley. (Supplied: Sussan Ley)

"In some states, you get a ticket to get on the Greyhound if you're homeless and the state wants you to leave," Ms Ley said.

"There were some returning prisoners, there were some nuns, there were veterans, there were many assistance dogs.

"I saw very, very few children.

"There were people whose lives were in transition and disarray, and that's what struck me from the moment I got on the first bus.

"There's several buses to get from the top of North Dakota to the bottom of Texas but it's hard to describe the expression on someone's face that comes from a lifetime of being overlooked.

"When I sat next to people and saw them in their most unguarded moments, the gap between what they hopefully looked into a future with and the reality that gradually settled on them was apparent.

"And what I mean by that is that I was often in awe of the dignity and the humanity of so many people that I travelled with."

America's 'incredible disconnection'

Asked what she learned about those "overlooked" Americans, Ms Ley said it was their disconnect from the political class that confronted her.

Donald Trump promised to make the United States better. (Supplied: Sussan Ley)

"The disconnection really was quite confronting," she told 7.30.

"I expected as I travelled to still see that clenched fist sense of pride in the US, in the flag, in the identity of the country.

"I've got to be honest, I didn't see that.

"It doesn't mean it didn't exist in people's hearts, but I didn't see it expressed, what I saw was incredible disconnection.

"I saw disconnection as a human condition rather than a political constituency. And people were simply not interested in the institutions and the organisations that ostensibly are there to represent them, to look after them and to be there for them.

"If you look back over history, you see the public in America and obviously around the world engaged, active, angry. What I saw was just an incredible stepping back and disinterest."

Ms Ley says what she saw was a people disconnected with their politicians. (Reuters: Kylie Cooper)

Asked to reconcile her understanding of the downtrodden, Ms Ley said it had been a constant.

"It was always there," she said.

" But remember that when you speak as a politician, you speak as a politician. You don't always speak with your own voice. "

Ms Ley said now that she has returned she will not be back in politics. That chapter is closed and she has no regrets.

"If I think about my time in politics, I'm proud of what I achieved," she said.

"I don't dwell on it because I'm very much focused on the next chapter of my life."

What that is Ms Ley says she is still unsure of but hopes it leads to a better Australia.

"I want to contribute to public life for the benefit of my grandchildren and their future in this country and to make it a better place," she said.

"How that happens, I'm not yet sure, but I am committed to that mission."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Cats confirm Kolodjashnij unavailable to play amid concussion waiver saga
World.content:
The player at the centre of a concussion waiver controversy, Geelong's Jake Kolodjashnij, will not play this weekend as the club prepares to find out whether it will face sanctions.

It emerged last Thursday that the Cats struck a secret agreement with a player, who had had a history of concussions.

Kolodjashnij went public confirming he was the player involved.

The waiver has since been removed from his contract.

"Geelong Cats defender Jake Kolodjashnij will be unavailable for selection at AFL or VFL level this weekend," the club said a statement late on Tuesday.

"The care and wellbeing of Jake remains the club's priority, and the club will continue to support him and his family through this period."

The Cats had until the end of Tuesday to respond to the "please explain" from the AFL over the concussion waiver that Kolodjashnij signed but which was never seen by the AFL or the AFLPA.

Geelong Cats board holds crisis meeting over concussion deal Geelong is about to reply to the AFL's please explain as the Cats brace for a potential massive penalty over the secret concussion deal with Jake Kolodjashnij.

Amid speculation over the futures of Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking and AFL chairman Craig Drummond, the club board had held a crisis meeting on Monday to work out its response to the league.

Hocking was Cats chief executive and Drummond was the club president when the deal was struck two years ago with Koladjashnij.

The Geelong defender signed a waiver that meant he effectively took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to indemnify the club and its medical staff from potential court action.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Media reports on Tuesday said that the AFL Commission had hired independent legal counsel to help determine whether the Cats should face sanctions over the issue.

The 31-year-old Kolodjashnij was drafted by the club in 2013 and he has played 209 games for Geelong.

He last played at AFL level for the Cats against GWS a month ago.

His twin brother Kade, who played for Gold Coast and Melbourne, was forced to retire in 2020 due to concussion issues.

World.title: Sydney fugitive arrested in Lebanon accused of running crime syndicate
World.content:
For years, fugitive George Dib had been a mystery.

The son of a respected service station entrepreneur, Mr Dib first appeared on the radar of law enforcement in 2013, then he vanished.

But Australian authorities had been watching.

Mr Dib, arrested last week in Lebanon, is now facing the possibility of spending decades in a Middle Eastern jail over claims he directed a global organised crime syndicate while on the run.

"He is suspected of brokering and organising multiple drug shipments to Australia on behalf of a wide range of criminal syndicates from around the world during the past 11 years," the Australian Federal Police (AFP) said after his capture in Lebanon last week.

His father is not accused of any wrongdoing.

Fugitives join forces overseas

For more than a decade, George Dib has been the source of underworld and police intrigue.

Though never convicted of a crime, Mr Dib was suspected to be part of the "Aussie Cartel", before it was systematically dismantled in Türkiye in 2023.

But according to an intelligence file from the NSW Crime Commission obtained by the ABC, Mr Dib is accused of being a main player in another offshore drug conglomerate.

A NSW Police mugshot of Rafat Alameddine, who has since fled to Lebanon. (Supplied: NSW Police)

The report names Mr Dib alongside fellow Lebanese fugitives Bilal Haouchar and Alameddine crime family boss Rafat Alameddine among other alleged Sydney criminals who joined forces.

Alameddine is wanted by NSW Police accused of two murders at the height of the Alameddines' gang war with the Hamzy family in 2021.

Haouchar himself was sentenced to eight years in jail by a Beirut court in May 2025 for a raft of drug crimes he committed while on the run from Australia.

Haouchar remains locked up in a Lebanese jail after AFP intelligence helped to jail him there. (Supplied: NSW Police)

Mr Dib, Alameddine and Haouchar are accused of sending threatening messages dubbed 'AUS weekly market updates' to Sydney's criminal milieu "in an attempt to set the distribution price of cocaine at $225,000 per kilogram".

Fall of 'The Commission'

It is alleged Mr Dib's coalition of criminals' rise came as another toppled.

The "AUS weekly market updates" landed in the inboxes of gangsters across Sydney in June 2023.

Just days earlier, the final domino of rival drug cartel "The Commission" fell when Alen Moradian was shot dead inside a Bondi car park.

Crime boss Alen Moradian. (Supplied: Nine Entertainment)

The Commission operated under a similar rule of law, spreading similar threatening message throughout the underworld through 2022 to 2023.

"To the drop kick wannabe gangsters who just called out the Commission. "You shouldn't try to claim things you did not know. "We have been dominating Sydney for the past 3 years now and like puppy dogs you have all submitted each time. "We are well aware who is responsible, writing up that message to throw the scene off won't work. "And you/they/them pop your head out of hiding you can bet your dollar we will be there to chop it off. "The weak dog who wrote that message has most likely paid us before and now feeling tough, nevertheless no stone will unturned. No friend will be loyal. "Watch this and you will know what we are about."

Though its authors were not clarified in the NSW Crime Commission intelligence, the following message was spread the day after Moradian was killed.

"To every one trying to call the shots that are hiding in different countries and playing with NSW prices. "We regret to inform your commission we control the prices in NSW from now on. "This is not just a warning but a threat to everyone who thinks they can run the streets here. "All NSW crews have come together to end your so called commission. Please remember the bullets dont rust here especially when you guys want to threaten familys we will also not toelerate this and will respond with kidnapping knee capping and if we hear any of your crews are trying to control prices under your guidelines we will come after anyone from your commission. "You guys will now follow our rules and respect us prices will be dropping at anyones will … "Thank you."

Mr Dib, nicknamed "Junior", according to Lebanese media, was picked up by the Information Branch of the Internal Security Force last week during a night-time raid.

With him in custody are about a dozen figures with links to Sydney's organised crime scene, sources told the ABC.

The intelligence that helped capture Mr Dib was provided by the AFP to Lebanese authorities by Operation Gain.

The unit is credited with taking down the "Aussie Cartel", led by drug lord Hakan Ayik out of Istanbul in 2023, and disrupting the activities of several wanted fugitives.

World.title: Alleged 2007 murder at Adelaide party involved 'payback', court told
World.content:
A man standing trial for murder over a fatal birthday party stabbing almost 20 years ago was allegedly among a group of men who stormed the celebrations seeking "payback", a court has heard.

Kimlong Rim, 38, is standing trial in South Australia's Supreme Court after pleading not guilty to the murder of Thea Kheav, 21, outside a party at Parafield Gardens, in Adelaide's north, in December 2007.

Opening the trial on Tuesday, prosecutor Kos Lesses told the jury that while Mr Rim did not inflict the fatal stab wound, he was among a group of four men accused of murdering Mr Kheav.

He said Mr Kheav was a guest at the 18th birthday party, which he had attended with his brothers.

"An argument broke out with one of the Kheav brothers and one of the men from the accused's group," Mr Lesses said.

He told the jury that that man had left the party "in an angry state" but later returned in a convoy of cars with "a large group of men", including Mr Rim and three others allegedly involved in the murder.

"[They] armed themselves with bottles and planks of wood, along with a machete-type knife," Mr Lesses said.

"They arrived at that party as a group and it's alleged they disrupted the party as a group. It's alleged they were working as a team, or a group.

"As a result of that group attack, Thea Kheav was fatally stabbed and died at the scene of this birthday party."

Kimlong Rim (left) is standing trial after pleading not guilty to the 2007 murder of Thea Kheav. (ABC News)

Mr Lesses told the jury the altercation took part in two stages, beginning when Mr Kheav was first struck with a bottle while standing next to a woman.

The jury was also told the second stage involved Mr Kheav's attempt to flee into the backyard of the house.

Mr Lesses said Mr Kheav had tried to climb over gates, but he was pulled to the ground where he was "kicked and punched, along with being stabbed in the chest with a long-bladed knife".

Crime about 'payback', court told

Mr Lesses said that despite the efforts of paramedics, Mr Kheav was unable to be resuscitated.

His cause of death was later determined to be a single stab wound to his chest, but he also had other injuries on his body, including a cut to his face.

Mr Lesses said the alleged crime was "borne out of a retaliation".

"It's about an armed group of men who retaliated by attending as a group to disrupt the party and effect payback on one of the Kheav brothers," Mr Lesses said.

Police attended the scene after a party was held at a Parafield Gardens house. (ABC News: ABC News)

Mr Lesses told the jury the alleged murder weapon was never recovered but had been described as "looking like a machete".

Mr Rim's defence barrister, Ryan Williams SC, told the jury it was not disputed his client was at the party and had "engaged in deplorable behaviour", but he said Mr Rim was not a murderer.

"What is in dispute is this idea that he is a murderer," he said.

" Put simply, ladies and gentlemen, the issues in dispute do not concern whether or not he, together with others, acted generally angrily, violently or whatever … but whether what he did, what he actually had in his mind, make him a murderer. "

Justice Rachael Gray, who is presiding over the trial, urged the 14-person jury to keep an open mind until it retires to consider a verdict.

The trial is expected to continue for three weeks.

World.title: Man tells jury he saw farmer accused of triple murder shoot family
World.content:
The trial of a Queensland cattle farmer accused of a triple murder and an attempted murder in 2022 has heard from a man who says he witnessed the shooting and survived a bullet wound himself.

Darryl Valroy Young, 63, pleaded not guilty to three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder in the Supreme Court in Townsville.

The jury trial, expected to run for three weeks, has heard the Bogie farmer and owner of Shannonvale Station is accused of killing his neighbour Graham Tighe, as well as Mr Tighe's mother Maree Schwarz and stepfather Mervyn Schwarz by shooting each of them with a rifle.

Darryl Valroy Young took notes with pen and paper as Ross Tighe gave evidence. (ABC News: Carole Howlett)

The trial has also heard that Mr Young is accused of shooting Graham's brother, Ross Tighe, who survived the incident on August 4, 2022.

Mr Young's defence lawyer has argued the farmer never saw the family he is accused of shooting on the day of the alleged incident.

Ross Tighe, 34, gave evidence on Tuesday via video link from a courtroom in Mackay, south of Townsville.

He told the court the family took two utes to meet Mr Young at the gate of Shannonvale Station on the day of the alleged shooting where there was a tense exchange.

Ross Tighe told the court he saw Mr Young shoot Maree Schwarz and Mervyn Schwarz (pictured) with a rifle. (Supplied)

Brother describes shooting

He said Mr Young refused to shake Mervyn Schwarz's hand and then retrieved a rifle from the back seat of his ute and began firing.

"He shot Merv in the face — then I turned around to start running," Mr Tighe said.

"I ran between the utes to get behind them for cover — when I turned, I'm pretty sure I got shot in the stomach and it went into my hip.

"I saw Graham had been shot as well on the ground towards the back of the utes."

Ross Tighe said he saw Mr Young shoot his brother Graham Tighe (pictured). (Facebook)

Mr Tighe told the court he then looked for his mother.

"She had been shot, she was sort of on her knees, hiding her stomach," he said.

'I knew they were dead'

Mr Tighe said after the shooting he ran downhill in an attempt to hide from Mr Young.

"I tried to run, my right leg kept falling over, I fell down like five or six times trying to get to where I ran towards," he said.

"I was running and when I stopped to lie down to hide I heard two more gunshots.

"I tried to cover myself with grass really quickly."

He said after about10 minutes he returned to the gate and heard the engine of one of his family's two utes running.

"I knew they were all going to be dead so I was trying not to look, I didn't look for mum and then I opened the car door because the ignition was on and she was there," he said.

"She was f**king shot … through the window."

Mr Tighe said he drove away in another car, found help and was taken to Mackay Base Hospital via rescue helicopter.

Cattle accusations

The trial heard Mr Young's Shannonvale Station shared a boundary with Sutherland Station which was jointly owned by Mervyn Schwarz, Maree Schwarz and Graham Tighe.

Ross Tighe said there was an unfenced area where the cattle stations met.

He said that Mr Young had accused his brother, Graham Tighe, of causing stress to cattle by "galloping them".

He said that on the morning of the alleged shooting Mr Young accused the family of stealing his calves.

Ross Tighe told the court that no cattle had been galloped, nor were any calves stolen.

He also denied he or his family members were armed on that day.

Ross Tighe told the court he ran away from Darryl Valroy Young as he fired bullets from a rifle. (ABC News: Carole Howlett)

Cross examination begins

Mr Young's defence lawyer Anthony J Kimmins began to cross examine Ross Tighe on Tuesday.

He asked Mr Tighe about the cattle business his family ran.

Mr Tighe explained he was a manager of a 10,500 acre cattle station in Roma which, like Sutherland Station at Bogie, was owned by his brother, stepfather and mother.

He said his family owned a property at Tara and two smaller properties but said he was not on any property titles.

He said he took a weekly wage for his role in the family business as did his partner at the time and had endeavoured to purchase one of the family's smaller properties.

Mr Kimmins also questioned Mr Tighe about a short pigging trip he went on with Mr Young and his son Derrick Young as well as a fence, kilometres in length, which the families installed together.

Cross examination of Mr Tighe will resume on Wednesday.

The trial continues.

World.title: The RBA's best guess is that it's done hiking interest rates
World.content:
Every second meeting, the Reserve Bank's boffins produce a set of economic forecasts that guides the board's thinking for the next three months.

The latest set of forecasts is good news for mortgage borrowers fearing further rate hikes.

Inflation was dramatically lower than the RBA expected just three months ago in May, even though oil prices behaved much as expected.

What's more, the bank continues to expect inflation to fall to the mid-point of its 2-3 per cent target range by the end of 2027, even though rates are tipped to be lower.

The RBA uses market pricing for future interest rates in its forecasts, so as not to given any hints about its own forward view, and traders now expect the cash rate to be about the same at the end of the forecast period in December 2028 as it is now — 4.35 per cent.

RBA keeps rate at 4.35pc The Reserve Bank has kept interest rates on hold at its August meeting, after three rate hikes earlier this year.

The Reserve Bank's governor Michele Bullock, learning from the mistakes of her predecessor Philip Lowe, is always reticent about giving so-called forward guidance on interest rates, that is a view on where they'll likely be at some point in the future.

At today's press conference, she came about as close to doing so as I have ever heard.

Referring to the bank's forecast that inflation would be at the mid-point of the target band by the end of 2027, she said, "This is a reasonable time to get inflation back down to target."

Reading between the lines, that tells you that if the economy continues tracking close to the RBA's current forecasts then it will see no need for further rate rises.

The RBA's forecasts show it thinks inflation will return to target with the current cash rate. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

'May be a need for further interest rate rises'

But before borrowers break out the champagne, or trade the baked beans for Wagyu and shiraz, Ms Bullock used much of her press conference to emphasise that higher rates aren't off the table just yet.

Loading...

"We'll still need to see some further progress before the board can be confident we're going to get inflation back to target with current monetary policy settings," she said.

"In waiting, the board isn't ruling out there may be a need for further interest rate rises if we look like we're off a path that takes us with inflation remaining above the target for much longer in the forecasts."

Just to make sure there was no doubt, Ms Bullock reiterated that a reduction in rates was not even discussed at the board meeting, as well as offering her personal view.

" We already raised three times, and we will go again if we need to. And I think personally that it's quite possible we may need to go, but we will wait and see what the data tells us. "

For those of us attending the Statement on Monetary Policy and briefed by the RBA's chief economist Sarah Hunter, it's clear why Michele Bullock is at pains to keep a rate hike firmly on the table.

There's a litany of upside risks to the RBA's inflation forecasts, the realisation of any of which could delay the return to target beyond a "reasonable time" and see the bank hike again.

The global economy could keep growing more strongly than expected.

The Middle East oil crisis could flare up or keep dragging on, sending oil prices back over $US100 a barrel.

The energy price shock we've already had might only just be filtering through to broader price rises, especially with the fuel excise cut having temporarily mitigated some of the pain.

The major risks to the central bank's inflation forecasts, including the Middle East conflict and energy shock, are to the upside. (Reuters: Hamad I Mohammed)

The capacity constraints in the economy could worsen rather than improve, with productivity again going backwards and the RBA lowering its already weak forecasts.

That weak productivity is already evident in stubborn domestic inflation, such as in the services sector, while the data centre construction boom threatens to soak up scarce tradies and push building costs to yet fresh heights.

To top it off, the looming El Niño risks slashing food production and raising prices.

Loading

Complacency the biggest inflation threat

Meanwhile, there's just one major downside risk to inflation identified by the RBA, which is a deeper-than-expected housing market downturn that dents residential building demand and sees nervy home owners close their wallets as prices keep falling.

In the presser, Bullock herself said repeatedly that housing is not the bank's focus right now.

"That isn't really the main game here for us at the moment," she told reporters.

"The main game here for us is excess capacity, tight labour market, particularly in some areas like construction, the Middle East conflict, the AI boom, these are all the things that are front of mind in terms of risks to the inflation outlook."

With most of the risks to the upside, Michele Bullock was most keen to address the greatest risk of all — complacency.

"It's important that people believe we will act if we need to," she said.

ABC Business Daily The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news.

At this point, the Reserve Bank's greatest enemy is a widespread expectation that there won't be any further rate hikes.

Well-practised in jawboning, the RBA governor was today playing the role of a financial Jaws: "Just when you thought it was safe to go back into the market …", as they would say in the movie.

Bullock knows full well that further rate hikes risk pushing unemployment above 5 per cent and tipping the economy into recession.

The RBA board will take that risk if it has to, but it would rather not.

World.title: Veteran Manly prop Nathan Brown outlines NRL exit plan
World.content:
Manly prop Nathan Brown has revealed he decided at the start of the season this would be his last in the NRL, as the veteran forward eyes a move to the Super League.

Off contract at the end of 2026, Brown has confirmed he will finish up at Manly this year as the Sea Eagles begin a changing of the guard in the forward pack.

Brown's final month at Manly will take on even more importance on Friday night, after he was called in to start for the first time in two years against the Dolphins amid the Sea Eagles' forwards shortage.

The 33-year-old is still hoping to exit the NRL in a finals series, with Manly likely needing to win their last four games to return to the top eight.

Munster free to play Melbourne Storm five-eighth Cameron Munster avoids suspension after the NRL match review committee downgrades his dangerous contact charge from Saturday's win over Manly.

"I just knew it was my time to call it quits in the NRL … I made my debut in 2013, so it's my 14th year. When your time's up, your time is up," Brown told AAP.

"The last thing I wanted to do was sit on the fence with whether I want to stay or go overseas.

"It's just made everything a lot easier to go all in this year and enjoy every moment, every training session and every game."

Brown was regarded as one of the most aggressive forwards in the game when he debuted at Wests Tigers in 2013, as well as during a two-year stint at South Sydney.

Nathan Brown played six seasons at the Eels, making his Origin debut while at the club. (Getty Images: Anthony Au-Yeung)

He came into his own at Parramatta, playing two State of Origins for NSW in 2020 and the 2022 grand final for the Eels before reviving his career with a train-and-trial deal at Manly in 2024.

"I find it funny [looking back at old footage)]" said Brown, who is on track to reach 200 games this month.

"When I started, I was a lot bigger. I wasn't really that fit. I was a bit overweight for my size and my position. And I had a different attitude back then.

"But at the same time, you learn a lot from it. You feel grateful that you had to go through those things."

Brown's NRL retirement comes with fellow veteran Manly prop Siua Taukeiaho off contract after breaking his leg in two places in May.

The Sea Eagles have signed props Davvy Moale and Toni Mataele for next year, while Kayliss Fatialofa will arrive as a highly-heralded second rower.

Teenage prop Simi Laiafi has also shown promise starting this year alongside Taniela Paseka, and looms as a long-term prospect.

Brown said he was proud of the impact he was able to have off the bench this year, still hitting the line with gusto.

"You don't want to be finishing by just clutching at the straws and hanging on by a thread," he said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I feel like I can probably still physically play another year in the NRL. But in the mental side of things, I'm just ready."

Manly expect to be without prop Paseka for at least a fortnight after he injured his knee against Melbourne last week, in a seismic blow to their finals chances.

Ethan Bullemor (concussion) remains sidelined, while Kobe Hetherington (biceps) last week joined Taukeiaho in being out for the season.

Second-rower Ben Trbojevic (concussion) is also still out, while his superstar brother Tom has been kept on ice for another week in his return from a hamstring injury.

AAP

World.title: Canberra Institute of Technology CEO Margot McNeill resigns
World.content:
Canberra Institute of Technology (CIT) chief executive Margot McNeill has resigned from the role after months of pressure to step down.

Dr McNeill's appointment as CIT CEO was brought into question earlier this year after revelations she had failed to disclose an investigation into misconduct in her previous role at TAFE NSW.

In the statement announcing her resignation, Dr McNeill said her decision was "tremendously difficult".

"It has become clear that this decision is in the best interest of the CIT community, especially students and staff, about whom I care deeply. Equally, it is in my best interest, including that of my family," she said.

Dr McNeill was appointed as CEO in June 2025.

In May this year, Dr McNeill came under further pressure to resign after an ACT Legislative Assembly inquiry found she "should have disclosed the information about the misconduct investigation or findings to the CIT board in a timely manner and that she did not".

Dr McNeill had repeatedly said she was under a strict obligation not to share the existence of the investigation, but TAFE NSW has publicly contradicted that.

Her evidence before the initial committee triggered another assembly probe, which questioned whether Dr McNeill had misled the assembly.

Its findings, released last week, criticised Dr McNeill as having been "deliberately obstructive" and "combative".

Dr McNeill's legal case against TAFE NSW is ongoing in the NSW Supreme Court.

'A dream opportunity'

Dr McNeill has been on extended leave amid the controversy.

On Friday last week, Mitch Pirie was appointed acting CEO.

Until now he has been the ACT government's acting deputy under treasurer.

Mitch Pirie has been appointed the acting CEO of CIT. (LinkedIn: Mitch Pirie)

In a statement about her resignation, Dr McNeill said it had been "a source of great pride" to lead the "much-loved Canberra institution.

"Sector leaders encouraged me to apply for this role in recognition of my extensive expertise in tertiary harmonisation and education excellence," she said.

"It was a dream opportunity to use my experience and leadership to position CIT as a hub for innovation during such an exciting period in tertiary education transformation."

Dr McNeill added that she continued to be passionate about the value of the vocational education and training sector, which she had "dedicated 40 years of [her] life to".

In a statement, CIT said its board had accepted Dr McNeill's resignation from the position.

"Dr McNeill led CIT over the last 13 months, bringing considerable expertise and energy to the role and introduced significant changes to CIT's operations, including reductions in executive staffing and increased staff communications," the statement said.

World.title: Educators on the line in proposed Zoos Victoria job cuts
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaAnimals Educators on the line in proposed Zoos Victoria job cuts Kieran Rooney August 11, 2026 — 7:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than a third of educator positions could be cut from Zoos Victoria under proposed redundancies, prompting fears the visits by 150,000 students each year will be cut and the standard of teaching affected. The Age revealed in June that Zoos Victoria was preparing a restructure that would cut up to 70 full-time roles from its 950-strong workforce – a figure the organisation has pushed back on as it consults staff about the changes. Among the most contentious proposals is a 38 per cent reduction in education staff at Melbourne Zoo – from roughly 6.2 full-time staff to 3.8 – who assist in teaching students and other groups about wildlife and conservation. A baby giraffe at Melbourne Zoo. Jo Howell The Community and Public Sector Union and United Workers Union said on Monday that about 600 staff – almost two-thirds of the organisation’s workforce – had responded to the proposed changes, which would be finalised later this month.



CPSU state secretary Jiselle Hanna said any cuts to education staff would devastate the 150,000 students who visited Melbourne Zoo, Werribee Zoo, Healesville Sanctuary and Kyabram Fauna Park every year. Related Article Animals Bailout backing was offered to Zoos Victoria a year before job cuts “Staff are telling us that they will not be able to maintain the volume of visits or the standard of education for young learners if these cuts go ahead,” Hanna said. “If this restructure is genuinely being driven by financial pressures, then why would cuts be made to an entity that brings in millions of dollars annually through school visits? “The impacted staff are highly skilled workers with decades of experience. They keep visitors educated, entertained and, most importantly, safe.”



The CPSU and the United Workers Union have urgently demanded Zoos Victoria wind back the scale of the cuts, arguing it will have flow-on effects across all parts of the organisation as staff are asked to handle new responsibilities. “This restructure process has demonstrated how out of touch the executive team is with the realities of the zoo and the work that zoo staff undertake,” Hanna said. A Zoos Victoria spokesperson said frontline services would not be impacted, as official consultation continued before a final decision was announced on August 25. “Our employees have provided valuable feedback through this consultation process, and we are considering this feedback carefully,” the spokesperson said. “Zoos Victoria will remain a world-class wildlife destination, and our commitment to fighting wildlife extinction remains.”



The Age has previously reported staff concerns that the restructure could also affect wildlife and conservation roles across the organisation, however, Zoos Victoria says frontline and animal care roles will not be directly affected. Related Article Animals Zoos Victoria to cut up to 70 jobs, including in conservation and wildlife Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell said Zoos Victoria should be upfront about what the cuts would mean for conservation programs. “With bird flu ravaging our state and our volunteer wildlife carers under enormous strain, we simply can’t afford to lose any of the dedicated Zoos Victoria teams whose job it is to respond to injured wildlife and protect threatened species,” she said. “It’s simply not good enough to say there won’t be cuts to frontline services without being clear about what happens to the conservation and wildlife rescue work that sits behind them.”

World.title: Labor blasted for restricting prisoner rights after gangland boss’s court victory
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaPrisons Labor blasted for restricting prisoner rights after gangland boss’s court victory Lachlan Abbott and Erin Pearson August 11, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wrongfully imprisoned academic Kylie Moore-Gilbert, the ombudsman and a chorus of human rights advocates have voiced serious unease about the Carroll government’s plan to curtail the right of Victorian prisoners to access fresh air daily. Labor is poised to pass legislation with opposition support in the upper house this week to make the right to open air for at least an hour each day “subject to operational considerations” in prisons, despite conceding this breaches Victoria’s human rights charter. Kylie Moore-Gilbert spent years imprisoned in Iran on trumped-up espionage charges. Scott McNaughton The Victorian Ombudsman wrote to the leaders of both major parties this month to express concern about the bill, which opponents say does not adhere to the international minimum standards for prisoners, a set of rules named after Nelson Mandela. The government argues the change is necessary to prevent lawsuits such as that brought by murderer and crime boss George Marrogi, who won a Supreme Court judgment in January that found some of his maximum-security units did not provide adequate open-air access.



Amendments to the Corrections Act would allow the state to limit a prisoner’s open-air rights “on an ongoing basis or for extended periods of time”, according to the bill’s explanatory memorandum. The legislation also stops the state from paying damages for any previous breaches of a prisoner’s open-air rights, despite corrections being plagued with prolonged lockdowns in recent years. Moore-Gilbert, who spent 804 days detained in Iran, said even the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps provided her access to fresh air while she was imprisoned. “This terror organisation gave me a minimum of 30 minutes a day outside, even when I was held in solitary confinement,” she said.



“Why on earth is the Victorian government proposing to lower its human rights standards beneath those of even the despotic regime in Iran?” Related Article Crime Underworld kingpin wins court battle over ‘inhumane’ prison conditions Then-corrections minister Paul Hamer told parliament in June there “may not be any suitable infrastructure solutions available” to provide high-risk prisoners like Marrogi with open air, as the recent Supreme Court decision required. The murderer and drug trafficker is one of the most challenging prisoners in Victoria, having run a $55 million drug empire from behind bars and once spraying prison guards with faeces. Marrogi’s lawsuit revealed corrections officials believed he had previously plotted to break out from Barwon Prison via helicopter.



Prison managers argued different types of roof mesh were necessary for Marrogi’s rear yards to prevent escape, self-harm, weather damage, and contraband being thrown in. Justice Claire Harris, however, ruled certain partially covered cells in the Exford unit at the Metropolitan Remand Centre, plus the Olearia, Melaleuca and Acacia units at Barwon Prison, did not provide adequate open-air access. Harris said there was no “clear bright line” for what constituted being “in open air” but noted the current right relied on experiencing weather, suggesting exposure to the elements such as rain, wind and sun outside was required. Her decision has been appealed.



Opposition police spokesman Brad Battin told parliament the Coalition would support proposed changes to open-air rights as it recognised they were not always practical. “I think it is important that the management of the prison can make a decision in the best interests of staff – not in the best interests of prisoners – to protect the staff who are within that prison,” he said. Jailed crime boss George Marrogi claims he’s being treated cruelly in prison. However, ombudsman Marlo Baragwanath told this masthead: “If these changes are passed into law, they’ll have wide-ranging and significant human rights implications for anyone in custody.” Marrogi’s lawyer, Zyg Zayler, said changing the law after Harris’ decision reflected poorly on Victoria.



“The quality of our society is determined by how we treat our most difficult people,” he said. “Maybe their prospects would be better if we didn’t treat them inhumanely.” Former prisoner Kelly Flanagan said her mental health suffered enormously when she was stuck inside at the Dame Phyllis Frost Centre, where an 18-year-old died last month. Wiradjuri woman Kelly Flanagan outside the Dame Phyllis Frost Centre last year. Luis Enrique Ascui “You’re stripping them of everything that makes them human by taking away their fresh air,” Flanagan said. A state government spokesperson said the open-air right for Victorian prisoners remained, and the changes were “operational decisions” to ensure access could be managed safely.



“This brings us into line with other jurisdictions like NSW, and makes a longstanding practice clear in law,” they said. NSW prisoners confined to their cell are allowed an hour each day for exercise in the open air subject to “practical limitations” but only those “that may from time to time arise”. Normal prisoners are allowed at least two hours outside. The Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service said making open-air rights subject to “operational considerations” was a “vague and open-ended excuse” to deny prisoners fresh air. Australian Lawyers Alliance spokesman Greg Barns, SC, also took issue with retrospective legislation removing compensation rights and called for it to be withdrawn.



Liberty Victoria president Gemma Cafarella said the bill marked just the fifth time a declaration to override Victoria’s human rights charter had been used since it was enacted in 2006. Liberal MP Chris Crewther said last month the government had “not adequately explained why an indefinite exclusion is necessary” compared with a normal five-year exemption. A protest against the bill is planned outside Victorian parliament on Wednesday before a vote in the Legislative Council is expected on Thursday. World.title: ‘Training objects for violence’: Cops, experts fear perverse motive behind ‘sex doll murder scene’
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWCrime ‘Training objects for violence’: Cops, experts fear perverse motive behind ‘sex doll murder scene’ Perry Duffin and Riley Walter August 11, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content A sex doll found in a suitcase on a remote stretch of NSW road was dressed like a sex worker with mock bruises and injuries, sparking fears among police and experts that whoever dumped it was acting out a violent fantasy against women. Discovery of the doll on Sunday triggered a short-lived murder investigation when it was located by two men during a bathroom break on a road south of Goulburn. The suitcase containing the doll was discovered metres from the roadside close to the pine tree. Kate Geraghty So disturbing were the doll’s features – a head of rain-matted hair, a nose piercing and markings that resembled bruising and grazes – the men thought they had uncovered an awful tragedy.



Police close to the investigation but not authorised to speak publicly are now concerned the person who dumped the doll might have been acting out a violent fetish. Caitlin Roper, campaigns manager for anti-sexploitation movement Collective Shout, told this masthead the dumping of sex dolls was not uncommon. A sex doll in a packing crate at a sex culture festival in China in 2013. Newer models are much more life-like and can be customised to meet buyers’ desires. NYT “People discover what they initially believe is a woman’s body – often mutilated, ripped apart or decapitated – but is actually a doll,” she said. “These dolls become training objects for violence against women and children.”



Roper has spent hours on sex-doll forums, monitoring owners’ who say they are buying dolls to practise extreme sexual abuse. In 2022, she published a book Sex Dolls, Robots and Woman Hating: The Case for Resistance, documenting her findings. “They shared realistic scenarios of predation that they acted out on their dolls. One user posted photographs of a doll bound with rope, explaining that he was practising how to tie women up and render them helpless,” she said. Superintendent Linda Bradbury revealed that the suitcase did not contain human remains - but instead a sex doll. KATE GERAGHTY “Other men described being so rough that they broke their dolls and had to send them away for repairs. One lamented that his doll would not fight back, saying, ‘If Tonya fought back, I’d be in heaven’.” As with the find on the weekend, many on the forum adorned their doll with fake bruises, cuts, blood and injuries.



Roper said there are multiple cases involving the owners of adult and child sex dolls – the latter are illegal in Australia – going on to carry out violence against women and girls. She pointed to the recent case of Perth man Jason William Forbes, a doll owner, who plotted to kidnap a young girl and keep her as a sex slave in his attic. “[Forbes] allegedly developed an elaborate plot to abduct a child. He had soundproofed an attic, researched chloroform, looked up schools and childcare centres, and marked locations on a map,” Roper said. “He was intercepted after purchasing a second doll.” Doll owner Jason William Forbes plotted to kidnap a girl and hold her captive in the attic of his Perth home. Roper said sex dolls, even childlike ones, are often dismissed as fantasies or mere objects. But many of the men she witnessed online have treated their dolls as partners.



“These are not simply sex toys; they are replicas of human beings that some owners regard as partners.” Criminologist and former NSW Police detective Vince Hurley said using child-like sex dolls could desensitise offenders and normalise abuse of children. It could also evolve into in-person offending. ‘The issue of consent doesn’t even come into it because they just use these sex dolls as they see fit, whenever they see fit.’ Vince Hurley, criminologist “It could reinforce any sexual attraction to children over time that might traverse into the real world,” Hurley said. “There would be nothing to say that it stops in their fake or false reality and then doesn’t transition into a real child.”



Men using sex dolls, similar to those using artificial intelligence chatbots, avoid rejection. Doing so warps their perception of relationships and consent, he said. “They will always have this perception that women will always be accepting of their behaviour and their attitudes because the chatbots never contradict them,” he said. “The issue of consent doesn’t even come into it because they just use these sex dolls as they see fit, whenever they see fit.” The Australian market for sex dolls Life-like sex dolls similar to the one found on Sunday are readily available online and can be customised to meet buyers’ desires.



Related Article Updated

Crime Police said a body was found in a suitcase. It turned out to be a sex doll High-end dolls retail for thousands of dollars. The growing market represents what police say is a worrying trend. In June, Australian Federal Police arrested a 31-year-old Quakers Hill man for trying to import a child sex doll, and allegedly found a second at his home. AFP Commander Jo Cameron said child-like sex dolls may desensitise users from the physical, emotional and psychological harm inflicted on real children. “Child-like sex dolls are not harmless objects – they are illegal to possess and can contribute to the exploitation of victims in the community,” Cameron said. World.title: Kids’ mental health unit shut as staff investigated for use of force
World.content:
A children’s mental health unit has been closed and five of its staff stood down amid allegations of bullying and the use of force against vulnerable young patients. The unit at a major Melbourne hospital has halted admissions to its inpatient unit – which treats children under 13 for severe mental health conditions – and has been referring families to another facility since the allegations emerged last Wednesday. Sources familiar with the investigation, but who are not authorised to speak publicly, said allegations of bullying surfaced a week ago following an outside-of-work gathering between multiple staff. Claims that some staff members used force against young patients also emerged. Related Article Opinion

Mental health I’m a psychiatrist of 40 years. It’s mass gaslighting to claim we’ve made progress Patrick McGorry Psychiatrist and mental health advocate Although five staff members connected with the unit have been stood down pending an investigation, not all are alleged to have used force on patients.



A hospital spokesperson confirmed investigations were under way, but said it would not be appropriate to comment on the specific allegations or individuals involved. The Department of Health and Safer Care Victoria have been advised of the allegations, and mandatory notifications have been made to the Commission for Children and Young People. “We take these allegations seriously and acted quickly when these concerns were raised,” the hospital spokesperson said. “Our priority is to ensure children and their families continue to have access to the mental health care they need while admissions to the unit are paused.” A state government spokesperson said the allegations were “disturbing and completely unacceptable”.



“Everyone deserves to feel safe whether they’re at work or seeking care in our health services,” the spokesperson said. The hospital’s specialist unit is an acute mental health service which caters for children up to 12 years old with severe or complex mental health conditions, who typically stay for two to four weeks, and are accompanied in the unit by a parent or caregiver throughout their treatment. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Rewritten mental health report scrubs critical findings, doubles progress Because the unit is staffed by a small team and all require specialist skills, the standing down of five of its members means that it cannot continue to operate with its current staffing levels. Children requiring urgent mental health care who present to the hospital will continue to be assessed by its clinicians, and will be supported to appropriate care pathways while admissions are paused.



The allegations come as pressure also mounts on the Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service (PYMHWS), following revelations in The Age on Tuesday that its fly-in, fly-out CEO Dr Leanne Geppert lives in Queensland as concerns of violence, drug use and patient deaths are being raised by its mental health workforce. It also follows revelations in The Age this week that a landmark report into Victoria’s progress following the mental health royal commission had been significantly altered to remove remarks critical of the state government’s progress. Writing in The Age, internationally renowned youth mental health pioneer Professor Pat McGorry accused the state government of gaslighting families and clinicians over its failed implementation of Victoria’s mental health reforms. “The risks to patients, to staff through both moral and physical injury, and to the wider community have continued to worsen as the workforce wilts and demand surges,” the former Australian of the Year writes. “This is the worst-kept secret in Victoria and a once-in-a-generation opportunity has so far been squandered. It is a classic case of implementation failure, which no amount of spin can conceal.”



Mental Health Minister Ingrid Stitt told parliament on Tuesday she had appointed a new chair to PYMHWS and had spoken to her about Geppert. Dr Leanne Geppert has been reappointed as the Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service’s CEO despite living in Queensland. “I have made my expectations very clear to her about the way in which the CEO’s work arrangements ought to occur,” Stitt said. “I am confident that the new chair has a very strong focus on the leadership requirements of the service and also of the clinical governance arrangements that are in place.” Stitt said her department had been following up concerns raised by McGorry about the service.



But she rejected allegations the government had tampered with the independent report into how Victoria was progressing on mental health reforms. Stitt said the initial version was an “early draft”, and between December 2025 and June 2026 the department had “provided factual and technical feedback” before its public release. This characterisation has been rejected by three senior mental health figures familiar with the report’s delay but who refused to discuss the circumstances of its rewriting on the record, fearing reprisals from the government and further financial cuts to vital services. Opposition mental health spokeswoman Emma Kealy said this masthead’s reports showed the government did not want scrutiny on a system taxpayers funded directly. “Victorians pay a dedicated Mental Health and Wellbeing Levy because Labor told them every dollar was needed to rebuild a broken system. They have every right to expect complete transparency about whether that reform is actually happening,” she said. World.title: Finally, the deli sandwich we’ve been searching for in Brisbane
World.content:
Eating outSandwich Watch Finally, the deli sandwich we’ve been searching for in Brisbane Deli sangers are easy to both overdo and underdo. This one gets it just right. Matt Shea August 11, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Deli sandwiches are hard. In some ways, they’re naturally restrained, meaning they can easily slip into boring. On the other hand, stack them with too many ingredients and the flavour signal gets lost in the noise. Anytime’s deli sandwich. Markus Ravik But we might have just found Brisbane’s – or the CBD’s, at least – best deli sandwich. Read on for instructions. Seek out Anytime Coffee



Anytime is hidden up a laneway near the intersection of Mary and Edward streets. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Little more than a timber-and-brick counter operation wedged beneath a fire escape, it was opened in early 2020 by Tom Cooney and Jack Wakefield (who have starred on Sandwich Watch with their exceptional work at Riser Bread). Now it’s operated by Marcus Allison and Matthew Burt. Related Article Brisbane’s best cafes and bakeries (on the northside) in 2026 Allison and Burt also own John Mills Himself in the CBD, and Allison owns Bunker and Bessa in Milton. In short, these blokes have the specialty coffee covered. But while Anytime’s sandwiches have always been at least pretty good, two have registered with this column recently. We love the chicken sandwich with tarragon mayo, but then there are a lot of very good chicken sangers around town at the moment. With that in mind, it’s perhaps Anytime’s deli sandwich that’s the true standout.



Anytime Coffee’s deli sandwich Deli sandwiches require precision. Get the ratio wrong between the meats and the rest of the ingredients (or even within the meats themselves) and you throw off the balance. Use too much in the way of condiments and you’ll end up with soggy bread. You’ll find Anytime Coffee hidden in a laneway near the intersection of Mary and Edward streets. Markus Ravik But Anytime’s take is about as precise as it gets – which is impressive when you discover how much is going on under the bonnet. Allison credits former Anytime chef Shane Neilson as the sandwich’s creator, although he says there have been minor tweaks since. “To my understanding at least, the deli sandwich was driven by Shane, predominantly,” Allison says. “Pretty much everything lived in Shane’s head, historically, and once we took over, I spent a lot of time with him, systemising it back of house.”



For meats, Anytime uses leg ham, salami cotto, and capocollo sourced from Rayner’s Meats in New Farm. That’s then layered with rocket, pickled red onion, and a green olive and guindilla mix that’s arguably the sandwich’s secret weapon. “It’s really important, for sure,” Allison says. “It brings that tang, that acid, and that heat helps offset the richness of the meats. “The sandwich also has a green dressing that has apple cider vinegar, dijon and parsley. That does a lot of heavy lifting.” Related Article Guy Grossi is gone. In his place, a Michelin-trained gun Sealing it all off is some provolone dolce. It’s there for its creamy texture and to protect the bread, which is why the Anytime crew has opted for a milder take on the semi-hard Italian cheese.



Talking bread, all this is squeezed between two slices of a light-rye sourdough tin loaf that’s produced by NYC Bagel for Anytime from a Riser Bread recipe (because Riser’s opening hours don’t align with Anytime’s). “We get that bread in every day, obviously, and it’s the right mix to soak up any residual juiciness but hold it together,” Allison says. “I love how it works. It’s such a good bread across a bunch of our sandwiches and toasties.” The perfect deli sandwich? If not perfect, this thing comes pretty close. This humble little thing is close to being the perfect deli sandwich. Markus Ravik



There’s so much good stuff here – the crunch of the rocket, the sweetness of the pickle, and the creamy texture of the cheese – but, really, what makes this thing so special is the interplay of the olive-guindilla mix and green dressing with the meats – particularly the rich umami of the salami cotto and capocollo. It’s all a bit sensational. And the perfectly weighted bread makes it a cinch to eat, when a lot of deli sandwiches are served on a harder roll-like bread that can encourage the ingredients to slip out the side. Anytime is always efficient, but get there off-peak if you’re in a hurry. Markus Ravik “It’s that classic combo of heat and sweet and salty and acid and fat and texture and colour. I think that’s what [Neilson] nailed, and that’s what we’ve really tried to dial in slightly with a few more systems back-of-house. “Deli sandwiches are often an extreme sandwich, but that’s OK … the tarragon is more of an everyday sandwich; but this has that sense of adventure to it that balances out the menu.”
